task_text: Map census tract population adjacency. The script processes U.S. Census Bureau tabular population data (from local 'population_temp' text files) to build a neighborhood graph of census tracts and counties, where each tract/county is linked to its spatially adjacent neighbors (sharing a boundary or intersection). It loads vector layers of state-level census tracts or counties (e.g., 'AL_counties.shp'), computes centroids, calculates pairwise spatial adjacency (not distance), and writes a CSV file per state (e.g., 'AL_features.csv') containing each GEOID20, its corresponding population value from the parsed tabular data, and a comma-separated list of adjacent GEOIDs. The script also updates the input layer in-place with no persistent GIS output—its primary output is the adjacency-population CSV.

Classify vegetation health status. The script converts loaded raster layers (assumed to be vegetation indices like NDVI, inferred from band selection logic and class labels) into 5-class vector polygons representing vegetation health status: 'Não-Vegetação/Água', 'Estresse Severo/Degradação', 'Estresse Moderado/Baixa Biomassa', 'Saúde Razoável', and 'Saudável e Vigoroso'. It performs equal-interval reclassification of raster values (using band 1 for single-band rasters or band 3 — interpreted as NDVI — for multi-band rasters), followed by polygonization, saving outputs as GeoPackage (.gpkg) files in a fixed local directory, and applies categorized symbology based on the 'DN' field with predefined colors and no stroke to emulate raster appearance.

Reclassify and fuse NLCD tree canopy with land cover. The script fuses high-resolution NLCD 2016 Tree Canopy data with NLCD 2016 Land Cover data for Alaska to produce a harmonized, reprojected (EPSG:4326), urban-cleaned, grass-replaced, HD-resampled, and spatially smoothed land cover raster. It first reclassifies tree canopy classes (41–43) into a unified forest class, warps both layers to WGS84, overlays tree canopy onto land cover while preserving native forest classes, replaces non-forest urban/clutter classes (e.g., 21–24, 31, 71–75, 81–82, 90, 95) with grass-compatible codes (e.g., 26, 27, 18, 19, 35), reclassifies urban impervious surfaces into simplified urban categories (10, 1, 2), applies GRASS median filtering to remove noise and road clutter from urban pixels, merges the cleaned urban layer with the grass-replaced base, upsamples to higher resolution (8× finer grid), smooths features using GRASS r.neighbors (size=11), and compresses to 8-bit LZW GeoTIFF — resulting in NLCD_2016_Alaska152-142_59_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff for flight simulation scenery generation.

Calculate point-based upslope catchments. The script computes the upslope contributing area (catchment) for each point feature in an input vector layer using a digital elevation model (DEM). It iterates over each point, invokes SAGA's 'upslopearea' algorithm to generate a raster catchment mask (with value 100 indicating the contributing area), polygonizes the raster, selects only polygons where DN = 100, and exports each as a separate ESRI Shapefile (e.g., 'area_1.shp', 'area_2.shp') into a user-specified output folder. No aggregation or summary is performed — outputs are individual catchment polygons per outflow point.

Calculate point-based catchment areas. The script calculates upslope catchment areas for input point locations using a digital elevation model (DEM) and the SAGA 'upslopearea' algorithm, then polygonizes the resulting raster catchments. It supports grouping points by a unique field (e.g., site ID) or processing each feature individually (by FID), outputs vector layers (GPKG single-file or ESRI Shapefile per catchment), and optionally loads results into QGIS. The workflow relies entirely on local raster/vector inputs — no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or cloud-based Earth Engine assets are used; all geoprocessing is performed via QGIS Processing Toolbox algorithms ('saga:upslopearea', 'gdal:polygonize'). Study area, time range, satellite data, and bands are not specified — the script is purely DEM-driven hydrological delineation.

Compute elevation-based stage-volume relationship. The script computes a stage-volume curve for a terrain by iteratively applying the QGIS 'Raster Surface Volume' tool across 11 elevation levels (from DTM minimum to maximum in 10% increments), converting each resulting volume from m³ to km³, appending level and absolute volume (km³) attributes, and merging all per-level vector tables into a single shapefile (stagevolume.shp) with an associated DBF table (stagevolume.dbf) containing elevation levels and corresponding cumulative absolute volumes.

Compute stage-volume relationship. The script computes a stage-volume curve for a given DEM by iteratively applying the 'raster surface volume' algorithm at n_increments (10) equally spaced elevation levels between the DEM's minimum and maximum values. For each level, it runs QGIS's native:rastersurfacevolume to calculate volume above/below that level, extracts the absolute volume (converted to km³), appends Level and VolAbsKm3 fields, and merges all resulting DBF tables into a single output vector layer (DBF format). The output is a tabular dataset with columns 'Level' (elevation in map units) and 'VolAbsKm3' (cumulative volume in cubic kilometers), intended for visualization via DataPlotly or spreadsheet software. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial inputs beyond the user-provided DEM raster layer are specified in the code.

Buffer polygon centroids. The script computes the centroid point of each input polygon feature and generates a circular buffer around each centroid with a user-specified distance. The output is a new vector layer of polygons representing these buffers, preserving one buffer per original polygon (no dissolution), with geometry derived solely from centroid locations—not the original polygon shapes or extents.

Set Z coordinate from DEM. The script replaces the Z (elevation) coordinates of 3D vector features (points, lines, or polygons) in an input vector layer with elevation values sampled from a user-provided Digital Elevation Model (DEM) raster at each feature’s XY location, optionally applying a constant vertical offset. It preserves original geometry XY positions while updating only the Z component per vertex using nearest-neighbor sampling from the DEM band (band 1), and supports processing either all features or only selected ones; output is the in-place edited vector layer with updated 3D geometry.

Reproject GeoPackage vector layers. The script reprojects all vector layers contained in an input GeoPackage (.gpkg) file to a user-specified Coordinate Reference System (CRS), preserving geometry integrity via QgsCoordinateTransform; it then packages the reprojected layers into a new output GeoPackage file. The workflow includes: (1) enumerating sublayers from the input GPKG using OGR subLayers(), (2) constructing individual QgsVectorLayer URIs per layer, (3) applying coordinate transformation per feature geometry using QgsCoordinateTransform (not relying solely on 'native:reprojectlayer' output due to memory layer handling), (4) optionally filtering to only 'instantiated' layers (though logic is flawed — Instanciado flag does not affect layer inclusion as both branches append to `layers`), and (5) aggregating all transformed layers and packaging them into a single output GPKG using 'native:package' with OVERWRITE=False.

Clean vector geometry nulls and duplicates. The script performs lightweight geometric cleanup on an input vector layer by (1) identifying and deleting features with null or empty geometries directly from the original layer, logging their IDs and reasons (e.g., 'null geometry', 'empty geometry'), and exporting their attributes—including auxiliary fields 'lf_orig_id' and 'lf_reason'—to a no-geometry output table; and (2) removing duplicate vertices from line and polygon features using QGIS's native:removeduplicatevertices algorithm, but only for remaining non-null/non-empty features and only if the layer geometry type is line or polygon; invalid geometries are explicitly excluded from correction or deletion. The tool operates in-place (with optional save/commit control) and preserves attribute integrity while producing a clean vector layer and a side-table of removed features.

Extract forest stand and ancillary layers. The script extracts forest stand-level vector and raster datasets from the Swiss TBk (Bestandeskarte) 2012 forest inventory dataset, using a user-defined extraction perimeter (a vector boundary). It first subsets the main stand map (TBk_Bestandeskarte.shp) by spatial intersection, then generates buffered-and-dissolved vector and raster extraction masks from the selected stands. Subsequently, it clips all listed vector datasets (e.g., local densities, simplified stands) using the vector mask (‘are within’ predicate), and clips all listed raster datasets (e.g., digital terrain models, VHM derivatives, classified rasters) using the raster mask via GDAL’s cliprasterbymasklayer. Outputs are written to a structured subdirectory preserving relative paths, enabling localized analysis of forest structure, topography, and classification products for a specific area.

Extract forest stand and density data. The script extracts forest-related vector and raster datasets spatially constrained to a user-defined extraction perimeter: (1) TBk_Bestandeskarte (forest stand map) is clipped via intersection with the perimeter; (2) local_densities (vector layer of forest density metrics) is extracted only where features fall entirely within a buffered-and-dissolved version of the clipped stands; (3) vhm_10m (a 10 m resolution canopy height model raster) is clipped using a buffered-and-dissolved polygon derived from the clipped stands, with buffer size configurable (default 10 m). Outputs are three geospatial products: a clipped stand vector layer, a clipped density vector layer, and a masked canopy height raster — all aligned to the operational forest inventory boundary.

Detect forest stand clearing change. The script computes two raster outputs quantifying forest structural change between two versions of a forest stand map (TBk): (1) 'change_DG' — a categorical raster encoding four canopy presence states (no canopy→no canopy=1, no→yes=2, yes→no=11, yes→yes=12) derived from binary dominant layer (DG) rasters; (2) 'change_DG_hdom' — an enhanced change raster that flags stands ≥ hdom threshold (default 25 m) where height reduction exceeds a negative difference threshold (default 7 m) as 'cleared' (value 100), otherwise retains the original change_DG code or sets to 0 if below hdom threshold. Workflow involves rasterizing hdom attributes from old and new stand boundary vector layers, aligning extents via intersect, and applying GDAL raster calculator expressions with conditional logic to derive both outputs.

Clean forest stand polygons. The script cleans a forest stand map (Bestandeskarte) by removing small polygon features (< 100 m²), filtering out null or missing area values, fixing invalid geometries (e.g., self-intersections, gaps), and standardizing the primary identifier field: it drops the original 'ID' field and replaces it with a new, unique, auto-incremented integer field named 'ID', ensuring no duplicate or non-geometric features remain in the output vector layer.

Extract forest stand perimeter. The script extracts forest stand map polygons (from a .gpkg file) that intersect with a user-provided perimeter vector layer. It then optionally extracts associated raster and vector layers (e.g., degree-of-cover rasters, VHM derivatives, coniferous rasters, intermediate layers, local densities) by clipping or subsetting them to the spatial extent of the extracted stands — using resolution-adapted buffered masks for rasters and a small-buffered polygon for vectors. Outputs include: (1) a clipped .gpkg containing only the intersecting TBk stands; (2) copied or clipped auxiliary geodata (rasters as GeoTIFFs, vectors as .gpkg), preserving relative folder structure; (3) optional copy of the TBk QGIS project file (.qgz); all placed in a new output folder named after the input TBk project directory. Raster clipping behavior is configurable: VHM and coniferous layers can be clipped either by mask (default for DG/VHM-detail) or by extent (default for MG rasters and toggleable for VHM layers).

Compute hdom-VHM height difference raster. The script computes the pixel-wise difference between a rasterized stand-level dominant height (hdom) layer and a 10 m VHM (Vegetation Height Model) raster, producing a continuous 'diff_hdom_vhm' raster where positive values indicate VHM exceeds hdom (e.g., emergent trees), negative values indicate VHM is below hdom (e.g., understory or errors), and zero indicates agreement. It also generates a point vector layer sampling every 10 m VHM pixel (with attribute 'VHM_10m') for visualization and validation.

Merge forest stand maps. The script merges multiple TBk (Toolkit Bestandeskarte) forest stand vector layers into a single unified layer, preserving spatial and attribute integrity. It systematically renames the original 'ID' field to 'ID_pre_merge', then appends a unique prefix (alphabetical A, B, C… or numerical 1, 2, 3…) to generate a globally unique 'ID' across all input layers. The prefix is also stored in a new string or integer field 'ID_meta'. Sorting of input layers is performed by geographic order — first by descending YMAX (most northern), then ascending XMIN (most western), using 1 km² grid-aligned coordinates — ensuring deterministic merge sequence. Finally, redundant fields ('layer', 'path') added during merging are dropped. Output is a single QGIS vector layer with three key attributes: 'ID' (e.g., 'A_123'), 'ID_pre_merge' (original ID), and 'ID_meta' (prefix).

Prepare VHM and MG rasters. The script prepares two key forest structure rasters for the TBk (Toolkit Bestandeskarte) workflow: (1) a detailed Vegetation Height Model (VHM) — optionally cropped to a polygon mask, converted to BYTE datatype, reclassified to enforce min/max/NA constraints (e.g., 0–60 m, NA=255), and resampled to 1.5 m and 10 m resolutions using max aggregation; and (2) a Forest Mixture Degree (MG) raster — aligned spatially and pixel-aligned to the 10 m VHM, rescaled by a user-defined factor (default 100, optimized for WSL’s 0–10,000 values), and optionally reclassified into a binary coniferous proportion layer (0–100) based on user-specified Laubholz (deciduous) and Nadelholz (coniferous) value ranges (e.g., LH: 1–50 → 0%, NH: 50–100 → 100%). Outputs include five georeferenced GeoTIFFs: VHM_detail.tif, VHM_10m.tif, VHM_150cm.tif, MG_10m.tif, and optionally MG_10m_binary.tif — all with LZW compression, BIGTIFF support, and consistent extent/resolution for downstream stand delineation.

Prepare VHM raster for forest stand mapping. The script prepares a Vegetation Height Model (VHM) raster as input for the TBk (Toolkit Bestandeskarte) forest stand mapping system. It performs: (1) optional conversion to BYTE datatype with user-defined NA value; (2) optional cropping to a vector mask polygon (either via GDAL’s cliprasterbymasklayer or via rasterization + masking using QgsRasterCalculator); (3) reclassification of outlier height values to a specified min–max range (e.g., 0–60 m); and (4) aggregation to two output resolutions — 10 m (for coarser stand delineation) and 1.5 m (150 cm, for fine-scale detail) — both using maximum resampling. Outputs are three GeoTIFFs: vhm_detail.tif (reclassified original resolution), vhm_10m.tif, and vhm_150cm.tif, all LZW-compressed and optionally BIGTIFF-enabled.

Optimize spatial join for forest stand attributes. The script performs an optimized spatial join between two vector layers: a primary layer (e.g., forest stand polygons or management units) and a secondary attribute layer (e.g., vegetation zones). It ensures performance by first checking and creating spatial indices on the primary layer, converting the secondary layer to singlepart geometries, fixing geometries using the 'Structure' method, indexing the cleaned singlepart layer, and then executing a one-to-one spatial join ('largest overlap only') with intersection predicate. The output is the primary layer enriched with selected fields (e.g., 'Code') from the secondary layer, prefixed (e.g., 'VegZone_'). No raster data, time-series, or satellite imagery is involved — this is a pure vector geoprocessing workflow for forest stand mapping (per plugin name 'TBk: Toolkit Bestandeskarte'). Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinates are not specified in the code.

Compute road segment slope from DEM. The script computes slope for individual road network segments by splitting edges into fixed-length segments, sampling elevation values at segment endpoints from a digital elevation model (DEM), calculating absolute slope as percent rise over run, and aggregating statistics (min/max/mean) per original edge. Outputs include: (1) GeoPackage of slope-annotated segments (segments_slope.gpkg), (2) GeoPackage of edges with aggregated slope metrics (edges_slope.gpkg), (3) GeoPackage of segments exceeding a user-defined slope threshold (very_steep_segments.gpkg), and (4) JSON summary statistics (stats_slope.json) containing segment lengths, slopes, and descriptive statistics (min, max, mean). Visualization layers are added to QGIS based on user flags (plot_intermediate/plot_results).

Extract urban population raster patches. The script clips the GHS Population 2020 raster (GHS_POP_E2020_GLOBE_R2022A_54009_100_V1_0.tif) to individual urban area (UA) boundaries defined in the 'UA_mask_small.shp' vector layer — sourced from the GHSL Urban Centre Database (UCDB) v2015MT — producing per-urban-area clipped rasters (e.g., '12914.tif') and corresponding polygonized rasters ('12914.shp') where each polygon represents a contiguous cell group with identical population count (VALUE). The workflow uses QGIS GDAL-based raster clipping and native pixel-to-polygon conversion. Input raster resolution is 100 m, projected in EPSG:54009 (World Mollweide); output rasters retain original resolution and nodata handling defaults. Study area is global (implied by 'GLOBE' in dataset name), but processing is applied per urban center ID (ID_HDC_G0), with 3261 urban areas iterated. No temporal filtering or modeling is performed — it is a static, spatial subsetting and vectorization task.

Generate Manning's roughness coefficient raster. The script generates a Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) raster layer by spatially joining ESA WorldCover 2021 land cover classification (at 10 m resolution, reprojected to EPSG:4326) with user-selected hydrological roughness class (Low/Medium/High) via lookup-table-driven raster algebra. It first clips the ESA WorldCover 2021 VRT dataset to the input Area of Interest (AOI) polygon (buffered by ~2 pixels), then applies a GDAL raster calculator expression that maps each ESA land cover grid_code (e.g., 10 — trees, 40 — cropland) to its corresponding Manning’s n-value using CSV-based lookup tables (low_n.csv, med_n.csv, high_n.csv), producing a continuous n-value raster. Optional outputs include the clipped ESA WorldCover raster and automatic QGIS styling using prepackaged .qml files.

Prepare vector-based predictor raster. The script converts an input vector layer (points, lines, or polygons) into a raster aligned precisely with a reference raster’s CRS, extent, and pixel grid. In Presence mode, it rasterizes features—optionally buffered—and optionally uses a numeric field to assign pixel values; in Proximity mode, it first creates a binary presence raster and then computes Euclidean distance to the nearest feature, outputting a continuous distance surface. The result is a spatially consistent, pixel-aligned predictor raster suitable for land-cover change modeling in MOLUSCE.

Identify 30-km service areas around Italian municipalities. The script computes 30-kilometer buffer zones around all Italian municipalities with ≥5,000 inhabitants (using ISTAT 2020 population data), excludes municipal capoluoghi (provincial capitals, identified by CC_UTS = '0'), intersects the resulting buffered area with Italy’s national administrative boundary (dissolved regions), and outputs a cleaned vector layer containing only the non-capoluogo 30-km service zones clipped to regional boundaries — intended for spatial analysis of accessibility, service coverage, or territorial planning in Italy.

Compute concave hull geometry. The script computes a concave hull polygon from an input point layer using the alpha shapes algorithm. It performs Delaunay triangulation, calculates maximum edge lengths across triangles, filters out triangles with edges longer than alpha * max_edge_length, dissolves the remaining triangles into a single polygonal geometry, and optionally removes interior rings (holes) or splits multipart geometries into singleparts. The output is a vector polygon layer representing the concave hull.

PyQGIS environment setup and GIS layer operations. The script is a comprehensive PyQGIS tutorial notebook that demonstrates core GIS workflows in QGIS Python API: initializing the environment, accessing interface objects (canvas, project), loading vector/raster/online/XYZ layers, navigating the map (zoom to active layer, full extent, selected features), inspecting layers and features, performing attribute and geometry operations (selection by expression, field addition, area calculation), applying symbology (single symbol, graduated renderer), configuring labeling, checking and reprojecting CRS, running geoprocessing algorithms (buffer, clip), manipulating raster rendering (band combination, contrast stretch), exporting data (selected features, map images), and handling messages/logging. It does not perform Earth observation analysis or modeling — it is purely a GIS software automation and desktop GIS scripting guide.

Generate digital surface model. The script downloads, unzips, reprojects (from EPSG:31256 to EPSG:4326), and merges 97 individual DSM GeoTIFF files (each named like 'XX_YY_dom.tif') sourced from the City of Vienna's MA41 geodata portal. It produces a single merged, georeferenced DSM raster ('dsm.tif') in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), intended as input for 3D urban modeling in QGIS. The workflow is fully automated via QGIS Processing Toolbox GDAL algorithms (warpreproject, merge) and custom plugin utilities for downloading and unzipping.

Generate urban orthoimagery mosaic. The script downloads, unzips, reprojects, and merges orthophoto raster tiles from the City of Vienna's MA41 geodata portal (region codes like '22_4', '32_2', etc.) into a single EPSG:4326 GeoTIFF mosaic named 'ortho.jpg'. It uses QGIS Processing GDAL algorithms ('gdal:warpreproject' and 'gdal:merge') to reproject from EPSG:31256 (MGI / Austria Lambert) to WGS84 and merge all tiles. The final raster is added as a QGIS raster layer under the name 'ortho'.

Compute zonal elevation statistics. The script computes zonal statistics (specifically mean elevation) from an SRTM digital elevation model raster for seismic zones defined in a vector layer. It first fixes invalid geometries in the input 'seismic_zones.shp' using QGIS's native:fixgeometries algorithm, then performs zonal statistics (mean) using native:zonalstatisticsfb, prefixing output columns with 'elevation_'. The output is a vector layer with added statistical fields, loaded into the QGIS project.

Calculate elevation statistics for seismic zones. The script computes zonal statistics (mean elevation) from an SRTM digital elevation model raster for seismic zone polygons. It first fixes invalid geometries in the input vector layer 'seismic_zones.shp', then runs 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' to calculate mean values (statistic ID 2) from band 1 of 'srtm.tif', prefixing output columns with 'elevation_'. The result is saved as a GeoPackage 'seismic_zones_with_elevation.gpkg' containing the original polygon attributes plus the computed elevation statistics.

Estimate floodwater depth. The script estimates spatially distributed floodwater depth by combining a flood inundation polygon (e.g., derived from remote sensing or field mapping) with a digital elevation model (DEM). It first clips the DEM to the inundation extent, converts the polygon boundary to a polyline and rasterizes it, then extracts elevation values along that boundary. Using GRASS7's r.grow.distance, it computes the Euclidean distance-transformed elevation (i.e., the nearest boundary elevation assigned to each cell), effectively approximating the local floodwater level. Finally, it subtracts the original clipped DEM from this approximated water surface to derive raw water depth, applies a SAGA Gaussian low-pass filter for smoothing, and outputs both the unfiltered and filtered water depth rasters.

Estimate floodwater depth from inundation polygons. The script estimates floodwater depth using a digital elevation model (DEM) and an inundation polygon input. It computes the shore/boundary raster by rasterizing polygon boundaries, sampling DEM values along them, smoothing with configurable iterations, filtering using slope thresholds (via grass7:r.slope.aspect), and applying ocean boundary removal. Then it grows the boundary using grass7:r.grow.distance with selectable distance metrics, subtracts the grown surface from the clipped DEM to compute water depth, masks results to the inundation extent, and optionally applies a low-pass filter (3x3 average kernel) for smoothing. Outputs include: (1) water depth raster, (2) smoothed water depth raster, and (3) shore-boundary raster.

Generate flow map from edge features. The script converts a vector line layer representing origin-destination edges (e.g., migration, transport, or movement flows) into a bundled, visually aggregated flow map using force-directed edge bundling. It optionally groups edges by a cluster field, applies iterative physics-based layout (force-directed edge bundling), segments bundled lines, and merges overlapping segments within a user-defined tolerance (MAX_DISTANCE). Outputs include a new line layer where each feature is either a bundled edge (if MAX_DISTANCE = 0) or a collapsed segment with attributes including CLUSTER, PATH, and OVERLAP_COUNT — enabling cartographic flow visualization with width/opacity encoding of overlap intensity.

Prepare SUEWS urban typology database. The script prepares input data for the SUEWS (Surface Urban Energy and Water Balance Scheme) model by integrating user-provided geospatial layers (polygon grid, DSM, DEM, optional typology layer), morphometric files (LCF, IMP, IMPveg), and meteorological forcing data. It computes grid-level land cover fractions, roughness parameters (z0, zd), building/vegetation heights, frontal area index (FAI), porosity, vertical morphology (via Spartacus option), anthropogenic emission profiles, irrigation schedules, snow parameters, conductance properties, and initial states (e.g., LAI, albedo, porosity, deciduous capacity) based on selected typologies and regional/country-level parameterization from an Excel database. The primary output is a validated YAML configuration file (e.g., 'prefix.yml') compatible with the SuPy/SUEWS modeling framework, alongside a re-formatted meteorological time-series text file ('prefix_YYYY_data_R.txt').

Compute centroids from buffered vector features. The script buffers input vector features with a fixed distance of 10 units and 5 segments per quarter-circle, then computes centroids of the resulting buffered polygons. It uses QGIS native algorithms 'native:buffer' and 'native:centroids', outputs point geometry, and explicitly sets the output type to QgsProcessing.TypeVectorPoint. The final output is the centroid layer derived from the buffer result.

Modify DEM for earthworks design. The script modifies an input digital elevation model (DEM) by carving (cut) and filling terrain around a user-provided platform vector layer (e.g., road alignment or construction footprint), using specified platform base level, cut slope (1:H), and fill slope (1:H). It generates concentric buffer rings around the platform, computes spatially varying cut and fill elevation levels as functions of distance and slope, rasterizes those levels onto two copies of the DEM, and then merges them via conditional raster algebra to produce a final modified DEM where cut areas lower terrain and fill areas raise it — respecting slope constraints and platform geometry.

Build polygons from center points and boundaries. The script constructs polygon features from input center point features and boundary line layers, optionally constrained by additional line or polygon layers and a geographic boundary. It computes polygons using geometric operations including clipping, spatial joins, polygon-to-line conversion, line explosion, spatial indexing, dissolving, and multipart-to-single-part conversion. Outputs include the generated polygons, flags for invalid polygon geometries (e.g., out-of-bounds angles), flags for unused boundary lines, and general processing flags. The algorithm supports spatial partitioning to handle large geographic boundaries in parallel via thread pooling.

Generate shaded bathymetry raster. The script generates a visually enhanced shaded bathymetry raster by combining a pseudocolor-rendered RGB representation of a single-band bathymetric (depth) raster with a derived shading layer (hillshade, slope, combined, or multidirectional), applying vertical exaggeration, CRS-aware scaling, and optional alpha channel; outputs a georeferenced, optionally compressed, shaded raster in GeoTIFF format.

Generate elevation contours. The script generates vector contour lines from an input raster layer (e.g., DEM or bathymetric grid), applying GDAL's contouring algorithm with user-specified interval, then smooths the geometry, reprojects to match the input raster’s CRS, optionally reverses line direction for Z-positive-down rasters (e.g., bathymetry), adds line length attributes for filtering, and applies a standardized QGIS style with symbology and labeling optimized for marine/terrestrial topographic interpretation.

Rasterize building and tree canopy height. The script converts vector layers of buildings (polygons) and trees (points) into two aligned raster layers: (1) a building height raster derived by rasterizing the building polygon layer using its 'Height [m]' attribute, and (2) a tree height raster derived by first buffering each tree point by its 'Radius [m]' attribute (creating variable-distance circular buffers), then rasterizing the resulting buffered polygons using the 'Height [m]' attribute from the original tree points. Both rasters are generated at 0.5 m resolution within a user-defined analysis extent and saved as Float32 GeoTIFFs ('BuildingTerrain_raster.tif' and 'Tree_raster.tif') for downstream urban 3D modeling or solar radiation/urban climate analysis.

Identify most isolated point. The script computes the most spatially isolated point within an input point layer by calculating the minimum distance from each point to its nearest neighbor, identifying the point with the maximum such minimum distance (i.e., the point farthest from any other point), then outputs that point as a feature and a circular buffer around it with radius equal to that maximum nearest-neighbor distance. The isolation metric is derived via Voronoi-based or direct pairwise distance logic (external `isolation()` function from `becagislibrary.voronoi`), and the buffer distance is dynamically reprojected to degrees if the input CRS is geographic using Gaussian mean Earth radius approximation.

Compute maximum inscribed circle. The script computes the Maximum Inscribed Circle (MIC) for each input polygon feature — i.e., the largest possible circle fully contained within the polygon boundary. It implements a geometric algorithm (imported from `becagis.becagislibrary.geometry.mic`) that iteratively refines a candidate center and radius using tolerance-controlled spatial search, leveraging QGIS native processing (e.g., `native:buffer` with dynamic radius field `'dist_pole'`). Outputs are two vector layers: (1) point layer representing MIC centers (with attribute `'dist_pole'` storing the radius), and (2) corresponding circular polygon layer generated via buffering those points using the radius attribute. The workflow handles both projected and geographic CRS by dynamically converting linear tolerance (meters) to angular units using Gaussian mean Earth radius approximation.

Clip TerraClimate temperature variable. The script downloads a remote TerraClimate NetCDF dataset for a user-specified variable (e.g., 'tmax', 'tmin') and year (1958–2024) from THREDDS, spatially subsets it to the bounding box of an input polygon layer (with optional buffer), sanitizes CF-compliant metadata (removing conflicting _FillValue, scale_factor, etc.), writes the subset as a temporary GeoTIFF with float32 dtype and -9999 nodata, then applies GDAL-based raster clipping using the dissolved input vector layer as a mask to produce a final clipped GeoTIFF aligned to the geometry’s extent and shape. Outputs include the clipped GeoTIFF file and automatic QGIS layer loading.

Split RGB bands. The script splits a multi-band raster image into its red (R), green (G), and blue (B) spectral bands using SAGA's 'splitrgbbands' algorithm, then converts each extracted band to a standardized raster format (via GDAL translate) with consistent data type, nodata handling, and CRS alignment. It outputs six rasters: three raw band layers (BLUE, GREEN, RED) and three converted/normalized versions (R_conv, G_conv, B_conv), enabling downstream spectral analysis or visualization workflows requiring isolated RGB components.

Identify overlapping map labels. The script identifies geometric overlaps between rendered map labels (text features) from user-selected vector layers within a geographic boundary, using QGIS's native label rendering engine at a specified cartographic scale. It extracts labels via 'native:extractlabels', filters them by layer name, computes precise polygon geometries for each label using a DPI- and scale-aware label size calculator, then detects intersections between these label polygons. The output is a vector layer of dissolved polygon flags marking areas where two or more labels overlap — intended as QA/QC feedback for cartographic finishing workflows in Brazilian Army topographic mapping.

Merge river segments by name. The script merges line features representing river segments (from a drainage layer) that share the same 'nome' (name) attribute and are geometrically connected (intersecting), producing a topologically simplified, merged MultiLineString layer. It performs: (1) adding an auto-incremental ID field; (2) building spatial index; (3) dissolving the polygon frame layer; (4) clipping drainage lines to the dissolved frame; (5) merging connected lines with identical names (prioritizing longest segment per group); (6) converting frame polygons to lines; (7) splitting merged rivers at frame boundaries; and (8) outputting the final clipped-and-merged river layer with original attributes and MultiLineString geometry.

Adjust contour line orientation. The script adjusts the geometric orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise) of input contour line features based on their vertex winding order. It computes the signed area accumulation via cross products of consecutive edge vectors to determine current orientation, identifies contours requiring reversal to match the user-specified orientation (CW or CCW), temporarily caches and extracts those features by ID, reverses their direction using QGIS's native:reverselinedirection algorithm, and updates the original layer in-place with corrected geometries. No new output layer is created — edits are applied directly to the source vector layer.

Configure legal boundary superposition. The script configures the 'sobreposto' (superposed) and 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' (show approximate label) attributes in the input legal boundary line layer ('llp_limite_legal_l') based on spatial relationships with filtered infrastructure and drainage layers. It first filters visible and polygon-situated drainage, visible road, and visible railway layers; merges them; computes the difference between the legal boundary and the dissolved/moldura outline; then performs intersect and difference operations against the merged infrastructure layer. Features intersecting infrastructure are assigned 'sobreposto' = 1, while non-intersecting features (i.e., outside infrastructure) are assigned 'sobreposto' = 2 — both set 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' = 1. The original legal boundary layer is edited in-place to replace all features with these updated geometries and attributes.

Configure line feature topographic overlay. The script configures cartographic line features (edicao_limite_especial_l) by evaluating their spatial relationship with selected infrastructure and natural linear layers (drenagem, via deslocamento, ferrovia) within a map frame (moldura). It filters those layers by visibility and situacao_em_poligono attributes, merges them, clips the polygonal limit layer (llp_limite_especial_a) to the dissolved moldura, converts the clipped polygon boundary to lines, computes intersections and differences between those boundary lines and the merged infrastructure layer, then updates the input line layer with new 'sobreposto' (1 = overlaid/intersected, 2 = non-overlaid/difference) and 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' attributes — effectively classifying each output line segment as either topographically overlaid or non-overlaid relative to key linear infrastructure within the cartographic frame.

Compute canopy height from GEDI and DEM-derived ground surface. The script computes canopy height as the difference between a canopy surface raster and a ground surface raster (e.g., digital terrain model), clamping negative values to zero. It then merges the resulting canopy height raster with optional GEDI raster input (likely waveform or RH metrics) and converts all merged raster pixels to vector points, assigning the pixel value (canopy height or merged band value) as an attribute. The final output is a point vector layer where each point represents a raster cell centroid and carries the computed canopy height (or merged value) in the 'VALUE' field.

Convert CSV point data to gridded ocean depth maps. The script converts tabular CSV files containing latitude, longitude, and depth (Z) measurements into georeferenced point vector layers (shapefiles), reprojects them to a user-specified CRS, and optionally generates interpolated raster grids (e.g., .img) using GDAL rasterize + fillnodata. It supports batch or single-file processing, auto-detects lat/lon field names (e.g., 'lat', 'lon', 'x', 'y'), computes an adaptive grid resolution based on point density statistics (median points per grid cell), and adds both the vector point layer and final raster grid to the QGIS project.

Extract river surface from thermal imagery. The script identifies river surfaces in thermal infrared raster data by thresholding pixel temperatures (T ≤ threshold_c, e.g., 15°C), applying morphological cleanup via GDAL sieve to remove small noise patches (< min_patch_pixels, e.g., 1000 pixels), and masking the original thermal raster to retain only thermally cold (river-like) regions. Outputs include: (1) a raw binary mask (rmr_*.tif), (2) a nodata-annotated version for inspection (rmrnd_*.tif), (3) a cleaned binary mask (rmc_*.tif), and (4) the final masked thermal raster (RiverFinal_*.tif) where non-river pixels are set to NODATA_OUTSIDE (−9999), with transparency applied in QGIS for visualization.

Extract thermal patches from river temperature raster. The script extracts contiguous thermal anomaly patches from a pre-processed river temperature raster by (1) automatically computing the minimum valid temperature value within the river raster, (2) defining a patch range as [min_temp, min_temp + patch_threshold], (3) generating a binary mask where pixels fall within that range, (4) converting 0s to NoData, and (5) applying a sieve filter to remove isolated pixels smaller than min_patch_pixels. Outputs are three rasters: raw binary mask (_raw.tif), NoData-corrected mask (_nodata.tif), and cleaned, speckle-filtered final thermal patch layer (.tif), added to QGIS with name 'ThermalPatches_<input_name>'.

Simplify NUTS3 administrative boundaries. The script simplifies the geometry of the NUTS3 administrative layer for Finland (NUTS3_FIN_pop) using a tolerance of 5000 map units (likely meters), then retains only the 'name' and 'pop' attributes. The output is a simplified, attribute-filtered vector layer of Finnish NUTS3 regions. No time-series, imagery, or classification is involved; the workflow consists solely of two QGIS geoprocessing algorithms: 'native:simplifygeometries' (Douglas-Peucker method) and 'native:retainfields'. The study area is explicitly Finland (inferred from 'NUTS3_FIN_pop' in the file path), and the input is a local GeoPackage layer — no satellite, sensor, or band data is used.

Export administrative units from CAOP. The script processes the Portuguese CAOP (Carta Administrativa Oficial de Portugal) vector dataset to extract, refactor, and export three hierarchical administrative unit layers—freguesia (parish), concelho (municipality), and distrito (district)—into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database. It first clips the CAOP layer to a user-defined Area de Trabalho (work area), identifies unique concelhos and distritos within that area, then extracts all corresponding CAOP features for those units. For freguesia, it retains original attributes and adds temporal metadata (current timestamp and user-provided publication date). For concelho and distrito, it dissolves geometries by DICOFRE-derived codes (4-digit for concelho, 2-digit for distrito), refactors fields to standardize naming (e.g., 'nome' = concelho/distrito name), and exports each dissolved layer to dedicated PostGIS tables ('freguesia', 'concelho', 'distrito') with geometry column 'geometria' and primary key 'identificador'.

Split catchments by 0.1-degree grid lines. The script spatially partitions GRDC global daily discharge catchment shapefiles (pre-smoothed) into sub-catchment polygons aligned with a 0.1-degree regular latitude-longitude grid (defined by 'lines_p1deg.shp'). For each input catchment, it performs three sequential GIS operations: (1) splits the catchment polygon(s) using the grid line layer via QGIS 'native:splitwithlines'; (2) appends area geometry columns (in m²) to the split features using 'qgis:exportaddgeometrycolumns'; and (3) computes centroids of each resulting sub-polygon using 'native:centroids'. Outputs are three per-catchment shapefiles: '_p1degsplit.shp' (topologically split polygons), '_p1degsplit_areas.shp' (with 'area_2' field in m²), and '_p1degsplit_centroids.shp' (point layer with same attributes plus centroid geometry), all stored in a dedicated processing directory for downstream fractional area assignment to meteorological forcing grids.

Export contours to 3D CAD. The script exports vector contour lines (2D or 3D) to a georeferenced, elevation-preserving 3D DXF file compatible with AutoCAD and other CAD software. It detects whether the input line layer has Z-dimension (WKB type > 1000); if not, it uses GRASS v.to.3d to lift lines into 3D using a user-specified numeric elevation field. The output DXF is reprojected to a target CRS (defaulting to input CRS), written in a selected AutoCAD version (R2000–R2018), and retains Z-coordinates for all vertices — enabling direct use in civil engineering and terrain modeling workflows. No raster data, satellite imagery, time-series, or classification is involved; the process is purely vector-based geometric transformation and CAD export.

Calculate RUSLE rainfall erosivity per parcel. The script computes the R-factor (rainfall erosivity) from climate data for each input parcel using a spatially weighted approach: it intersects parcels with a climate shapefile, calculates the percent area of overlap, generates one random point per intersected polygon, retrieves the R-value at that point’s latitude/longitude via an external API (UsleClimateApi.get_r_value), computes area-weighted R-values, and aggregates the sum of area-weighted R by parcel 'title' attribute. The final output is a JSON-serialized pandas Series mapping parcel titles to their total area-weighted R-value, representing spatially distributed rainfall erosivity for RUSLE modeling.

Calculate RUSLE rainfall erosivity. The script calculates the R-factor (rainfall erosivity) of the RUSLE model for agricultural parcels by spatially intersecting parcel boundaries with climate data polygons, computing area-weighted R-values using point-based interpolation via UsleClimateApi.get_r_value(x,y), and aggregating results by 'title' field. Key steps include geometry fixing, reprojection to ESRI:102003 (USA Albers Equal Area Conic), area calculation, intersection with climate polygons, percent-area weighting, random point sampling per polygon, XY coordinate extraction in EPSG:4326, and application of an external climate API to derive R-values from latitude/longitude. Inputs are two local shapefiles: 'ClimateShapeFile.shp' (climate zones or stations) and a parcels shapefile passed as sys.argv[1]; no satellite or Earth Engine imagery is used — all operations occur in QGIS Processing via PyQGIS. The output is a JSON-serialized pandas Series mapping 'title' (e.g., parcel or climate zone identifier) to summed area-weighted R-values. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified.

Count languages per country. The script computes the number of distinct languages (from the World Language Database, WLDS) intersecting each sovereign country (from Natural Earth admin-0 boundaries), producing a CSV table ('nlangs_country.csv') where each row corresponds to a country (ADMIN field) and contains the count of languages (GID) falling within its territory. It achieves this by first repairing geometries of both input layers, then performing a vector intersection to associate each language polygon with its containing country, and finally aggregating counts per country using QGIS's 'Statistics by Categories' tool.

Extract hydroconditioning adaptations for inundation. The script filters and clips line- and horseshoe-shaped hydrological adaptation features (e.g., culverts, flow regulators, DHM fixes) from vector layers using a DTM mask polygon. It selects only those features intersecting the mask and further filters them by attribute values ('Generel', 'Havstigning', or 'DHMfix') in the 'brugesher'/'brugesHer' field. Outputs are three shapefiles: HorseshoesAdaptations.shp, LineAdaptations.shp, and DHMFixAdaptations.shp — all clipped to the mask and attribute-filtered for use in hydrological inundation modeling and DTM conditioning.

Model anthropogenic heat flux. The script calculates anthropogenic heat flux (W/m²) per grid cell by integrating four components: (1) population-derived metabolic + domestic heat (using a 10m population raster), (2) traffic-related heat (from OSM road length weighted by highway class multipliers and/or ANAS-style traffic volume proxies), (3) industrial waste heat (from E-PRTR/IED facility point data, de-duplicated by site ID and reporting year, then spatially redistributed within 150m buffers proportionally to building surface area inside each intersecting grid cell), and (4) morphological fallbacks (BSF and ISF) when population or industry data are missing. Outputs include two fields in the input vector layer: 'anthro_heat' (total anthropogenic heat flux) and 'industry_heat' (industrial component only, for LCZ 1 vs LCZ 10 disambiguation).

Calculate urban aspect ratio. The script computes the Aspect Ratio (H/W) for urban and natural land cover cells by geometrically measuring building height (z_h) and inter-building spacing (using spatial index and nearest-neighbor distances in metric CRS), and for tree-covered areas, it estimates vegetative aspect ratio using canopy height (from canopy_height_10m.tif) and tree spacing derived either from Copernicus Tree Cover Density (TCD) or a binary canopy mask. It outputs a vector layer with an updated 'aspect_ratio' field (rounded to 2 decimals), capped at 3.0 for urban cells and supporting LCZ classification (e.g., LCZ A–G), with diagnostics on building vs. tree spacing usage.

Calculate building impervious pervious fractions. The script computes Building Surface Fraction (BSF), Impervious Surface Fraction (ISF), and Pervious Surface Fraction (PSF) for polygonal urban cells (e.g., LCZ grid cells). It first derives BSF by spatially intersecting input vector cells with a local 3D building layer (buildings_lod1.gpkg); then computes ISF and PSF either (a) using Copernicus High-Resolution Layer (HRL) imperviousness raster (subtracting BSF from HRL to isolate non-building impervious surfaces, with PSF as remainder) or (b) falling back to ESA WorldCover land use/land cover (10m) raster, aggregating predefined pervious (e.g., classes 10,20,30,40,60,90,95,100) and excluded (70,80) classes, adjusting ISF by removing building contribution and normalizing all three fractions to sum to 100%. Outputs are written as rounded float attributes ('building_frac', 'impervious_frac', 'pervious_frac') directly into the input vector layer.

Classify terrain roughness length. The script computes terrain roughness length (z0) and assigns a terrain roughness classification (integers 2–8) to each polygon feature in the input vector layer, based on building fraction, vegetation (tree) fraction, and roughness height (z_h). It first attempts to retrieve or compute missing inputs (z_h from buildings and canopy rasters; building_frac from building vector layer; tree_frac from canopy height raster using a >2.0 m threshold), then applies a rule-based decision matrix combining building and tree fractions with z_h thresholds to assign both the discrete terrain roughness class and continuous z0 value (in meters) per feature.

Calculate spatial smoothness of polygon attribute. The script computes a 'smoothness' metric for a numeric attribute field across a polygon layer by evaluating the absolute differences between each polygon's attribute value and those of its topologically adjacent (edge-sharing or overlapping) neighbors. It builds a spatial index to efficiently identify neighbors, handles null/zero values by imputing zero and applying a penalty (2× the focal value), normalizes the total absolute influence by the product of total neighbor comparisons and the global value range (max−min), and returns a unitless percentage smoothness score (0–100), total neighbor connections, the full topological influence dictionary per polygon, and a continuity ratio (percentage of non-zero/nonnull features).

Estimate service supply density. The script converts point locations of service facilities (e.g., hospitals, schools, shops) into a continuous raster surface representing supply intensity (i.e., kernel density estimation) within a user-defined radius (in meters), using a quartic kernel and raw density output; it then clips the resulting heatmap to the exact geometry of a provided study area boundary vector layer, ensuring no extrapolation beyond the analysis zone. The final output is a clipped, georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layer named 'Supply_Density' with values representing estimated service supply per unit area (e.g., count per km²), suitable for accessibility or equity analysis.

Model service supply density. The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous raster surface representing supply intensity using kernel density estimation. It uses QGIS's 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm with a quartic kernel, radius scaled to 2× the input radius for visual spread, and outputs a clipped, styled raster layer named 'Supply_DensityRaster'. The styling applies a red-to-green color ramp (Red=low supply, Green=high supply) based on observed density value statistics. Inputs include a user-provided supply_pois vector layer (e.g., hospitals, clinics), a study_area_layer boundary, radius (m), cell_size (m), and workspace metadata. No satellite imagery or time-series analysis is involved — the analysis is purely spatial and static, relying solely on vector POI locations and geometric parameters. Study area extent is used to constrain output raster bounds; clipping is performed via 'gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer'. Output is a styled QgsRasterLayer ready for visualization in QGIS.

Map service supply density. The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation (quartic kernel) with a user-specified radius (e.g., 1000 m) and cell size, then clips the resulting heatmap raster to a provided study area boundary. It applies a custom red-to-green color ramp renderer (Red=low supply, Green=high supply) for visualization. Inputs include a QgsVectorLayer of service POIs (e.g., hospitals, clinics), a study area QgsVectorLayer, analysis radius in meters, and output cell size in meters. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or time-series analysis is performed — the analysis is purely spatial and static, based on point locations. The final output is a styled QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster' representing supply density per unit area (raw kernel density units), clipped to the study extent.

Model service supply density. The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data (e.g., hospitals, clinics, schools) into a continuous raster surface representing spatial supply intensity — i.e., kernel density estimation of service access potential within a user-defined radius (e.g., 1 km), reprojected to Web Mercator for metric accuracy, clipped to the study area boundary, and styled with a red-to-green color ramp where red indicates low supply density and green indicates high supply density. The output is a georeferenced, styled QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster' suitable for equity or accessibility analysis in urban or regional planning contexts.

Model service supply density. The script converts point-based service infrastructure locations (e.g., hospitals, clinics, schools) into a continuous raster surface representing supply intensity (density per unit area), using kernel density estimation with a configurable radius and cell size. It reprojects inputs to EPSG:3857 for metric accuracy, generates a heatmap (quartic kernel, 2× input radius for visual spread), clips the result to the study area boundary, reprojects back to the original CRS (typically EPSG:4326), and applies a red-to-green color ramp renderer where red indicates low supply density and green indicates high supply density — enabling spatial assessment of service accessibility gaps.

Estimate service supply density. The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface (raster) using kernel density estimation. It reprojects both the POI layer and study area boundary to EPSG:3857 for metric-consistent distance calculations, generates a heatmap with a user-defined radius (heatmap_radius) and cell size, clips the resulting density surface to the study area, and reprojects the final raster back to the original CRS of the input POIs (e.g., EPSG:4326). The output is a styled QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster', visualized with a red-to-green color ramp indicating low-to-high supply intensity. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or time-series analysis is performed; inputs are static vector layers (supply_pois and study_area_layer), and all geoprocessing is done via QGIS native and GDAL algorithms. The study area and POIs are assumed to be pre-acquired (e.g., from OSM queries), but no specific source identifiers, time range, or geographic names are embedded in the code.

Join reference points with modeled width. The script filters reference points (PtRef) that intersect with ecological aquatic units (UEA) from a hydrographic network (CRHQ), then joins them with the 'PtRef_mod_lotique' attribute table to attach the 'Largeur_mod' (modeled width) value. It outputs a point layer where each point retains its original geometry and gains the 'Largeur_mod' attribute, representing the CRHQ-modeled width of the reference point along lotic watercourses.

Apply NCS decision tree rules. The script enforces hierarchical, biome-conditional rules from the Nature-based Solutions (NCS) framework to generate a single binary raster mask (Protect / Manage / Restore) from a set of input NCS pathway rasters. It first groups pathways by biome (cropland, wetlands, grass/savanna/shrub) and action type (Protect/Manage/Restore), then applies strict spatial precedence: cropland actions override all others in cropland areas; wetland actions override non-cropland actions in wetland areas; forest restoration is further constrained to exclude native grass/savanna/shrub areas (biodiversity safeguard); finally, action hierarchy (Protect > Manage > Restore) is enforced via sequential masking. The output is a final binary (0/1) raster indicating presence of the user-selected action, with all conflicting or lower-priority actions removed.

Compute zonal statistics for magnetic and geophysical fields over grounded ice units. The script computes zonal statistics (mean, std, min, max) of multiple geophysical raster datasets — including Dziadek’s ASE magnetic compilation (250 m), ANTGG Bouguer anomaly (10 km), ICESat-derived dmdt (mass change), PISM basal drag coefficient (beta), BedMachine bedrock roughness, and pre-processed gravity/magnetics rasters — over vector polygons representing grounded ice units in the Amundsen Sea Embayment (ASE). It begins by loading and repairing input vector geometry, unions it with grounding line and catchment boundaries, filters to 'Grounded' ice only, clips to the ASE bounding box, decomposes multipart features, eliminates small slivers (<10 km²), adds geometry columns (area), then sequentially appends zonal statistics from each raster. The final output is a GeoJSON vector layer containing all computed statistics per polygon, saved to disk and added to the QGIS project.

Generate DFM confidence map. The script computes a Digital Feature Model (DFM) Confidence Map using the CRAN decision tree methodology. It takes as input a DEM/DFM raster, a ground point density layer, and a low vegetation density layer; resamples them to target resolutions (0.25m, 0.5m, 1m, or 2m); reclassifies ground density and vegetation layers using resolution-specific thresholds; computes slope from the DEM; reclassifies slope into five categories (≤12.5°, 12.5–22.5°, 22.5–42.5°, ≥42.5°); then applies a series of weighted raster algebra operations (e.g., 'Calc1a', 'Calc4b', 'Calc5a') that combine density, slope, and vegetation classes with multiplicative weights (1× to 6×) to quantify spatial confidence in DFM accuracy—higher values indicate lower confidence (i.e., higher uncertainty due to vegetation occlusion, low point density, or steep terrain). Final outputs are resolution-specific confidence rasters (e.g., 'DFM CM 0.5m'), styled with a QML file and optionally loaded into QGIS.

Generate hybrid DFM interpolation. The script computes a hybrid digital feature model (DFM) by combining IDW and TLI (TIN-based linear interpolation) rasters using a confidence map to spatially weight contributions: IDW dominates in low-confidence zones (confidence levels 1–3), TLI in high-confidence zones (4–6), with a transitional buffer zone derived via raster morphological operations (r.grow, r.buffer) and algebraic blending. Outputs a final patched, reprojected hybrid DFM raster (DFM_hybrid.tif → dfmpatched.tif) optionally loaded into the QGIS project.

Align rasters to reference grid. The script aligns one or more input rasters to a user-specified reference raster by matching its CRS, cell size, origin (grid alignment), and extent. It optionally applies masking using a vector polygon layer (with optional buffering) to clip outputs to the mask geometry. All aligned rasters are saved as GeoTIFF files in a user-defined output directory, preserving original names (with disambiguating suffixes if needed). The algorithm uses GDAL Warp for reprojection/resampling and GDAL Clip Raster by Mask Layer for masking, with support for 11 resampling methods including near, bilinear, cubic, lanczos, average, mode, min, max, med, q1, and q3.

Modify land cover raster with vector field values. The script modifies a land cover raster by overwriting pixel values within polygon boundaries using the numeric land cover code from a specified field in the input vector layer. It first creates a copy of the input raster (via GDAL clip-by-extent), then performs an in-place rasterization (gdal:rasterize_over) that replaces overlapping raster pixels with the attribute value from each polygon, producing a modified land cover raster where designated areas reflect updated land cover codes.

Modify land cover by name. The script modifies a land cover raster by overwriting pixel values within user-defined polygon areas with a new land cover code, determined by matching a user-provided land cover name (e.g., 'Urban') against a custom lookup table containing 'lc_name' and corresponding integer 'lc_value' fields. It first clips the input raster to its own extent (effectively copying it), then rasterizes the input vector polygons onto that copy using the matched lc_value as the burn-in value, producing a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced.

Modify land cover raster. The script modifies pixels in an input land cover raster (e.g., NLCD or C-CAP) within polygon areas defined by a vector layer, overwriting them with a user-selected land cover class value (e.g., 'Developed, High Intensity' → value 24). It first clips the input raster to preserve its extent and data type, then rasterizes the input vector polygons using a fixed land cover code derived from CSV-sourced NLCD/C-CAP classification coefficients. The output is a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced with the selected class’s numeric code. No time-series analysis, spectral computation, or classification modeling is performed — it is a deterministic spatial overwrite operation. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the algorithm is generic and data-source-agnostic, relying solely on user-provided raster and vector inputs and local CSV coefficient files.

Rasterize hydrologic soil group and K-factor. The script converts a vector polygon layer representing soil properties into two raster outputs: (1) a Hydrologic Soil Group (HSG) raster where categorical HSG values ('A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A/D', 'B/D', 'C/D', 'W', or Null) are mapped to integer codes (1–9) via field calculation and then rasterized; and (2) a K-Factor raster where numeric erodibility values from a user-specified attribute field are directly rasterized. Input validation ensures HSG field values conform strictly to USDA NRCS-approved codes. Both rasters inherit the input layer’s CRS and are generated at a user-defined cell size using GDAL’s rasterize algorithm.

Convert radar reflectivity to GeoTIFF. The script converts NetCDF-formatted meteorological radar data (specifically 'Band1', representing radar reflectivity in dBZ) into a georeferenced GeoTIFF file projected to WGS84 UTM Zone 17S (EPSG:32717). It applies a user-defined NoData threshold (default 25 dBZ) to mask low-reflectivity values as NaN, computes geographic transform from latitude/longitude arrays, writes the masked reflectivity array to a temporary GeoTIFF in WGS84 lat/lon, then attempts robust reprojection to UTM 17S using multiple fallback GDAL/QGIS methods. Finally, it loads the output raster into QGIS with a custom pseudo-color ramp optimized for precipitation intensity (0–250 dBZ), applying transparency for near-zero values and setting CRS explicitly to EPSG:32717.

Locate nearest meteo stations. The script computes the centroid of a user-provided basin polygon, then identifies the N (default 4) meteorological stations nearest to that centroid using a distance matrix and spatial join. It outputs a vector layer of the selected stations, enriched with distance and association attributes from the distance matrix.

Compare park cooling effects on air temperature. The script compares two urban microclimate scenarios (reference vs. alternative) to quantify differences in park-induced cooling effects—specifically the spatial pattern and magnitude of air temperature modification (ΔT) and absolute temperature (T) at day (14:00) and night (2:00) hours, as well as derived building energy savings and thermal discomfort reduction. It validates geometric consistency between scenarios (park boundaries must be identical; building footprints/heights may differ only for 'buildings characteristics' change), computes raster-based differences, generates isovalue contour layers (geojson) for visualization, and returns aggregated city-scale metrics including mean ΔT per scenario, total energy saved, and degree-hour comfort improvements.

Convert building plan boundary to XPlanGML. The script converts one or more user-drawn or loaded polygon features (Bebauungsplan umring / building plan boundary) from a QGIS vector layer into a standards-compliant XPlanung GML v5.4 file (xplan.gml), embedded in a ZIP archive. It performs geometry preprocessing (reprojection to specified CRS, CCW orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M dropping), validates input constraints (character set, length, required fields), injects metadata (name, number, AGS, plan type, legal status, dates, municipality/Ortsteil, planner), replaces placeholder GML geometries and bounding boxes with actual feature geometry and extent, assigns UUID-based gml:id and xlink:href attributes per XPlanGML v5.4 schema requirements, and sanitizes filenames for xPlanBox compatibility (German umlauts → ae/oe/ue/ss, non-alphanumeric → underscore). The output is a ZIP archive named after the sanitized plan name containing exactly one xplan.gml file.

Subtract polygon from raster plan. The script performs a geospatial raster masking operation: it takes an input raster layer (representing a planning document, e.g., a zoning or development plan) and subtracts (i.e., masks out) the area covered by a user-provided polygon vector layer. Internally, it first generates a bounding extent layer from the raster, segments the polygon for geometric robustness, computes a vector difference (extent minus polygon), then uses that resulting geometry as a mask to clip the original raster — optionally setting palette index 0 as NoData. The output is a new raster where the polygon area is removed (transparent/NoData), preserving only the original raster outside the polygon. This is intended for XPlan-compliant digital planning documents (e.g., German Bauleitplanung), specifically for generating 'Umring' (outline/perimeter) rasters in KRZN-XPlanBox.

Convert plan boundary to XPlanGML. The script converts one or more user-provided polygon vector layers (representing Flächennutzungsplan 'Umring' boundaries) into a valid XPlanung GML v6.0 XML file embedded in a ZIP archive. It performs geometric preprocessing (reprojection to specified CRS, CCW orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M dropping), extracts the bounding box and GML3 geometry of the first feature, populates an XPlanGML template with user inputs (name, AGS, planart, rechtsstand, dates, etc.), dynamically assigns UUIDs to GML elements, updates srsName and bounding coordinates, conditionally removes or populates date fields based on Rechtsstand selection, sanitizes the plan name for xPlanBox compliance, and writes the final GML to 'xplan.gml' inside a ZIP archive. The study area is not defined by remote sensing data but by the input vector layer provided by the user in QGIS; no satellite, sensor, or band processing occurs.

Convert landscape plan boundary to XPlanGML. The script converts one or more polygon features representing landscape plan boundaries (Umringpolygon(e)) from a QGIS vector layer into a valid XPlanung GML v6.0 XML file, packaged in a ZIP archive. It performs geometric preprocessing (reprojection to user-specified CRS, CCW polygon orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M value dropping), validates input constraints (character set and length of plan name for xPlanBox compatibility), injects user-provided metadata (name, number, Bundesland, AGS, planart, Rechtsstand, dates, etc.), replaces template placeholders with real geometry (GML3-encoded MultiSurface/Polygon), updates UUIDs and xlink references, adjusts bounding box coordinates from the input geometry, and handles conditional date fields (aufstellungsbeschlussDatum, inkrafttretenDatum, untergangsDatum) based on Rechtsstand selection. The output is a standards-compliant XPlan-Archiv (.zip containing xplan.gml) ready for ingestion into xPlanBox or other XPlanung-compliant systems. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis is involved — it is a vector-based metadata + geometry serialization workflow.

Replace spatial extent geometry. The script replaces the raeumlicherGeltungsbereich (spatial extent) geometry in an XPlanGML file with a new polygon geometry provided as a QGIS vector layer, while preserving all other attributes and metadata; it validates XPlanGML structure (single *_Bereich, correct namespace, srsName), reprojects and cleans the input polygon (force CCW winding, remove duplicate vertices, drop Z/M), updates both the root and plan-level boundedBy envelopes, replaces the existing raeumlicherGeltungsbereich element with a newly generated GML3 MultiSurface/Polygon conforming to GML 3.2 and the original coordinate reference system, and writes the modified XPlanGML to the specified output file.

Extract local elevation maxima. The script identifies local elevation maxima (spot heights) within user-defined circular neighborhoods across a digital elevation model (DEM). It first computes the maximum value in each neighborhood using GRASS r.neighbors, then isolates cells where the original DEM value equals that neighborhood maximum (i.e., local peaks), nulls all zero-valued pixels, converts remaining pixels to vector points, and finally filters those points to retain only those intersecting the input coastline polygon—yielding on-land spot height candidates as point features with elevation values.

Generate distance-based environmental variable. The script generates a continuous raster surface representing Euclidean distance from vector features (e.g., rivers, roads, urban nuclei) within user-defined territorial boundaries and maximum distance. It rasterizes clipped input vector features to a zero-initialized reference grid, computes proximity (distance) raster up to a specified maximum distance, fills null values with a user-defined fill value, and masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster—producing a standardized distance raster suitable for MaxEnt species distribution modeling.

Delimit habitat suitability zones. The script reclassifies a Maxent-generated ASCII habitat suitability raster into discrete ecological or management zones (e.g., 'High', 'Medium', 'Low' suitability) using user-defined thresholds (Min/Max value ranges per category) from a CSV-based typology layer; it then converts the reclassified raster to vector polygons, producing both a thematic raster and a polygon vector layer where each feature represents a spatially contiguous zone of uniform suitability class.

Generate distance-based environmental variable raster. The script generates a continuous raster surface representing Euclidean distance from input vector features (e.g., rivers, roads, urban nuclei) within user-defined territorial boundaries. It rasterizes clipped vector features to a zero-initialized reference raster grid, computes proximity (distance) up to a specified maximum distance, fills null pixels with a user-defined control value, and masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster layer. The output is a standardized-resolution distance raster suitable for Maxent species distribution modeling. No satellite imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved; all operations are vector-to-raster conversion and distance transformation using QGIS Processing algorithms (qgis:rastercalculator, native:clip, gdal:rasterize, gdal:proximity, grass7:r.null, saga:rastermasking). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

Compute zonal statistics for environmental variables. The script computes comprehensive zonal statistics (mean, median, min, max, std, variance, sum, count, range, minority, majority, uniqueness) of a continuous environmental raster variable within circular buffers (user-defined radius) centered on species occurrence point locations. It outputs a point feature layer where each original occurrence point is replaced by its buffer centroid and enriched with the computed raster statistics as attributes prefixed with 'Sta_'. The workflow consists of three deterministic QGIS native processing steps: (1) buffering input points, (2) computing zonal statistics over the buffered polygons using the environmental raster, and (3) computing centroids of the buffered polygons to return point geometry aligned with original occurrences while retaining all statistics.

Delimit raster variable by negative buffer zone. The script processes an input environmental raster (e.g., for MaxEnt modeling) by first generating a zero-valued raster of identical extent, converting it to a polygon, applying a *negative* distance buffer (i.e., an inward shrinkage) to create a perimeter mask, and finally clipping the original raster to that buffered polygon. This effectively removes peripheral pixels — such as coastal edges, administrative boundaries, or island fringes — to avoid edge artifacts in species distribution modeling. The output is a spatially constrained raster where only the interior region (retracted by the specified negative distance) remains, with outer pixels masked out.

Rasterize and fill linear or isolated environmental features. The script converts linear or isolated vector-based environmental features (e.g., rivers, roads, protected areas, settlements) into a standardized raster layer for Maxent modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to territorial influence boundaries, then rasterizes it using a specified numeric field and user-defined pixel resolution, fills NoData cells with a user-controlled fill value, and finally masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster—producing a ready-to-use, spatially constrained environmental variable raster aligned with Maxent requirements.

Rasterize categorical vector variable. The script rasterizes a categorical environmental vector layer (e.g., land cover, habitat type, or administrative zoning) into a standardized-resolution raster aligned to a territorial boundary mask, specifically for Maxent species distribution modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to a territorial influence boundary using spatial intersection, then rasterizes the clipped features using a specified numeric field (categorical ID), and finally masks and resamples the resulting raster to match the extent, resolution, and geometry of the provided territorial limits layer — ensuring pixel alignment and NoData handling suitable for ecological niche modeling.

Generate microshed basins. The script runs GRASS r.watershed on a user-provided DEM raster to compute watershed basins using a user-specified cell-count threshold (e.g., minimum exterior basin size of 1000 cells, recommended for ~2–3 km²). It outputs a uniquely labeled integer raster where each pixel value corresponds to a distinct microshed basin ID. Optionally, it polygonizes that raster into a vector layer (GeoPackage or similar) with a 'basin_id' attribute. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is embedded in the code — inputs are generic QGIS raster layers supplied by the user at runtime. The workflow relies entirely on local DEM input and GRASS GIS hydrological modeling, not remote sensing imagery or temporal analysis.

Compute network betweenness centrality. The script computes betweenness centrality for road/path network segments within 30 selected municipalities in the Madrid region (Comunidad de Madrid, Spain), using a pre-existing vector network layer and administrative boundary polygons. It first filters the polygon layer to retain only municipalities with specific INE boundary codes (e.g., '28005', '28006', ...), splits the network layer along those municipal boundaries, then iteratively applies GRASS v.net.centrality (betweenness mode) to each municipality’s subset of the split network. Outputs include individual GeoPackage layers per municipality containing centrality values (as attribute 'centrality'), and a final merged GeoPackage layer aggregating all municipal centrality results for downstream spatial analysis and visualization in QGIS.

Generate village interior sampling polygons. The script generates a set of non-overlapping 100 m × 100 m rectangular polygons distributed randomly inside the interior (buffered-in) boundary of a selected village polygon. It first extracts one selected (or first) village feature from an active QGIS vector layer, applies an inward buffer (−70 m), generates random points inside that buffered area, then converts each point into a centered rectangle. The final output is a shapefile of these rectangles stored in a predefined local folder (e.g., 'C:\Users\atree\Desktop\QC_polygons') named after the village (e.g., 'village_name_polygons.shp'). This is intended for spatial sampling or field survey planning within village boundaries.

Delineate catchments and correct structure locations. The script processes point-based water-harvesting structure locations (anicut, pokher, taal) in Karauli district, Rajasthan, India. It first corrects each input point’s location by identifying the nearest high-flow-accumulation pixel within a 200m buffer of the original point using FABDEM-derived flow accumulation raster. Then, for pokher and taal structures, it traces upstream drainage lines by iteratively stepping to the lowest-flow-accumulation pixel within successive 25m buffers along the flow path (using FABDEM drainage direction), generating polylines of specified lengths (300m for pokher, 1000m for taal). Finally, it delineates the contributing catchment for each corrected point using GRASS r.water.outlet on the drainage direction raster, polygonizes the catchment, and outputs combined vector layers: original points, corrected points, structure-specific buffers (250m for anicut/pokher/taal), drainage lines (for pokher/taal), and catchment polygons — all georeferenced in EPSG:4326.

Estimate water storage volume. The script estimates the volume of water that can be stored by a check dam or johad structure (a traditional rainwater harvesting structure) based on high-resolution elevation data (FABDEM, ALOS, or CartoSat), flow accumulation, and drainage direction rasters.
