Output includes one KML per visible vector layer, each containing only geometries within the selected property boundary and named using a user-specified attribute field.

Generate building detection training chips. The script generates synthetic training chip pairs (satellite image PNG + binary building mask PNG) for deep learning models (e.g., Mask R-CNN, U-Net). It loads a satellite GeoTIFF basemap and an OSM building vector layer, reprojects the vector to match the raster CRS, rasterizes buildings into a pixel-aligned binary mask GeoTIFF, computes a regular grid of chip extents over a user-defined AOI, clips and resizes both image and mask to fixed dimensions (e.g., 256×256 px), filters out chips with insufficient building coverage (< min_positive_ratio), and logs dataset statistics including total chips, exported count, skip/fail rates, and average building pixel coverage.

Update urban point attributes. The script updates a point layer representing current land surface conditions by identifying points located within future urbanization polygons, then modifies their attributes: (1) sets 'ALB' (albedo) to the value from the 'ALBFUT' field of the intersecting urban polygon; (2) sets 'HAUTA' (tree height) to 0; (3) sets 'URB' (urban flag) to 1; (4) sets 'OCCSOL' (land cover class) to 6 (indicating an urban class); finally merges updated points with unmodified points (those outside future urban zones) and removes the temporary 'ALBFUT' join field, producing a fully updated point layer with consistent urban attribute assignments.

Estimate floodwater depth. The script estimates floodwater depth using a digital elevation model (DEM) and a user-provided inundation polygon. It follows the FwDET v2.1 method (Cohen et al., 2022): (1) clips the DEM to the inundation polygon extent; (2) rasterizes the inundation boundary (polygon-to-line → raster); (3) samples DEM elevations along that boundary; (4) smooths boundary elevations via iterative neighborhood maximum filtering; (5) applies slope-based filtering using GRASS r.slope.aspect (with threshold in percent); (6) grows the smoothed boundary outward using GRASS r.grow.distance with configurable distance metric (euclidean, squared, etc.); (7) computes water depth as the difference between the grown distance surface and the clipped DEM; (8) masks depths to the inundation area; and (9) optionally applies a low-pass 3×3 average filter. Outputs are three rasters: shore-boundary elevation, interpolated water depth, and smoothed water depth. No satellite or time-series data is used — inputs are static local raster (DEM) and vector (inundation polygon) layers. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified in the code.

Compute slope and aspect from DTM. The script processes raw digital terrain model (DTM) GeoTIFF files by reprojecting them to EPSG:7791, then computing slope and aspect rasters for each input DTM tile; it also derives and exports the spatial extent of each reprojected DTM as a shapefile. Outputs include per-tile slope rasters, aspect rasters, and tile boundary shapefiles, organized in dedicated subfolders (slope/, aspect/, tile/, dtm/).

Clip raster by vector mask. The script clips an input raster file to the spatial extents and geometry of a provided vector mask layer (Shapefile), reprojecting the raster to the mask layer's coordinate reference system first. It produces a single clipped GeoTIFF output file ('clipped.tif') and removes the intermediate reprojected raster. The operation is projection-aware and handles format-agnostic rasters using GDAL-based QGIS processing algorithms.

Model school suitability location. The script computes a final school suitability map by integrating normalized population density, road proximity, slope, land use/land cover suitability, and water body proximity rasters. It applies a custom weighted formula that reduces city-center bias via a Gaussian-adjusted population term (penalizing high-density areas), then normalizes the raw output to 0–1. Outputs are two GeoTIFFs: an unnormalized raw suitability raster and a normalized 0–1 suitability raster for decision support in educational infrastructure planning.

Aggregate flood hazard layers. The script performs spatial upscaling (coarsening) of high-resolution flood modeling outputs—specifically DEM (digital elevation model), WSE (water surface elevation), and WSH (water surface height/depth)—using two physics-informed averaging methods from Bryant et al. (2023): (1) 'WSH Averaging', where WSH is directly averaged and WSE is reconstructed as DEM + WSH; and (2) 'WSE Averaging', where WSE is first averaged, then filtered against the coarsened DEM to retain only wet cells (WSE > DEM), and WSH is derived as WSE − DEM. Outputs are three coarsened rasters at user-specified scale: DEM_s2, WSE_s2, and WSH_s2, all aligned and consistent with hydrologic constraints.

Apply linear fuzzification to indicator raster. The script performs spatial fuzzification of a geospatial indicator (e.g., soil moisture, temperature, or land degradation index) by converting its crisp raster values into fuzzy membership values between 0 and 1 using a linear membership function. It first extracts a user-defined WKT polygon area, reads indicator point data from a PostGIS table ('pixels') filtered by 'indicator_id', spatially joins those points to a regular grid (cell size configurable), rasterizes the joined grid with indicator 'value' as burn-in, applies either direct or inverse linear fuzzification based on 'relationship' (mapping [min,max] → [0,1] or [max,min] → [0,1]), converts the resulting fuzzy raster back to points, appends the 'indicator_id', and exports the fuzzy point layer to the 'fuzzy_view' table in PostGIS. The output is a georeferenced point layer where each point holds a fuzzy membership value and its associated indicator ID.

Convert raster pixels to point features. The script processes a raster input layer by reprojecting it to EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator), clipping it to a user-provided polygon study area, converting the resulting clipped raster pixels to vector point features (one point per pixel, retaining pixel values in a 'VALUE' field), adding a constant integer attribute 'project_indicator_id' to all points, and finally appending those points to a PostGIS table named 'pixels' in the 'integral' database under the 'public' schema. The output is a persistent spatial table of georeferenced pixel points with indicator metadata, enabling subsequent SQL-based aggregation or spatiotemporal analysis.

Convert CHM to forest polygons. The script converts a Canopy Height Model (CHM) raster into a binary forest/non-forest raster using height and density thresholds, followed by morphological closing/opening (with adaptive kernel size derived from minimum width and area constraints), removal of small connected components (< minArea m²) in both forest and non-forest masks, optional integration of user-provided forest/no-forest mask rasters (e.g., SIBOSCO/NOBOSCO), and final vectorization into polygon features with area (ha) attribute and style application. Outputs include a classified forest raster layer and an optional smoothed, single-part polygon layer with area calculation.

Estimate glacier thickness distribution. The script estimates spatially distributed glacier ice thickness for the Juncal Norte glacier system (Chilean Andes) using Farinotti et al. (2019) gridded thickness data, reprojects and masks it to EPSG:32719, replaces zero values with NaN, and integrates it with Landsat-derived NDSI, Random Forest classification, DEMs, model ID rasters, and debris cover to generate a structured CSV containing per-pixel glacier attributes: U_ID, MOD_ID, GLAC_ID, MOD_H (model DEM elevation), GLAC_H (glacier surface elevation), DEB (debris flag), FRAC_GLAC (glacier coverage fraction), and ICE_DEPTH (thickness). This CSV serves as input for glacio-hydrological modeling (e.g., in PCRaster).

Reclassify and smooth NLCD land cover. The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for Alaska, specifically the 2016 Tree Canopy and Land Cover layers. It performs a sequence of geospatial operations: (1) reprojecting the input NLCD Land Cover raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reclassifying land cover classes into simplified grass-dominated values using a pixel-wise arithmetic expression mapping 20 original NLCD classes (e.g., 21=Developed, Open Space → 26; 41=Deciduous Forest → 23) to new integer codes; (3) separately reclassifying urban classes (21,22,23,24) into urban-subtype codes (10,1,1,2); (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to denoise and remove road/clutter artifacts from the urban layer; (5) compositing the cleaned urban layer over the grass-only layer using conditional pixel replacement (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8× finer resolution) via GDAL Warp with resampling; (7) spatially smoothing the high-resolution composite using GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and (8) compressing and exporting as an 8-bit LZW-compressed GeoTIFF. The final output is a smoothed, high-resolution, urban-prioritized, grass-background land cover raster in WGS84, named 'NLCD_2016_Alaska_SaintPaul-Island_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'. Input filenames and paths confirm the source is NLCD 2016, and the processing is explicitly scoped to Alaska, specifically Saint Paul Island and adjacent longitude bands (e.g., 'Alaska141-140_60').

Reclassify NLCD land cover. The script reclassifies and processes the NLCD (National Land Cover Database) 2016 land cover raster for Alaska's Diomede Island region. It performs a sequence of geospatial operations: (1) warping the input NLCD raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reassigning NLCD class values to simplified 'grass-only' categories using a deterministic pixel-wise expression mapping 20 original NLCD classes (e.g., 21=Developed, Open Space → 26; 41=Deciduous Forest → 23) to new land-cover-representative codes; (3) isolating urban classes (NLCD 21–24) into a binary/multi-value reclassified urban layer; (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to clean urban features by removing small clutter/road artifacts; (5) combining the cleaned urban layer with the grass-only layer via conditional raster algebra (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8× higher spatial resolution) the combined raster using GDAL Warp; (7) smoothing the high-resolution result with GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and (8) compressing to 8-bit GeoTIFF with LZW. The study area is explicitly Diomede Island, Alaska; the time range is fixed to 2016; the source is NLCD 2016 — a USGS-conducted, multi-source (Landsat-derived + ancillary) land cover product — not a raw satellite acquisition. No satellite or sensor metadata is embedded in the script; the input is a pre-processed, classified raster dataset.

Reclassify and combine NLCD land cover and tree canopy. The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) data for Alaska in 2016 to produce a refined, high-resolution, EPSG:4326-aligned land cover raster. It first reclassifies NLCD Tree Canopy (input: NLCD_2016_Tree_Canopy_Alaska162-154_56.tiff) into a single forest class (value 43) where canopy > 0; warps both tree canopy and NLCD Land Cover (input: NLCD_2016_Land_Cover_Alaska162-154_56.tiff) to WGS84 (EPSG:4326); combines them using conditional logic that prioritizes tree canopy over land cover except where land cover is already forest (41–43); replaces non-forest urban/clutter classes (e.g., 11, 21–24, 31, 51–52, 71–75, 81–82, 90, 95) with grass- or vegetation-appropriate NLCD codes (e.g., 41→23, 21→10, etc.); reclassifies urban classes (21–24) into simplified urban types; applies GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=7) to clean urban pixels; merges cleaned urban with grass-reclassified raster; upsamples the result by factor of 8 using gdal.Warp; smooths again with GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and compresses to 8-bit LZW GeoTIFF. The final output is NLCD_2016_Alaska162-154_59_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff — a high-definition, visually smoothed, reclassified land cover raster for flight simulation scenery generation. Study area is Alaska, tile identifier '162-154_56'; time range is 2016; no satellite/sensor is involved — inputs are derived NLCD raster products (not raw satellite imagery).

Compute raster statistics in geosquare grids. The script converts an input raster layer into a vector grid of equal-area geosquares (hierarchical H3-like or custom geohash-based polygons) aligned to a user-defined grid size (50 m to 10 km), clips the raster to a boundary polygon, and computes per-grid zonal statistics (Sum, Mean, Median, St Dev, Min, Max) for a selected raster band. It uses a two-level tiling strategy: first partitions the boundary into ~10 km parent cells (via `polyfill`), then subdivides each into child grids at the specified resolution (`parrent_to_allchildren`), filters children intersecting the boundary, and applies `zonalstatisticsfb` to assign the chosen statistic value to each grid cell. Output is a vector polygon layer with fields 'gid' (geosquare identifier) and 'value' (computed statistic).

Identify nearest gas leak to schools. The script identifies the publicly reported gas leak closest to each Massachusetts school by converting KML gas leak data to shapefile, reprojecting both gas leak and school point layers to EPSG:3857, performing a nearest-neighbor spatial join to assign the nearest gas leak (by 'Name' attribute) to each school, visualizing both layers in QGIS, and exporting the joined result—including school attributes and nearest leak name—as a CSV table with XYZ geometry coordinates.

Derive stream network and catchment velocity. The script performs hydrological terrain analysis on a DEM to derive flow direction, flow accumulation, Strahler stream order, and channel networks; it snaps a user-defined pour point to the extracted channels, computes the upslope contributing catchment, calculates a slope-area term (sqrt(slope) × sqrt(flow accumulation)) as a proxy for flow velocity potential, clips it to the catchment, computes its mean statistic, then derives a normalized velocity layer and its inverse (weight grid) for downstream hydrological modeling. Outputs include filled DEM, flow direction/accumulation rasters, Strahler-order rasters (full and thresholded ≥6), vectorized channels and catchment, slope raster, slope-area term raster (clipped), velocity raster, and weight raster.

Compute ground surface temperature. The script computes hourly ground surface temperature (in °C) for a grid of points across a user-defined study area, using material properties (albedo, emissivity, thermal conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, thickness), solar radiation and weather data (air temperature, humidity, sky temperature), shadow duration from precomputed rasters, ground heat conduction (using annual temperature wave propagation at 20 cm depth), and evapotranspiration (Penman-Monteith). It solves a nonlinear energy balance equation (radiation + convection + conduction + storage + latent heat) iteratively per hour per material-shadow combination, outputs a CSV with x/y coordinates and hourly/mean/min/max temperatures, and loads it as a styled point layer in QGIS.

Calculate centerline distance metrics. The script calculates four distance metrics along vector centerlines: (1) Distance (cumulative distance from the startpoint), (2) RDistance (reverse cumulative distance from the endpoint), (3) SP_Dist (shortest path distance from the startpoint of the longest shortest path), and (4) SP_RDist (reverse shortest path distance from the endpoint of the longest shortest path). It operates on input line features (centerlines), optionally densifying vertices at a user-specified interval or exploding lines at each vertex. It constructs a networkx graph where nodes are rounded coordinate endpoints of line segments and edges represent segments with weight = geometry length. Using Dijkstra’s algorithm, it identifies the two endpoints of the longest shortest path in each connected component, then computes distances relative to those endpoints. Outputs are line features with original attributes plus the four new numeric fields, preserving geometry. No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite imagery is involved — input is purely vector line geometry. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic location are not specified in the code.

Calculate polygon centerlines. The script calculates centerline(s) for each input polygon feature using Voronoi diagram-based skeletonization and graph-theoretic shortest-path analysis. It supports three methods: (1) 'Centerlines' — single shortest path between two endpoints derived from the largest connected component of the trimmed Voronoi graph; (2) 'All' — all shortest paths after iterative dangle trimming; (3) 'Circles' — edges belonging to cycles (loops) in the pruned graph. Input polygons are optionally simplified (Douglas-Peucker) and densified before vertex extraction. Outputs are line features with attributes: ID, Distance (distance from first endpoint), RDistance (distance from reverse endpoint), SP_Dist (shortest path distance from startpoint), and SP_RDist (reverse shortest path distance). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms (SAGA Thiessen polygons, polygon-to-lines, explode lines, select by location) and NetworkX for graph operations. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — input is vector polygon geometry only. Study area, time range, and external data sources are not specified.

Skeletonize raster centerlines. The script creates vector centerlines from a binary raster image by applying morphological skeletonization (either 'lee' or 'medial axis' method from scikit-image), followed by raster-to-vector conversion (GRASS r.to.vect), line splitting, exploding, and network-based topological cleaning to resolve spurious cycles and node intersections. The output is a vector line layer representing centerlines of rasterized linear features (e.g., rivers, roads, or other binary-valued linear objects). Input must be a single-band binary raster (values 0/1); no thresholding is performed internally — the script explicitly requires prior binarization via a separate 'Thresholding tool'. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic coordinates are embedded in the code; it is a generic, local raster processing algorithm operating on user-provided QGIS raster layers.

Compute passive visibility rasters. The script computes multiple passive visibility raster maps (GeoTIFF) by systematically varying observer height, target height, number of observation points (for polygon inputs), and surface elevation adjustments (MNS/MNE variations). For polygon inputs, it first samples points along the perimeter, computes individual viewsheds per point, then aggregates them into binary (full visibility), count-based, and fuzzy-logic visibility rasters. Outputs are stored in user-specified directories with structured filenames encoding parameter combinations (e.g., 'vpass_nbpt3_Hcible0_Hobs160_sursol_code1var5.tif'), and optionally launches a web interface for visualization.

Calculate passive visibility rasters with parameter variations. The script computes multiple passive visibility raster maps (GeoTIFF) by systematically varying observer height, target height, number of contour points (for polygon inputs), and surface elevation (MNS/MNE) parameters—either uniformly across all built/vegetation features or differentially per land cover type (using CSV-specified codes). For polygon inputs, it first generates random contour points, computes individual visibility rasters per point, then aggregates them via logical AND (pixel sees polygon only if it sees all points). Outputs include a folder of visibility rasters (1 = visible, 0 = not visible), optional web-visualizable GeoJSON points and EPSG:3857-reprojected rasters, and intermediate MNE/MNS rasters reflecting surface height perturbations.

Extract OSM roads and railways. The script extracts road and railway line features from an OpenStreetMap (.osm) vector layer based on user-selected highway and railway types (e.g., 'motorway', 'rail', 'cycleway'), clips them to a user-provided watershed polygon, and appends a 'demi_emp' (half-width in meters) attribute derived from standardized width values per feature type (e.g., 22.5 m for motorway, 5.486 m for rail), producing a new metric-projected line vector layer representing the morphologically relevant transport infrastructure within the watershed for MQI (Morphological Quality Index) calculation.

Snap stream network outlets to DEM-derived flow paths. The script extracts the downstream endpoints (outlets) of each river segment (UEA) from a vector stream network, interpolates points near the end of each line (at ~90% or length−30 m), rasterizes the stream network using a LiDAR-derived 10-m DEM, then snaps those interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within 40 m using a flow-path-aware algorithm (JensonSnapPourPoints); finally, it joins the original segment ID attribute from the stream layer to the snapped points. The output is a point vector layer where each feature represents a topologically consistent outlet location for an ecological aquatic unit (UEA), correctly aligned with the hydrologically conditioned DEM for subsequent MQI (Morphological Quality Index) computation.

Extract road railway cycleway network. The script extracts and filters road, railway, and cycleway vector layers from Quebec’s AQréseau+ geospatial datasets (MRNF and MELCCFP sources), clips them to a user-provided watershed polygon (or processes all features if the watershed is empty), applies attribute-based filtering to retain only morphologically relevant linear infrastructure (e.g., excluding tunnels, ferries, unmarked/unbuilt cycleways, and ferry railways), merges the three filtered line layers into a single unified transport network layer, and appends a 'demi_emp' (half-right-of-way) width attribute using rule-based lookup tables derived from official Quebec transportation design standards (Ministère des Transports du Québec, 2012). The output is a metric-projected QgsVectorLayer of lines with geometry and a calculated decimal width field, intended for use in computing the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) of river systems.

Filter river-proximate structures. The script identifies and filters point-based infrastructure structures (e.g., bridges, culverts, tunnels) and road-river intersections that are spatially coincident with or within 100 m of a river network. It first computes line intersections between roads and rivers, merges those intersection points with existing MTMD point structures, applies a 2 m buffer to each point, dissolves overlapping buffers, computes centroids of dissolved polygons (to aggregate nearby structures), then extracts only those centroids within 100 m of the river network. Finally, it assigns a unique integer ID (fid) to each retained point. The output is a cleaned, de-duplicated point layer of anthropogenic structures directly associated with the fluvial system for Morphological Quality Index (MQI) assessment.

Calculate Morphological Quality Index A1. The script calculates the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) component 'Indice A1' for river segments (UEAs) by quantifying upstream watershed land cover composition—specifically forest and agricultural area proportions—and applying a rule-based classification to assign an integer score (0–5) reflecting hydrogeomorphic alteration. It requires either a precomputed sub-watershed polygon layer with land-use attributes or generates it on-the-fly using a D8 flow direction raster, dam point layer, and land-use raster; then joins computed watershed-area, forest-area, and agri-area metrics back to the input stream network (line features), appending them along with the final A1 index to the output vector layer.

Calculate dam impact index A2. The script calculates the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) component 'Indice A2', which quantifies the hydrogeomorphological impact of upstream dams on river segments by computing the ratio of total dam-affected drainage area to total watershed area per segment. It uses a pre-segmented stream network (CRHQ UEA layer), optionally provided sub-watershed polygons (with land use), or generates them using a D8 flow direction raster (WBT D8 Pointer), dam point locations (CEHQ), and land use raster (MELCCFP). The workflow includes: (1) validating input fields (e.g., 'Id_UEA'); (2) generating sub-watersheds if not provided; (3) computing 'dam_area_sum' per watershed via spatial join/summarize; (4) applying a rule-based classification formula to derive integer 'Indice A2' scores (0–4) based on dam-area-to-watershed-area ratio thresholds; and (5) joining results back to the original stream network. Study area is implied to be Québec, Canada (via CEHQ, MELCCFP, CRHQ, LERGA/UQAC); data sources are provincial/national administrative datasets — no satellite imagery or time-series analysis is used. Outputs are a line vector layer (UEA segments) enriched with 'dam_area_sum_m2' and 'Indice A2' attributes.

Estimate land surface temperature. The script computes Land Surface Temperature (LST) and NDVI from Landsat 7 ETM+ top-of-atmosphere (TOA) or calibrated radiance raster inputs. It first converts band 6 (TIR) digital numbers to at-sensor spectral radiance using Landsat 7 ETM+ calibration parameters (gain = (12.650 − 3.200)/(255 − 1), offset = 3.200), then applies a single-channel LST algorithm: LST = (1282.71 / ln(666.09 / L) + 1) − 273.15, where L is the calculated radiance — consistent with the mono-window algorithm for Landsat 7 ETM+ band 6 (10.4–12.5 µm). Simultaneously, it computes NDVI using band 3 (red) and band 4 (NIR) as (B4 − B3)/(B4 + B3), clips both outputs to a user-provided ROI polygon, and applies pre-defined QGIS layer styles for visualization.

Estimate land surface temperature. The script computes Land Surface Temperature (LST) and NDVI from Landsat 8 thermal infrared (B10) and optical bands (B4, B5), using a single-channel algorithm that incorporates atmospheric correction via brightness temperature (TOABT), NDVI-derived vegetation proportion (PV), and emissivity estimation (E = 0.004×PV + 0.986). It outputs two clipped, ROI-masked rasters: NDVI (unitless, −1 to 1) and LST (in °C), both styled with predefined QML files for visualization.

Generate styled density grid. The script computes a point density heatmap by aggregating input point features into a regular (rectangle/diamond/hexagon) grid, counting points per cell (optionally weighted), filtering cells by minimum count, and applying a graduated color ramp style to the resulting polygon layer. It outputs a styled vector polygon layer representing spatial density distribution, with configurable grid geometry, units, color ramp, classification mode, and outline visibility.

Calculate polygon overlap density. The script computes the spatial density of overlapping polygons in a vector layer by performing a union operation to split all intersecting polygons into non-overlapping atomic parts, then aggregates each resulting geometry to count how many original input polygons contributed to it (NUMPOINTS), optionally listing their unique IDs (ID_LIST); finally, it filters out parts where the overlap count is below a user-defined threshold, outputting a cleaned polygon layer where each feature represents a spatially distinct zone with its associated overlap count and optional source ID list.

Identify high-altitude and steep-slope areas. The script identifies two distinct terrain-based environmental constraint zones within a user-defined rural property boundary: (1) areas with elevation > 1800 m above sea level, derived by binary thresholding a reprojected Digital Terrain Model (MDT), and (2) areas with slope > 45°, computed from the same MDT using the native slope algorithm; both outputs are vectorized, attribute-filtered (DN = 1), and clipped to the input property polygon, yielding two separate polygon layers suitable for APP (Permanent Preservation Area) identification under Brazilian environmental regulation (e.g., CAR/APP criteria).

Identify 25°–45° slope areas. The script computes terrain slope from a user-provided Digital Terrain Model (MDT) raster, reprojects it to a projected CRS (e.g., UTM), calculates slope in degrees using QGIS native:slope, applies a raster algebra condition '(A>=25)*(A<=45)' to isolate pixels within the 25°–45° range, converts the binary raster to polygons via gdal:polygonize, filters for DN=1 polygons (i.e., slope-valid areas), and clips the result to the input property boundary ('Área do imóvel'), producing a vector layer of polygons where terrain inclination falls strictly between 25 and 45 degrees — intended for identifying potential Areas of Permanent Preservation (APP) under Brazilian environmental regulation (Resolução CONAMA 303/2002).

Compute basin-averaged precipitation from gridded data. The script computes spatially weighted average precipitation over a catchment area using a gridded precipitation dataset. It reprojects the grid to EPSG:32632, clips it to the catchment boundary, calculates cell area, appends a constant field with total catchment area, computes weighting factors (cell area / catchment area), and then generates new weighted precipitation fields (e.g., 'DATA_20230101_pesata') by multiplying each 'DATA*' precipitation value by its corresponding weight. Outputs include: (1) clipped & reprojected grid, (2) clipped grid with area, catchment area constant, and weight fields, and (3) final layer with original precipitation fields plus their basin-weighted versions for downstream aggregation (e.g., summing weighted values yields basin-mean precipitation).

Derive waste dump elevation model. The script processes a DEM raster clipped to a waste dump polygon, computes the minimum positive elevation value within that clipped area, creates a constant raster layer with that minimum value, subtracts it from the clipped DEM to generate a relative elevation (height-above-base) raster, and then — though incorrectly configured — attempts to compute surface volume (but misuses the 'Create Constant Raster Layer' algorithm in place of 'raster surface volume'). The final output is a 'DerivedDem' raster representing elevation relative to the lowest positive terrain point inside the waste dump boundary.

Calculate street openness ratio. The script computes the street openness ratio (h/d ≤ 1) for urban blocks, where h is building height (derived from floor count × 3 m) and d is the perpendicular distance between opposing building façades across streets. It identifies façade segments perpendicular to street centerlines using azimuth matching (±6° and ±174°–186°), generates transects, clips them against buildings, retains only segments intersecting exactly two buildings (i.e., spanning the street width), measures their length (d), computes h/d, filters segments where h/d ≤ 1, and finally calculates the percentage of total block perimeter length covered by such favorable segments — outputting a grid-based polygon layer with the computed IA06 indicator value per cell.

Calculate pedestrian intersection density. The script computes pedestrian intersection density as a connectivity indicator for urban areas, by extracting street network intersections from OpenStreetMap (OSM) line data, filtering out dead-ends (intersections with <3 connected segments), aggregating remaining intersections into clusters to resolve topological noise, counting them per grid cell, and normalizing by grid cell area (km²) to produce a density metric (intersections/km²). Output is a vector feature class (polygon grid) with an attribute field named per NAMES_INDEX['IA12'][0] containing the computed density values.

Compute coastal elevation change. The script computes vertical change (erosion/accretion) between two point cloud datasets representing coastal topography at different times. It merges multiple old and new point clouds separately, converts each merged set to a 1-m resolution DEM raster (using Z attribute), assigns the project's CRS, then calculates the difference (New − Old) to produce a continuous-change raster ('temp.tif') representing elevation change in meters. The result is loaded into QGIS with a predefined style (style.qml) and exported as a styled GeoTIFF named after the user-specified 'Erosion Map Layer Name'.

Calculate annual solar shadow patterns. The script calculates solar shadow rasters for four key dates (March 20, June 21, September 23, and December 22, 2020) using a Digital Surface Model (DSM) and optional roof plane vector data. It generates continuous-shadow rasters via geometric shadow casting (using the external ShadowGenerator class), reclassifies them into binary shadow/no-shadow rasters, multiplies them to produce a composite annual shadow mask (where 1 = persistently sunlit, 0 = shaded on ≥1 date), and finally computes mean shade values per roof plane polygon using zonal statistics. Outputs include four date-specific shadow rasters, four binary rasters, one final multiplied binary shadow layer, and updated roof vector attributes ('Shade_mean').

Generate linear referencing marks. The script creates a point vector layer of linear referencing marks placed along input line geometry, with mandatory marks at distance = 0 (start) and full line length (end), plus inner marks either at fixed map-unit intervals or equally spaced by count. Each output point contains a numeric 'distance' field (accumulated length from line start) and a formatted 'label' string field (e.g., '123.45'), and is automatically styled with black cross markers (2 mm) and white Arial labels (8 pt) with black 0.8 mm buffer.

Delineate watershed subbasins. The script delineates a watershed basin and its internal subbasins from a digital elevation model (DEM), using GRASS GIS hydrological tools (r.fill.dir, r.watershed, r.water.outlet) in QGIS Processing. It snaps an outfall point to the nearest stream network, extracts streams at high resolution (r.stream.extract), and characterizes subbasins by intersecting them with reprojected and geometry-fixed land cover and soil vector layers. It computes hydrologic parameters including Manning’s n, retardance coefficient, runoff coefficient class, Hydrologic Soil Group (HSG), SCS Curve Number (CN), and area (ha) for each subbasin polygon — outputting three vector layers: Streams (detailed stream network), Basin (delineated watershed boundary), and Subbasins (attribute-rich, clipped, and area-calculated subbasin polygons).

Calculate SCS curve number and lag time. The script computes the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Curve Number (CN) and time of concentration (lag time) for each subbasin by integrating land cover, soil hydrologic group (HSG), and topographic parameters derived from a filled DEM. It first reprojects and fixes geometries of input vector layers (subbasins, land cover, soil type), then performs sequential intersections to spatially associate land cover classes and soil types per subbasin polygon. Using lookup rules, it assigns retardance coefficients, runoff coefficients (e.g., 'AS', 'CN', 'GPF'), HSG values ('A'–'D') based on soil texture, Manning’s n, and CN values per land-cover–HSG combination. It calculates weighted-average CN and n per subbasin using area-weighted aggregation. Then, using WhiteBoxTools, it clips the DEM to each subbasin, computes the longest flow path and average slope along that path, and applies the SCS lag equation: tc = (60 × (L × 3.28084)^0.8 × (1000/CN − 9)^0.7) / (1900 × S^0.5), clamping minimum tc to 5 minutes. Final output is a CSV file ('basin_summary.csv') containing per-subbasin records with ID, area (ha), weighted CN, weighted n, longest flow path (m), average slope (%), and lag time (min).

Delineate catchment basins. The script delineates catchment basins and subbasins from a digital elevation model (DEM) using hydrological terrain analysis. It reprojects the DEM to a specified CRS, fills sinks, computes flow direction and accumulation, extracts stream networks using a minimum contributing area threshold, vectorizes streams and basin raster outputs, snaps an outfall point to the nearest stream, derives the upstream contributing basin from that outfall using r.water.outlet, clips subbasins to the main basin boundary, and generates refined stream vectors within the delineated basin. Outputs include: (1) a vector layer of the full catchment basin, (2) a clipped vector layer of subbasins within that basin, and (3) a detailed stream network vector layer confined to the basin extent.

Extract slope-derived road candidate points. The script processes a precomputed slope raster (in degrees) to generate point shapefiles stratified by slope ranges (0–24°, 24–32°, 32–40°, 40–45°, and 0–45°), then excludes points within a 10-meter buffer of existing streams to produce a final shapefile of potential road alignment points ('GENERATED ROAD POINTS.shp') suitable for civil infrastructure planning.

Generate 3D arc geometry. The script generates a 3D polyline (LineStringZ) representing an arc derived from input 2D line geometries. It computes a circular arc approximation using the start/end points to estimate radius, buffers a point to create a circle polygon, applies sequential 3D affine transformations (rotation around y/z axes, z-axis scaling, and translation), aligns the result to the original geometry's centroid and bearing, and appends the resulting 3D geometry to a new memory layer with matching attributes. Input parameters control segmentation count, y-axis rotation angle (degrees), and vertical scaling factor.

Identify dangle line endpoints. The script identifies dangles (unconnected line endpoints) in an input vector line layer using QGIS's 'Identify Dangles' algorithm. It then spatially evaluates each dangle point against user-selected vector layers (points, lines, or polygons) by generating small buffers (0.000001 decimal degrees) around non-polygon layers and merging all candidate overlap layers. Using intersection and extract-by-location operations, it classifies dangles into two outputs: (1) 'DANGLES_Overlapping' — dangle points that intersect/overlap with any of the selected layers (with attribute 'layer_overlap' populated from the overlapping layer's 'layer' field), and (2) 'DANGLES_Non_Overlap' — dangle points that do not intersect any selected layer. The workflow preserves original dangle geometry (as points) and attributes, and handles mixed geometry types via buffering and spatial indexing for performance.

Extract headwater sources. The script identifies and extracts headwater (spring) locations from a linear stream/river network vector layer. It first identifies dangle vertices (unconnected endpoints) as candidate headwaters, then filters them by length criteria (minimum, maximum, or all), removes false positives near river mouths using a buffer-based spatial exclusion, and outputs two products: (1) Headwater_Lines — line segments representing the upstream-most reaches of headwater streams, attributed with their length ($length); and (2) Headwater_Points — point features at the upstream endpoints of those lines, inheriting original layer attributes plus length. The core logic relies on topological analysis (dangle detection via 'Identify Dangles'), network splitting, and spatial filtering (extract-by-location with NOT_INTERSECTS predicate against river mouth buffer).

Detect pseudo-node topological connectivity. The script identifies pseudo-nodes (line endpoints that are not properly connected to other line vertices) in an input polyline layer, then determines whether each pseudo-node spatially coincides with any vertex from user-selected vector layers (points, lines, or polygons). It outputs two point layers: (1) 'Pseudo-node Non_Overlap' — pseudo-nodes with no topological coincidence to any vertex of the selected layers; and (2) 'Pseudo-node Overlapping' — pseudo-nodes that do coincide with at least one vertex, enriched with a 'Layer_Name' attribute identifying which source layer contributed the coincident vertex. The workflow involves generating pseudo-nodes via a custom 'Continuous_Network_Analysis:Pseudo-node' algorithm, extracting all vertices from selected layers (handling multipoint, polyline, and polygon geometries by densifying to points), building a unified vertex layer with layer attribution, and performing spatial intersection/extract-by-location operations to classify pseudo-nodes based on vertex overlap.

Characterize pockmark depressions. The script characterizes delineated pockmark polygons (submarine or terrestrial depressions) using an input DEM by computing a comprehensive suite of morphometric, geometric, and volumetric attributes. It rasterizes pockmark polygons, fills DEM depressions to compute relative depth (depth below local spill point), calculates zonal statistics (mean, min, max, std dev, range, sum) on slope, absolute elevation, and relative depth rasters; derives Minimum Bounding Geometry (MBG) metrics (width, height, angle); computes shape descriptors (compactness, circularity, convexity, solidity, eccentricity, roughness index, dissection index, profile index, relief-area ratio); estimates pockmark volume in m³ from summed relative depths and pixel area; and optionally extracts pockmark centroids and intra-polygon local minima points (deepest points) via minimum filtering, raster comparison, point extraction, buffering/dissolving, and spatial joining with polygon attributes. Outputs include a fully attributed polygon layer, optional centroid points, and optional local minima points — all enriched with quantitative descriptors for geomorphic analysis.

Burn drainage into DEM. The script burns vector-based drainage features (e.g., rivers, canals, ditches) into a digital elevation model (DEM) by lowering elevation values along buffered drainage corridors using a two-stage vertical drop: a gradual (smooth) drop over a user-defined buffer distance, followed by an additional sharp drop directly on the drainage centerline. It rasterizes and aligns vector drainage layers to the DEM’s CRS and resolution, converts both DEM and drainage rasters to PCRaster format, applies PCRaster’s burndem operator with custom parameters (buffer size, smooth drop depth, sharp drop depth), and outputs a modified DEM raster where drainage networks are topographically enforced — critical for hydrological modeling accuracy.

Delineate stream network and catchment. The script delineates a stream network and its corresponding upstream catchment boundary for a user-defined outlet point within a specified study extent. It downloads a DEM from OpenTopography (e.g., SRTM or Copernicus), reprojects and converts it to PCRaster format, computes flow direction (LDD) using lddcreate, derives Strahler stream order, thresholds streams by order (e.g., ≥5), snaps the user-provided outlet point to the nearest stream cell within a tolerance buffer using flow accumulation maxima, computes the contributing catchment with catchment(), and outputs vectorized streams (as polylines) and a polygonized catchment boundary — all in the user-specified CRS.

Trim and extend fracture networks. The script performs topological editing of line vector layers representing fracture or lineament networks. It identifies and removes short isolated fractures (I-I branches), trims dangling line ends (I-C branches) within a user-defined distance, and extends dangling ends to intersect nearby lines within another user-defined distance. The workflow includes splitting lines at intersections, building a node degree graph to classify endpoints (isolated vs. connected), spatial indexing for efficient nearest-neighbor queries, geometry extension using QgsGeometry.extendLine(), intersection detection, and final line reconstruction. Outputs are a cleaned, topologically improved line vector layer with preserved attributes. No satellite imagery, temporal data, or raster processing is involved — this is a pure vector GIS topology repair tool operating on user-provided line features. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial data sources are not specified in the code.

Digitise fracture network. The script digitises a fracture network from a user-provided binary raster input by applying morphological skeletonization (either 'lee' thinning or medial axis transform), vectorizing the skeleton into linestrings, simplifying geometries using Douglas-Peucker if specified, splitting lines at intersections to ensure topological consistency, and pruning short isolated branches below a user-defined length threshold. The output is a topologically cleaned line vector layer representing fracture traces with x-node (crossing) intersections resolved into four-segment junctions. The script requires pre-processed binary input — no satellite data processing, thresholding, or temporal analysis is performed within this code; it operates purely on an existing raster layer supplied by the user.

Repair fracture network topology. The script repairs common topological errors in digitized fracture (e.g., fault or joint) networks. It merges V-shaped nodes (two-line endpoints meeting at a vertex), extends lines at sharp-angle vertices using a user-defined angle threshold and distance, optionally creates X-nodes (four-way intersections) at such vertices, removes closed loops/circles, and fixes multiple intersections (>4 line endpoints coincident at one location) by iteratively removing the shortest segment(s) associated with the smallest grouped fracture length (using 'Fault No' attribute if present). Input is a vector line layer; outputs are a repaired line layer and optionally an intermediate layer showing multiple-intersection repair steps. No satellite, image, or temporal data is involved — it is a pure vector topology correction tool for GIS digitization workflows.

Generate parallel line grid for fracture sampling. The script generates a vector layer of equally spaced, parallel line segments oriented at a user-specified rotation angle, clipped to the spatial extent of an input fracture network (linestring) or interpretation boundary (polygon). It computes the bearing of each line segment and retains only those aligned (within rounding tolerance) to the specified rotation. Output is a linestring feature class with integer 'Sample_No_' attribute, intended for geological fracture network sampling. No remote sensing data, time-series, or raster processing is involved — it is purely vector-based geometric construction and clipping using QGIS Processing algorithms ('qgis:creategrid' and 'native:rotatefeatures'). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensors are not specified.

Extract fracture network branches and nodes. The script extracts topological elements (branches and nodes) from a user-provided vector-based fracture network (linestring) within a specified sample area polygon (or contour grid), optionally constrained by an interpretation boundary polygon. It classifies node types (I, Y, X, U for unknown, E for edge, or numeric error codes) and branch connection types (e.g., 'I - I', 'I - Y', 'X - X') based on intersection degree and spatial containment. Outputs are two vector layers: (1) a line layer ('Branches') with attributes including 'Class' (node-pair topology), 'Connection', 'Weight', 'Sample_No_', and 'Length'; and (2) a point layer ('Nodes') with 'Class' and 'Sample_No_'. Symbology is applied via external QML files ('branches.qml', 'nodes.qml'). All inputs must share the project's CRS. No remote sensing imagery or time-series analysis is performed — the workflow is purely vector topology processing using QGIS native algorithms (e.g., splitwithlines, intersection, buffer, multiparttosingleparts, centroids). Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified.

Calculate shortest pathway along fracture network. The script computes the shortest geometrical or weighted cost distance pathway from source points (or polyline vertices) to edges in a fracture network vector layer. It builds a NetworkX graph where nodes are rounded coordinate pairs of line endpoints and source points, and edges are fracture segments with weights equal to their Euclidean length (or field-weighted length if a 'Weight Field' is provided). Source points are snapped to the nearest fracture endpoint using spatial indexing and distance minimization. For polyline sources, optional vertex densification is applied before extraction. The output is a line feature sink containing each fracture segment edge annotated with the minimum distance (or weighted distance) from any source point — i.e., the shortest path length to reach that segment from the nearest source. No raster data, time series, or satellite imagery is involved; input is purely vector-based (line and point/polyline layers), and all operations occur within QGIS Processing using native algorithms ('explodelines', 'densifygeometriesgivenaninterval', 'extractvertices') and NetworkX graph analysis. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

Classify hydrographic nodes. The script generates a vector layer of hydrographic nodes (points) derived from stream centerlines (eixo), classifying each node into one of six types based on topological connectivity (number of incident segments) and spatial overlap with auxiliary layers: '1' = upstream start, '2' = downstream end, '3' = confluence (≥3 connections), '4' = pseudo-node (2 connections, no overlap with barriers/waterfalls/wetlands), '5' = flow variation node (2 connections + overlap with waterfall or wetland), '6' = flow regulation node (2 connections + overlap with barrier). The workflow includes Z-aware geometry orientation, vertex extraction (start/end points), deduplication, spatial joining with input layers (barrier, waterfall, wetland), clipping to the working area, and attribute-driven classification using conditional logic on count and presence fields.

Identify road transport nodes. The script creates a vector layer of road transport nodes (‘Nós transporte rodoviário’) by extracting start and end vertices of road segment lines, removing duplicates, counting how many segments meet at each vertex (via spatial join summary), classifying node type based on connection count (1 = ‘fim de via’/dead-end, 2 = ‘pseudo-no’/dangling node, ≥3 = ‘juncao’/junction), and clipping the result to a user-provided polygonal ‘Área de trabalho’. The output is a point layer with attribute ‘valor_tipo_no_trans_rodov’ encoding node type as string values ‘4’, ‘3’, or ‘1’. All operations are purely vector-based; no raster or remote sensing data is used. Input data sources are two local vector layers: a line layer ‘segmentovia’ (road segments) and a polygon layer ‘readetrabalho’ (study area boundary). No time dimension, satellite, sensor, or band information is present.

Export lentic water features. The script exports polygon vector features representing lentic water bodies (e.g., lakes, reservoirs, ponds) from a QGIS input layer into the 'agua_lentica' table of a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART geodatabase). It refactors the input layer by adding standardized fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_agua_lentica' (a categorical code mapped via external lookup), 'cota_plena_armazenamento' (boolean flag cast as string), and 'mare' (boolean flag cast as string), then imports the enriched geometry (3D polygons) into PostGIS with fixed schema ('public.agua_lentica'), using 'geometria' as the geometry column and 'identificador' as primary key. No remote sensing or Earth observation processing occurs — it is a metadata-enriched vector data export workflow.

Export agricultural forested or shrubland area. The script exports a user-provided polygon vector layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'area_agricola_florestal_mato' in the 'public' schema, appending new records. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_areas_agricolas_florestais_matos' (a categorical value selected from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorAreasAgricolasFlorestaisMatos'), e.g., codes like 'A1', 'F2', 'M3'). The input must be a 2D polygon layer; no raster processing, remote sensing, or geospatial analysis is performed — only field refactoring and database insertion. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified — this is a pure vector data export workflow tied to the RECART database.

Export cable transport infrastructure area. The script exports a user-provided 2D polygon vector layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'area_infra_trans_cabo' in the 'public' schema, appending records using an existing configured PostgreSQL connection. It first adds a timestamp field 'inicio_objeto' (set to 'now()') via QGIS 'refactorfields', then imports the modified layer into PostGIS using GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or classification is performed — it is a pure vector data export and database ingestion workflow. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

Export railway transport infrastructure area. The script exports polygon features representing railway transport infrastructure areas from a QGIS vector layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'area_infra_trans_ferrov' in the 'public' schema. It refactors the input layer to include a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') and renames/extracts a user-specified string field (e.g., 'infra_trans_ferrov_id') from the input polygon layer. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or classification is performed — it is a data export and schema alignment workflow. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code; the input is generic and user-provided via QGIS interface.

Export road transport infrastructure area. The script exports polygon features representing areas of road transport infrastructure from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'area_infra_trans_rodov' in the 'public' schema. It refactors the input layer to include a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') and maps a user-specified string field (containing the road infrastructure ID) to a standardized field 'infra_trans_rodov_id'. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed — it is a metadata-preserving vector data export workflow using GDAL's PostGIS import driver. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code; the input is an arbitrary user-provided polygon layer with no embedded spatiotemporal constraints.

Export work area polygon. The script exports a user-provided 2D polygon vector layer as a 'work area' (área de trabalho) into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'area_trabalho') using a preconfigured connection. It appends new records with standardized fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'data' (user-specified date string, e.g., '1900-01-01'), 'nivel_de_detalhe' (enum value 'NdD1' or 'NdD2'), 'nome', 'nome_produtor', and 'nome_proprietario'. No geospatial analysis, classification, remote sensing, or raster operations are performed — it is a metadata-augmented vector data ingestion workflow targeting the RECART geodatabase. Study area, satellite data, sensors, bands, and time-series analysis are not involved.

Export artificialized area polygons. The script exports user-provided polygon vector layers representing 'artificialized areas' to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'areas_artificializadas') using a preconfigured connection. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type datetime) and 'valor_areas_artificializadas' (a categorical value selected from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorAreasArtificializadas'), stored as text). No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed — the script is purely a data export and field-refactoring workflow. Input must be 2D polygon geometry; no study area, time range, satellite data, or spectral operations are involved — all are not specified.

Export barrier infrastructure. The script exports vector features (lines or polygons) representing 'barreira' (barrier) elements from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'barreira' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type datetime) and 'valor_barreira' (a categorical value selected from a predefined enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorBarreira'), stored as text). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject these fields, then 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched features to the target PostGIS table using a preconfigured PostgreSQL connection. No remote sensing, time-series analysis, classification, or geospatial modeling is performed—the task is purely vector data ingestion and attribute enrichment. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

Export electric cable infrastructure. The script exports 2D linear vector features representing electric cables to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART schema), enriching them with standardized attribute values for 'valor_designacao_tensao' (voltage designation) and 'valor_posicao_vertical' (vertical position), while ensuring geometry compliance (2D only, no Z/M) and inserting into the 'cabo_electrico' table with auto-generated 'inicio_objeto' timestamp.

Export water conduit infrastructure. The script exports vector line features representing water conduits (e.g., pipes or channels) from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'conduta_de_agua' within the 'public' schema. It appends new records with standardized attributes: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_conduta_agua' (a categorical value mapped from an enumerated UI parameter, e.g., material or function type), and 'valor_posicao_vertical' (a categorical vertical position value, e.g., 'enterrada', 'aérea'). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject and rename fields, then 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched layer to the target PostGIS table via a preconfigured PostgreSQL connection. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or transformation beyond field injection and database export is performed. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not involved — this is a GIS data publishing utility for infrastructure asset management.

Export polygonal construction features. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing 'Construção poligonal' (polygonal constructions) from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'constru_polig' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_tipo_construcao' (a categorical string value selected via an enum parameter mapped from a predefined code list 'valorTipoConstrucao'). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject these fields, then 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched layer to the target PostGIS table using a preconfigured PostgreSQL connection. No remote sensing, raster, or time-series analysis is performed; it is a vector data ingestion and attribute enrichment workflow for a national cartographic database (RECART). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified.

Export linear construction features. The script exports user-provided 2D line vector features (e.g., roads, pipelines, power lines) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'constru_linear' in the 'public' schema. It adds mandatory metadata fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_construcao_linear' (mapped from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos), 'nome', 'suporte' (boolean), and 'largura' (string). Input geometry is sanitized to 2D (Z/M values dropped), and the output is appended to the target table using GDAL's PostGIS import driver with PROMOTETOMULTI=True and GEOCOLUMN='geometria'. The RECART database connection is provided externally via QGIS PostgreSQL connection manager — no study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are involved.

Export river area polygons. The script exports polygon vector layers representing river areas (curso_de_agua_area) from a QGIS processing input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART schema, public.curso_de_agua_area table). It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'delimitacao_conhecida' (boolean flag as string, e.g., 'False' or 'True'), then imports the refactored polygon layer using GDAL's PostGIS import algorithm. Input must be 3D polygon geometry. No remote sensing, image processing, classification, or temporal analysis is performed — it is a vector data export and metadata augmentation workflow.

Export river axis geometry. The script exports line vector features representing river axes (curso_de_agua_eixo) from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'curso_de_agua_eixo') using a preconfigured connection. It refactors the input line layer by adding or replacing fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_curso_de_agua' (mapped from an enumerated parameter), 'valor_posicao_vertical' (mapped from another enumerated parameter), 'delimitacao_conhecida' (boolean value cast to string), and 'ficticio' (boolean value cast to string). The input layer must be 3D line geometry, as noted in the shortHelpString. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed — it is a metadata-enriched vector data export workflow targeting RECART (a Portuguese topographic database). Study area, time range, satellite data, and imagery are not involved; the script operates solely on user-provided vector features and static lookup values.

Export contour line elevation attributes. The script processes 3D line vector layers representing contour lines, extracts and homogenizes Z (elevation) values per feature using majority Z from vertices, computes 'valor_tipo_curva' (contour type value) either manually via enumeration or automatically based on detail level (NdD1/NdD2) using modular arithmetic on z_majority to classify index/intermediate contours, refactors fields to include timestamp, computed contour type expression, and majority Z, optionally sets uniform Z across all vertices, and exports the resulting layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS table 'curva_de_nivel' in the RECART database schema.

Export local designation points. The script exports point features representing 'designação local' (local designation) from a QGIS vector layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS table named 'designacao_local' in the RECART database. It refactors the input point layer by adding three fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_local_nomeado' (a categorical code mapped from a user-selected enum value via get_lista_codigos('valorLocalNomeado')), and 'nome' (copied from a user-specified string field in the input layer). The geometry is preserved as 2D points. The target schema is 'public', with 'geometria' as the geometry column and 'identificador' as the primary key. No spatial filtering, reprojection, or temporal filtering is applied — the operation is purely attribute-driven ETL. Study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing operations are not involved; this is a GIS vector data publishing workflow.

Export building geometry and attributes. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing buildings to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'edificio' in the 'public' schema. It adds standardized metadata fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_elemento_edificio_xy' (categorical XY planimetric attribute code, e.g., 'Edifício' or 'Edifício em ruínas'), 'valor_elemento_edificio_z' (categorical Z vertical attribute code, e.g., 'Edifício com altura conhecida'), and 'altura_edificio' (numeric height value). The input layer must be 2D point or polygon; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing occurs. All parameters are user-provided via QGIS Processing interface; no hardcoded study area, time range, or remote sensing data is present.

Export petroleum gas chemical element. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing 'Elemento associado de petróleo, gás e substâncias químicas' (associated elements of petroleum, gas, and chemical substances) from a QGIS input layer into the PostgreSQL/PostGIS database RECART, under the table 'elem_assoc_pgq'. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_elemento_associado_pgq' (a categorical value selected via enum from a predefined code list). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject metadata fields and 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched layer to the target PostGIS table. No remote sensing data, image processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — it is a metadata-enriched vector data export task targeting an infrastructure-related thematic table in a national cartographic database (RECART). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified.

Export telecommunications infrastructure elements. The script exports point features representing 'Elemento associado de telecomunicações' (telecommunications-associated infrastructure elements) from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'elem_assoc_telecomunicacoes' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type datetime) and 'valor_elemento_associado_telecomunicacoes' (a categorical string value selected from a predefined enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorElementoAssociadoTelecomunicacoes')). The input must be a 2D point vector layer; no geoprocessing (e.g., reprojection, clipping, filtering) is performed beyond field refactoring and direct database insertion using GDAL's PostGIS import algorithm. The target database connection is preconfigured in QGIS as a PostgreSQL provider connection — no credentials or host details are exposed in the script. Study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing operations are absent; this is a pure vector data export workflow for national cartographic infrastructure (RECART).

Export water-associated infrastructure element. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing 'water-associated infrastructure elements' (e.g., valves, hydrants, manholes, etc.) from a QGIS input layer into the RECART PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table 'elem_assoc_agua'. It adds two mandatory fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_elemento_associado_agua' (a categorical code mapped from an enumerated UI parameter using external lookup via get_lista_codigos('valorElementoAssociadoAgua')). It enforces 2D geometry by dropping Z/M values, refactors schema, and imports into PostGIS with geometry type–aware configuration (GTYPE=3 for points, GTYPE=5 for polygons), appending to existing data in the 'public.elem_assoc_agua' table. No remote sensing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — this is a GIS data ingestion and metadata enrichment workflow targeting a national Portuguese cartographic database (RECART).

Export electricity-associated element. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing electricity-associated elements to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'elem_assoc_eletricidade' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_elemento_associado_electricidade' (a categorical code selected from a predefined list via QgsProcessingParameterEnum). Input geometry is sanitized to 2D (Z/M values dropped), and the export respects geometry type (points → POINT, polygons → POLYGON, with PROMOTETOMULTI enabled). The target database connection is user-selected via a preconfigured PostgreSQL provider connection. No remote sensing, classification, or temporal analysis is performed — this is a metadata-enriched vector data ingestion workflow.

Export land-water boundary. The script exports a vector line layer representing the land-water boundary (fronteira terra-água) into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'fronteira_terra_agua') using an existing QGIS PostgreSQL connection. It refactors the input line layer by adding three fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'data_fonte_dados' (user-provided date string, default '1900-01-01'), and 'ilha' (boolean flag indicating island context, stored as integer 0/1). The input must be a 3D line vector layer. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or classification is performed — it is a metadata-augmented database export workflow. Study area, satellite data, imagery, bands, classification, or time-based filtering are not involved; the only temporal element is a static user-provided date string used as an attribute value, not a temporal filter.

Export aerial transport infrastructure. The script exports point features representing aerial transport infrastructure (e.g., airports, heliports) from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'infra_trans_aereo' in the 'public' schema. It appends new records with standardized attributes: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_categoria_infra_trans_aereo' (e.g., 'aeródromo', 'heliporto'), and 'valor_tipo_infra_trans_aereo' (e.g., 'civil', 'militar', 'mistos'), sourced from enumerated domain lists via external utility function 'get_lista_codigos'. The input layer must be 2D points; no geoprocessing (e.g., reprojection, buffering, classification) is performed — only field refactoring and database insertion using GDAL's PostGIS import. Study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing operations are absent; this is a pure vector data ingestion workflow for a national cartographic database (RECART).

Export road transport infrastructure. The script exports point vector features representing road transport infrastructure to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'infra_trans_rodov') using a preconfigured connection. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_tipo_infra_trans_rodov' (a categorical string value selected from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoInfraTransRodov')). Input must be a 2D point layer. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing is performed — it is a metadata-augmented vector data export workflow.

Export navigable waterway transport infrastructure. The script exports point features representing navigable waterway transport infrastructure to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'infra_trans_via_navegavel') using a preconfigured connection. It adds three fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime), 'valor_tipo_infra_trans_via_navegavel' (categorical value mapped from a user-selected enum via get_lista_codigos), and 'nome' (user-provided string). Input must be a 2D point vector layer. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing is performed — it is a metadata-augmented vector data export workflow.

Export breakline geometry. The script exports 3D line vector features (breaklines) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'linha_de_quebra' in the 'public' schema. It adds three attributes: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_classifica' (a user-selected classification code from a predefined list), and 'valor_natureza_linha' (a user-selected line nature code from another predefined list). Input must be a 3D line vector layer; no raster, satellite, or image processing is performed. The workflow consists of two QGIS Processing steps: (1) refactoring fields to inject static values and timestamp, and (2) appending the result to an existing PostGIS connection. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis is involved — it is a metadata-augmented vector export tool.

Export margin polygon layer. The script exports a user-provided vector polygon layer representing 'Margem' (margin, likely hydrographic margin such as riverbank or shoreline) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'margem' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_tipo_margem' (a categorical value selected from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoMargem'), e.g., 'natural', 'artificial', etc.). The workflow consists of refactoring the input layer to inject these fields, then appending the result to the target PostGIS table using GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. No remote sensing data, image processing, classification, or temporal analysis is performed — it is a GIS data export and metadata enrichment workflow targeting the RECART geodatabase. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and spatial extent are not specified in the code.

Export urban furniture and signage. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) representing urban furniture and signage to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'mob_urbano_sinal' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_tipo_de_mob_urbano_sinal' (a categorical string value mapped from a user-selected enum, e.g., 'placa_indicativa', 'banco', etc., sourced from a lookup list 'valorTipoMobUrbSinal'). The input layer is refactored and appended to the target table using GDAL's PostGIS import algorithm. No spatial filtering, reprojection, or geometry transformation is applied beyond what is implicit in the GDAL driver settings (e.g., 'GTYPE': 0 → unknown geometry type handling). The study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and classification methods are not involved — this is a pure vector data export workflow with metadata enrichment.

Export spring point features. The script exports point features representing springs ('nascente') from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'nascente' in the 'public' schema. It first adds a timestamp field 'inicio_objeto' with the current datetime using 'qgis:refactorfields', then imports the modified layer into PostGIS via 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. The input layer must be 3D point geometry, and the target database connection is selected from pre-configured PostgreSQL connections in QGIS. No remote sensing, image processing, or spatial analysis is performed—the workflow is purely vector data export and schema enrichment.

Export road transport node. The script exports point features representing road transport nodes (e.g., intersections, terminals, or access points) from a QGIS vector layer to the 'no_trans_rodov' table in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART schema). It adds a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') and populates the 'valor_tipo_no_trans_rodov' field either with a user-selected enumerated value (mapped via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoNoTransRodov')) or dynamically using the content of a user-specified string field from the input layer. The workflow consists of two key steps: (1) refactoring the input point layer to add/replace fields using 'qgis:refactorfields', and (2) appending the result to the target PostGIS table 'public.no_trans_rodov' via GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. Input must be a 3D point vector layer; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing is involved. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

Export pipeline infrastructure data. The script exports vector line features representing oil pipelines, gas pipelines, or chemical substance transport infrastructure from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART) using predefined categorical attribute values. It adds two mandatory attributes—'valor_gasoduto_oleoduto_sub_quimicas' and 'valor_posicao_vertical'—mapped from user-selected enumeration options (retrieved via external utility 'get_lista_codigos'), and timestamps the record with 'inicio_objeto' = current time. The output is a persisted table 'oleoduto_gasoduto_subtancias_quimicas' in the 'public' schema of the target PostgreSQL connection. No remote sensing, image processing, or geospatial analysis is performed—the workflow is purely vector data ETL (Extract-Transform-Load) with field refactoring and PostGIS insertion. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

Export point of interest. The script exports vector features (points or polygons) from a QGIS input layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'ponto_interesse' in the 'public' schema, adding two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_tipo_ponto_interesse' (a categorical value selected from a predefined enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoPontoInteresse')). It uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' and 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. The target database connection is user-selected via a configured PostgreSQL provider connection. No remote sensing, image processing, or geospatial analysis is performed — only vector field augmentation and database export. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not involved or specified in the code.

Export 3D point elevation data. The script exports 3D point vector features (with Z/elevation values) from a QGIS input layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS table named 'ponto_cotado' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_classifica_las' (a user-selected LAS classification code from a predefined list, e.g., ground, vegetation, building). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms: 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject metadata fields, then 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched 3D points to the RECART database. Input must be a 3D point layer; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing occurs. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

Export waterfall point data. The script exports a vector point layer representing waterfall features ('queda_de_agua') from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'queda_de_agua'), using an existing configured connection. It first adds a timestamp field 'inicio_objeto' with the current time via 'qgis:refactorfields', then imports the modified layer into PostGIS using 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. The input layer must be 3D point geometry, and the target database is named 'RECART' per the parameter label and help text. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing occurs — it is purely a data export and schema enrichment workflow.

Export railway segment attributes.
