The script exports a user-provided vector line layer (representing railway segments) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'seg_via_ferrea' in the 'public' schema, enriching it with standardized categorical attribute values selected via QGIS Processing enum parameters (e.g., bitola category, line status, vertical position, line type, track type) and a boolean 'eletrific' flag. It adds a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') with current time and maps input geometry unchanged. The input must be 3D line geometry. No remote sensing or Earth observation data is used; all inputs are local vector layers and user-selected categorical codes sourced from an external utility function 'get_lista_codigos', implying lookup tables stored outside the script (e.g., RECART domain value lists). The target database connection is preconfigured in QGIS as a PostgreSQL provider connection.

Export road segment attributes. The script exports vector line features representing road segments to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'seg_via_rodov') using a preconfigured connection. It refactors the input line layer by injecting standardized attribute values—derived from QGIS enum parameters mapping to controlled vocabularies (e.g., 'valorEstadoViaRodov', 'valorSentido')—along with computed fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'num_vias_transito' (user-provided integer), and 'pavimentado' (boolean). The input layer must be 3D line geometry. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing is performed; the workflow is purely data structuring and database ingestion. Study area, time range, satellite data, and imagery processing are not involved—this is a GIS data publishing tool for the RECART national cartographic database.

Export geodetic signal points. The script exports point features representing geodetic signals (e.g., survey markers, benchmarks) from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'sinal_geodesico' in the 'public' schema. It appends standardized attribute values — 'valor_local_geodesico', 'valor_ordem', 'valor_tipo_sinal_geodesico', and 'data_revisao' — derived from user-selected enumerations and a string input, along with a timestamp ('inicio_objeto') set to 'now()'. The input layer must be 3D point geometry, and the export relies on an existing PostgreSQL connection configured in QGIS. No remote sensing or Earth observation data is used; all operations are vector-based attribute assignment and database ingestion.

Export wetland polygons. The script exports user-provided polygon vector layers representing wetlands to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART) with standardized attribute fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_zona_humida' (a categorical code mapped from an enumerated UI parameter), and 'mare' (a boolean flag). It performs field refactoring using QGIS's 'refactorfields' algorithm, then appends the result to the 'zona_humida' table in the 'public' schema. The input layer must be a 3D polygon vector layer; no remote sensing or raster processing is performed. All operations are vector-based and database-oriented. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified — the script is purely a metadata-enriched vector export workflow for a national cartographic database (RECART, Portugal).

Adapt species occurrence coordinates. The script processes point-based species occurrence records by clipping them to a user-defined influence boundary polygon, removing specified attribute fields (e.g., species name columns), and appending X/Y coordinate fields in the project CRS — producing a cleaned, Maxent-compatible CSV-ready point layer with geographic coordinates explicitly as attributes.

Setup TUFLOW hydrodynamic project. The script sets up a TUFLOW Catch (hydrodynamic) modeling project by generating folder structures, initializing configuration files (e.g., tfsettings.json), creating domain check GIS layers, generating empty model input files (e.g., .mif, .asc, .csv), and populating control file templates (e.g., .tcf). It dynamically loads existing project settings from 'tfsettings.json' when a project folder is selected, auto-fills executable paths, CRS, GIS format, and output format configurations, and optionally applies QGIS styling to domain check layers using a predefined QML file.

Generate LiDAR-derived terrain and density rasters. The script processes airborne LiDAR point cloud data (LAS/LAZ format) to generate four core raster products: (1) a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN)-based digital elevation model (DEM), (2) an Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)-interpolated surface, (3) ground point density (GPD) raster, and (4) low vegetation density (LVD) raster. It first optionally classifies unclassified input point clouds using LAStools, converts LAZ to LAS if needed, then applies WhiteboxTools algorithms (LidarTINGridding, LidarIdwInterpolation, LidarPointDensity with class exclusions) to compute surfaces and densities at a user-defined cell size. All outputs are resampled to the target resolution and reprojected to the specified CRS before being loaded into QGIS as named layers (e.g., 'TLI', 'IDW', 'Ground Point Density').

Generate archaeological terrain visualisations. The script takes a digital feature model (DFM) or DEM as input and generates five archaeologically significant terrain visualisations: Sky-View Factor (SVF), Visual Assessment Technique (VAT) via RVT Blender, Openness (OPN), Difference-from-Mean Elevation (DfME), and Hillshade (HS). Each output is saved as a temporary GeoTIFF, styled where applicable (e.g., DfME uses a predefined QML style), and loaded into the QGIS project with a user-defined prefix. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms interfacing with Relief Visualization Toolbox (RVT) and WhiteboxTools (wbt:DiffFromMeanElev), along with native QGIS hillshading.

Validate cartographic grid alignment. The script validates the geometric and attribute correctness of a user-provided cartographic grid (line layer) and grid numbering points (point layer) against a reference grid generated from a frame polygon and selected map scale (e.g., 1:5,000–1:250,000). It computes grid errors via symmetrical difference between reference and input grids, and identifies three types of point errors — missing points (present in reference but absent in input), incorrect points (mismatched 'numero' or 'direcao' attributes within tolerance), and extra points (present in input but not matched to any reference point within tolerance). Outputs are two error layers: a line layer of grid discrepancies labeled 'erro_grid', and a point layer of validation failures labeled 'ponto_faltante', 'ponto_incorreto', or 'ponto_extra', each retaining relevant attributes ('numero', 'direcao').

Calculate water table depth. The script calculates the depth to the water table (i.e., vertical distance from ground surface to groundwater level) by subtracting a water table elevation raster from a digital terrain model (DTM) raster. It performs spatial alignment (clipping and resampling to common extent, CRS, and cell size), raster arithmetic using QgsRasterCalculator, and outputs the result as an ASCII (.asc) grid with user-specified precision. Input rasters must be co-registered or are reprojected/clipped via GDAL translate; the output is a continuous-depth raster where positive values indicate depth below surface (e.g., 2.5 m), and negative values indicate perched or surface water conditions.

Classify hydrologic soil groups. The script creates a raster map of Hydrologic Soil Groups (HSG) — classified as A (1), B (2), C (3), or D (4) — by integrating soil property data (soil ID, maximum depth, minimum saturated hydraulic conductivity at 0–0.5 m, 0–0.6 m, and 0–1.0 m depths) with spatial rasters: a soil distribution map (thematic), digital elevation model (DEM), and water table elevation map. It first reclassifies the soil map using lookup tables derived from the source table to generate per-pixel max depth and min Ksat rasters; then computes water table depth as elevation minus water table elevation; finally applies the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) HSG classification logic from the National Engineering Handbook (Mockus et al., 2009), which conditions group assignment on combinations of soil depth, water table depth, and hydraulic conductivity thresholds — outputting a single-band integer raster (values 1–4, nodata = -9) in ASCII Grid or GDAL-compatible format.

Rasterize soil table fields. The script rasterizes numeric fields from a tabular dataset (e.g., soil properties) by spatially distributing their values across polygon features in a vector map (e.g., soil units or land parcels), using a reference raster’s georeferencing parameters (origin, cell size, extent). It performs a table-vector join on matching ID fields, then executes GDAL rasterization for each numeric field (excluding string and 'fid' fields), exporting each as an ASCII (.asc) raster file in the specified output folder. The workflow is designed for generating spatially explicit raster layers of agronomic or pedological attributes from IdrAgra database tables.

Rasterize time-series irrigation data. The script converts a vector layer containing polygons with temporal (datetime) and numeric attribute fields into a series of time-stamped raster maps — one per specified year — using GDAL rasterization. It selects features by year (via SQL-like datetime field filtering), writes year-specific subsets to temporary GeoPackage files, then burns the numeric data field values into rasters aligned to a user-defined extent and cell size. Outputs are ASCII (.asc) raster files named with a base name and year suffix (e.g., 'output_2000.asc'), each representing spatially distributed values (e.g., water demand, crop ID, or irrigation volume) for that year.

Calculate watershed curve number. The script calculates the spatially weighted average Curve Number (CN) for a user-defined watershed by intersecting Corine Land Cover (CLC) and soil/geology map layers, assigning SCS hydrologic soil groups (A–D) and land use classes (1–7), then combining them to retrieve CN values from condition-specific lookup tables (unfavorable/mean/favorable). It outputs: (1) a vector layer with per-polygon CN, land cover description, soil group, and basin percentage; (2) clipped Corine and soil layers; and (3) a detailed UTF-8 log file reporting class-wise coverage percentages, CN distribution, weighted mean CN, and urban cover quantification.

Update pipeline flow rates. The script updates flow rate attributes in a vector layer (e.g., pipelines or network segments) by joining and recalculating flow values from a separate flow rate data layer. It applies unit conversions (volume: e.g., L → m³ via user-defined conversion factors; time: day/hour/minute/second → seconds), optionally multiplies by fluid density (retrieved via `get_fluid_parameter` using ambient temperature/pressure and selected fluid), and outputs a new vector layer with updated flow rate values. The workflow includes scenario-based filtering of flow data, field calculation, column deletion, and attribute join — all performed using QGIS native processing algorithms (`extractbyexpression`, `fieldcalculator`, `deletecolumn`, `joinattributestable`).

Compute largest empty circle. The script computes the Largest Empty Circle (LEC) for a given point layer — i.e., the largest possible circle that can be inscribed in the convex hull of the point set without containing any input points in its interior. It first calculates the LEC center and radius using a Voronoi-based geometric algorithm (imported from becagislibrary.voronoi), then adjusts the radius for geographic CRS by converting meters to degrees using Gaussian mean Earth radius approximation, and finally outputs two vector layers: (1) a point feature representing the LEC center (with duplicate geometries removed), and (2) a buffered polygon (circle) centered at that point with radius equal to the LEC radius (64-segment approximation, dissolved).

Calculate distance to waterpoints for cattle GPS tracks. The script processes cattle GPS collar CSV data (latitude/longitude, timestamp) to compute distance-to-water (DTW) for each point within a specified paddock boundary. It first clips the GPS points to a 100-m buffer around the paddock polygon, then calculates the shortest Euclidean distance from each point to the nearest waterpoint (e.g., bores, dams, waterholes) within that paddock. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage (.gpkg) with original attributes plus 'q_datetime' (QDateTime), 'Date' (date-only), and 'dist_to_water_m' fields; (2) an Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx) exporting the DTW GeoPackage; and (3) daily movement statistics (distance traveled, speed, time spent near water) saved as both a tracks GeoPackage and Excel file.

Calculate distance to water points. The script processes GPS collar CSV data (e.g., No4_1168_20240715_132300.csv) to compute point-to-water distances for animal movement analysis within a defined paddock. It clips the GPS points to a buffered paddock boundary ('No_4_plus_100'), adds a QDateTime field from the 'Time' column, appends a Date field for Excel compatibility, computes Euclidean distance from each GPS point to all clipped waterpoints (from 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes' layer) in EPSG:9473 (GDA2020 MGA Zone 53), saves results as a GeoPackage (.gpkg), exports it to Excel (.xlsx), and further derives daily movement statistics (track length, displacement, etc.) with paddock name and collar ID metadata.

Rasterize XYZ bathymetry data. The script converts one or more plain-text XYZ files (containing Easting, Northing, and Depth/Elevation values) into georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layers. For each input file, it auto-detects or applies a user-specified grid resolution, preserves original Z values in direct rasterization mode, or fills gaps via IDW interpolation, outputs rasters with Float32 precision and optional LZW compression, and adds them to the QGIS project. It uses a robust VRT+GDAL bridge for reliable coordinate-aware rasterization and handles multiple files individually with per-file parameter optimization.

Model forest road wood flux. The script models the flow of harvested timber through a forest road network by generating wood-source points inside harvest polygons, assigning wood volume to the nearest road segments, and propagating flux downstream toward designated ending points (e.g., main road connections). It computes per-segment wood flux values, resolves network topology via k-d tree–accelerated spatial adjacency detection, infers directional flow using Dijkstra-based least-cost path search from line endpoints to user-provided termination points, and outputs a line vector layer with attributes: segment ID, total wood flux (volume or density-derived), upstream neighbor IDs, and downstream neighbor IDs. The algorithm enforces topological consistency by processing segments only after all upstream contributors have been resolved, preventing cycles and ensuring mass conservation in directed acyclic network traversal.

Retract line endpoints. The script retracts (shortens) the start and end segments of input line features by specified distances. It computes vertex offsets between original and extended lines, then calculates new first and last vertex coordinates to produce a modified line geometry where the start and end portions are removed—effectively 'retracting' the line inward along its direction. The output is a vector line layer with retracted geometries, supporting only single-part (non-multi-part) lines.

Download GeoDanmark infrastructure data. The script downloads and unpacks official Danish geospatial vector datasets from the Dataførderen API (GeoDanmark) for a user-specified entity (e.g., 'Vejmidte', 'Bygning', 'Jernbane') and temporal variant ('current', 'bitemporal', or 'temporal'), returning a QGIS feature layer (vector) in GeoPackage format. It performs HTTP GET authentication using username/password, downloads a zipped GeoPackage, unzips it via a custom 'Unzipper' script, and outputs the first extracted layer after applying a trivial filter ('1=1') to ensure valid feature sink handling.

Download cadastral parcel data. The script downloads and processes cadastral vector data from the Danish Datafordeler API, specifically targeting one of 20 predefined cadastral entity types (e.g., 'Jordstykke', 'Matrikelskel', 'BygningPaaFremmedGrundFlade') in either current, bitemporal, or temporal version. It performs an HTTP GET request to retrieve a GeoPackage (.gpkg) file, unzips it (via a custom 'Unzipper' script), and extracts all features (using expression '1=1') into a QGIS feature sink. The output is a vector layer containing the full geometry and attributes of the selected entity — no spatial subsetting, temporal filtering, or attribute transformation is applied. Study area is Denmark (inferred from 'datafordeler.dk', 'Matriklen', and entity names like 'Ejerlav', 'Sogn', 'Kommune'); time range is determined by the 'type' parameter ('current', 'bitemporal', 'temporal') but no explicit dates are hardcoded; data source is the Danish national cadastre (Matriklen2), delivered via REST API; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — this is authoritative vector cadastral data.

Match raster geotransform to reference grid. The script performs a two-step GDAL-based geospatial raster alignment: (1) clips the input 'modify' raster to the exact extent of the 'matchto' raster using gdal:translate with -projwin, and (2) resizes and overwrites the geotransform of the clipped raster to precisely match the pixel size, origin, rotation, and dimensions of the 'matchto' ASCII raster using -a_gt and -outsize. Outputs a new .asc file with identical spatial metadata (origin, resolution, extent, size) as the reference raster, enabling direct pixel-wise comparison or integration in fire modeling workflows requiring consistent AII (Area of Interest Index) grids.

Aggregate plancap-derived exfiltration per drainage area. The script spatially links plancaps (planning capacity units) and other point-based infrastructure datasets (VEs, BAG verblijfsobjecten, drinkwater connections) to drainage areas (bemalingsgebieden) using geometric intersection and spatial joins. It computes summary statistics—including counts and sums of exfiltration values (ExAFW_2124, ExAFW_2529, etc.) per BEM_ID—by first intersecting plancaps with drainage polygons, filtering for largest-area plancaps per drainage area (to resolve one-to-many), aggregating exfiltration by BEM_ID, and then joining these results with statistical summaries from VEs, VBOs, and drinkwater points. Outputs include: (1) ExAFW_per_bem_id — aggregated exfiltration and concatenated PC_IDs per drainage area; (2) Meerdere_plancaps_in_bemalingsgebied — drainage areas containing ≥2 plancaps; (3) Plancap_in_meerdere_bemalingsgebieden — plancaps overlapping ≥2 drainage areas; (4) PLANCAP_PC_ID — plancaps with auto-generated PC_ID field; (5) Bemalingsgebieden_joined_stats — final joined layer with all infrastructure statistics (VE counts/sums, VBO counts, drinkwater counts/sums, and plancap exfiltration); plus auxiliary stats layers for each source.

Convert kikker network to GeoDyn input. The script converts municipal sewer infrastructure data (kikker punten/lijnen) into GeoDyn-compatible input layers by spatially joining point features (e.g., manholes, pumps) and line features (e.g., pipes, channels) to drainage catchments (bemalingsgebieden), assigning standardized BEM_ID identifiers, retaining only required hydrological and infrastructural attributes (e.g., BERGING_M3, NUMMER, VAN_KNOOPN, NAAR_KNOOP, TTOTAAL_M3), and outputting three cleaned, attribute-joined layers: (1) polygon catchments with BEM_ID, (2) point features enriched with BEM_ID_SP and original kikker attributes, and (3) line features joined with BERGING_M3 and structural identifiers — all structured for direct ingestion into the GeoDyn hydraulic modeling suite.

Model coastal inundation extent. The script models incremental coastal inundation extents under rising sea levels by performing raster-based elevation thresholding (using a DTM), followed by cost-distance accumulation from a shoreline vector line to simulate overland flow paths across low-lying terrain. For each sea level increment (e.g., 2.1 m → 2.3 m), it generates: (1) a binary inundation mask (1 = below/equal to sea level, else NoData), (2) a distance accumulation raster measuring shortest path cost (in cells) from the densified shoreline to each inundated cell, (3) a final inundation raster where values represent the sea level elevation (in cm) assigned only to cells reachable within the cost distance, and (4) a vector polygon layer (GeoPackage) of the inundated area. Temporary rasters are cleaned up after each iteration.

Hydrologically condition DTM with burned streamlines. The script hydrologically conditions a digital terrain model (DTM) by burning linear hydrological adaptation features (e.g., streams, canals, or drainage lines) into it. It achieves this by: (1) dissolving input vector polylines; (2) extracting start/end vertices and sampling their Z-values from the DTM; (3) assigning linearly interpolated Z-values along each line segment based on distance from the start point and slope (ΔZ/length); (4) rasterizing the interpolated points; and (5) replacing original DTM pixel values with the interpolated Z-values where burn-in occurs, producing a hydrologically corrected DTM raster (e.g., 'DTM_with_hydro_adaptations.tif'). The output is a seamless, depression-free, flow-enforced elevation model suitable for hydrological modeling.

Burn building footprints into DTM. The script burns building footprint polygons into a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) raster by assigning a uniform elevation value (e.g., 20 m) to each building polygon, rasterizing the buildings to match the DTM’s resolution and extent, filling NoData cells with 0, and then summing the building-raster layer with the original DTM to produce an updated DTM where buildings are elevated as impermeable barriers — resulting in a modified terrain model (DHyM_with_buildings.tif) suitable for hydrological modeling requiring explicit representation of built infrastructure.

Burn buildings onto DTM. The script burns building footprints (as vector polygons) onto a digital terrain model (DTM) or digital height model (DHyM) by rasterizing building polygons with a user-specified height value, filling NoData cells with zero, and summing the resulting building-height raster with the input DTM to produce an augmented surface model where buildings are elevated above ground level. Inputs are a local DTM raster file (path provided), a vector layer of building polygons (OGR-readable, e.g., Shapefile or GeoPackage), and a scalar height value (e.g., 20.0 m). The workflow includes: (1) adding an 'elevation' attribute field to the building layer and populating it uniformly with the height value; (2) rasterizing the building layer using GDAL's rasterize algorithm aligned to the DTM’s extent, resolution, and CRS; (3) replacing NoData values in the rasterized output with 0 using QGIS's Fill NoData tool; (4) summing the processed building raster and the original DTM via raster calculator. Outputs are three geotiff files in the specified output folder: 'Building_raster.tif', 'Building_raster_NONull.tif', and 'DHyM_with_buildings.tif'. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial identifiers are referenced — all inputs are local file paths provided at runtime. The script operates entirely within QGIS Processing Framework using GDAL and native QGIS algorithms, with no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls or cloud-based assets.

Extract tent structures. The script identifies tent-like structures (e.g., IDP camp shelters) in RGB satellite imagery by computing two spectral indices — F1 (green/red/blue ratio-based edge contrast) and F3 (green minus min(red,blue), thresholded to zero) — normalizing them using linear fuzzy membership, applying Otsu thresholding and segmentation, intersecting the resulting binary built-up masks, masking out bare soil areas (derived from Soil Brightness Index sampled from user-provided bare-ground points), performing morphological opening to refine tent-shaped objects, and finally polygonizing and filtering for DN=1 to output a vector layer of tented structures. The workflow is explicitly designed for rapid identification of temporary shelters in humanitarian response contexts, with post-processing guidance for rectanglify and manual cleaning.

Extract pavement edge vertices. The script processes a vector layer named 'PAVEMENT_EDGE' to generate a coarse grid (2500 m spacing) over a fixed coordinate range in EPSG:2263 (NAD83 / NY Long Island), intersects the pavement edges with each grid cell, extracts all geometry vertices from the intersection result, and exports the vertex coordinates (as X,Y) to individual CSV files named '<i>_<j>.csv'. The grid is hardcoded to cover a region starting at (910000, 115000) with row/column indices i∈[0,4] and j∈[0,9], but the y-range calculation erroneously reuses 'i' instead of 'j', indicating an intent to tile a rectangular AOI — likely NYC metro area given EPSG:2263 and coordinate magnitudes. Output is a set of point-coordinate CSVs for downstream pavement geometry analysis or digitization QA.

Assess autobahn impact on valuable habitats. The script performs a spatial impact assessment of an autobahn infrastructure project on ecologically valuable habitats in Switzerland. It loads vector layers for environment (habitat classification with attributes 'ffh_typ_nr', 'geschuetzt_biotop', 'bedeutend_gruenland_typ') and autobahn linear infrastructure; creates nested buffers (20 m, 100 m, 300 m) to model physical footprint and broader ecological disturbance zones; unions these buffers into cumulative impact areas; intersects them with the environment layer to isolate affected habitat polygons; subsets and intersects valuable vs. non-valuable habitats using attribute queries; applies categorized symbology by habitat type ('ffh_typ_text', 'bfn_biotop_text') for visual differentiation; and overlays a semi-transparent raster basemap. Outputs include styled map layers: 'Impact Area Intersected', 'Valuable Intersected', and 'Non-Valuable Intersected' — enabling spatial quantification and visualization of habitat loss/fragmentation due to road construction.

Analyze autobahn impact on habitats. The script analyzes the spatial impact of Autobahn (highway) construction on terrestrial habitats in a Swiss study area using vector geoprocessing. It loads an Environment layer (containing habitat attributes such as 'ffh_typ_nr', 'geschuetzt_biotop', and 'bedeutend_gruenland_typ') and an Autobahn linear layer from local GeoPackage files. It creates three concentric buffers (20 m, 100 m, and 300 m) around the Autobahn to represent physical footprint and cumulative ecological impact zones, then unions them into a single 'Impact Area'. It intersects this impact zone with the Environment layer to extract 'Impact Area Intersected'. It then subsets valuable habitats (using attribute queries for FFH sites, protected biotopes, and significant grassland types) and non-valuable habitats, intersecting each with the impact area to produce 'Valuable Intersected' and 'Non-Valuable Intersected' layers. Final outputs include categorized symbology by habitat type (e.g., 'ffh_typ_text', 'bfn_biotop_text'), opacity-adjusted visual layers, and layer reordering for cartographic clarity — all within QGIS Desktop. No time-series analysis or remote sensing data is used; inputs are static vector layers. Study area is implied to be in Switzerland (CH) via file path '\svm-c113.hsr.ch\zkang\Desktop\QGIS-Steilkurs_MSE_Maerz_2017\...' and CRS EPSG:31467 (DHDN / Gauss-Krüger zone 3, used in Germany and parts of Switzerland).

Assess autobahn infrastructure impact on environment. The script performs a spatial impact assessment by generating concentric buffer zones (20m, 100m, 300m) around an Autobahn vector layer, unions them to create a cumulative 'Impact Area', and intersects this area with an 'Environment' vector layer to identify spatially overlapping zones — producing a final 'Intersected' vector layer representing environmentally sensitive areas affected by autobahn proximity.

Rasterize species range polygons. The script converts vector-based species range polygons into individual species-specific raster layers, where each raster encodes presence (value 1) for a single species within its geographic range; it first adds a presence field to the input polygon layer, then iterates over unique species values in the Species_Attribute field, exports one shapefile per species, and rasterizes each using GDAL with fixed dimensions (2000×1000 pixels), producing one GeoTIFF per species named after the species (with spaces replaced by underscores) in the specified output directory.

Resample Copernicus vegetation products. The script resamples Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) vegetation biophysical variables (e.g., NDVI, LAI, FAPAR) from native 333 m resolution to a consistent 1 km spatial resolution while preserving the original 1 km time-series spatial extent (−180° to 180° longitude, −60° to 80° latitude). It applies two parallel resampling pathways: (1) 'average' resampling for continuous variables (e.g., NDVI), including scaling and georeferenced cropping; (2) 'mode' resampling on a reclassified version of the input (using user-defined class intervals, e.g., [-1,1,1,1,255,0]) for categorical or integer-coded data. The final output is the pixel-wise multiplication of the average-resampled and mode-resampled rasters — effectively blending continuous-value smoothing with dominant-class preservation — then compressed and exported as a GeoTIFF.

Resample Copernicus vegetation product to 1km. The script resamples high-resolution (333m) Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) vegetation biophysical products (e.g., NDVI, LAI, FAPAR) — originally derived from Sentinel-3 — to a consistent 1 km spatial resolution matching legacy PROBA-V time series. It applies a two-path resampling workflow: (1) an 'average' resampling for continuous variables (preserving radiometric integrity via scaling and offset correction), and (2) a 'mode' resampling for categorical or integer-coded layers (e.g., land cover flags or quality masks); then combines them via raster algebra to produce a final 1 km output with UInt32 encoding, DEFLATE compression, and proper nodata handling. The reclassification step (using user-defined thresholds like [-0.08,0.92,1,0.92,255,0]) converts floating-point reflectance/indices into discrete classes before mode resampling, while the final formula applies offset removal and scaling (e.g., (PVo − (1−offset) − offset) × scaling) to restore integer physical units (e.g., scaled LAI × 250).

Resample Copernicus land cover raster. The script resamples input Copernicus Global Land (CGLS) vegetation-related rasters (e.g., NDVI, FAPAR, LAI) from native 333 m resolution to 1 km resolution while preserving the standard global spatial extent (−180° to +180° longitude, −60° to +80° latitude). It applies two parallel resampling workflows: one using 'average' (for continuous variables) and another using 'mode' (for categorical or discrete classes), followed by pixel-wise multiplication of the two outputs. The final output is a compressed GeoTIFF at 1 km resolution with DEFLATE compression. The script explicitly targets Copernicus GL products distributed via QGIS plugin interface, and references PROBA-V (pre-July 2020) and Sentinel-3 (post-July 2020) as underlying sensors — though no actual GEE data loading occurs in this code, as it operates purely on user-provided local raster layers within QGIS. All geospatial operations (reclassify, translate, clip, raster calculator) are executed via GDAL/QGIS Processing algorithms, not Earth Engine APIs. No time-series processing, cloud masking, or temporal filtering is performed — the script is strictly spatial resampling and reclassification.

Delineate forest stands from canopy height models. The script performs automated forest stand delineation using a 10m-resolution Vegetation Height Model (VHM) as primary input. It applies a hierarchical classification algorithm (run_stand_classification) that segments the VHM into homogeneous height-based stands, incorporating optional coniferous proportion and vegetation zone rasters for stratification. The workflow includes post-processing steps: simplification and elimination of small polygons, merging of geometrically and structurally similar neighboring stands (based on hdom relative difference), clipping to a user-provided perimeter boundary, gap elimination, calculation of dominant height (DG) using a higher-resolution (150 cm) VHM, addition of coniferous proportion attributes, attribution with forest site and vegetation zone codes via spatial join, and final cleanup (field removal, project packaging). Outputs include a GeoPackage vector layer (TBk_Bestandeskarte.gpkg) containing stand polygons with attributes such as DG, coniferous proportion, VegZone_Code, ForestSite, area, perimeter, and geometry; auxiliary files (log, config, tmp layers); and a QGIS project file.

Calculate area-weighted average perimeter. The script computes the Area-weighted Average Perimeter (AwaP) metric for urban blocks intersecting or contained within user-defined boundary polygons. It processes vector layers of urban blocks and boundaries through geometry cleaning (fix geometries, dissolve, multipart-to-singlepart, delete holes), optional dead-end removal via buffer-in/buffer-out morphological filtering, and spatial selection (intersection/within/partial overlap based on user thresholds). For each boundary polygon (or dissolved union), it calculates AwaP = Σ(Perimeter × Area) / Σ(Area) across qualifying blocks, then outputs either: (1) a set of styled block layers annotated with AwaP value per block (when coloring by Area or Perimeter), or (2) a boundary layer where each feature is attributed with its computed AwaP value (when coloring 'by AwaP', i.e., grid-cell-level AwaP mapping). Outputs are emitted as QgsVectorLayer objects with attribute tables containing 'awap_id', 'Area', 'Perimeter', and 'AwaP' fields.

Model reservoir inundation and dam-modified DEM. The script models the construction of a dam on an existing digital elevation model (DEM) by first buffering the dam crest vector layer, computing elevation-dependent fill levels along buffer rings using dam wall slope geometry (1:H), rasterizing those fill levels to create a water-surface elevation surface, then merging it with the original DEM via conditional raster algebra (keeping the higher of DEM or fill level at each cell) to produce a new DEM containing the raised dam structure. Finally, it uses GRASS r.lake to simulate flooding from a user-provided interior point up to a specified water level (dam top minus water depth), generating a raster of the resulting lake extent/depth. Outputs are (1) a new lake raster layer representing flooded area/depth, and (2) a modified DEM raster layer incorporating the engineered dam structure.

Calculate water depth from bathymetric point cloud. The script processes an airborne LiDAR point cloud (COPC format) classified with standard ASPRS classes to derive water depth. It first separates bathymetric points (Class 40) and water surface points (Class 41), then generates a 1 m resolution DTM (from Class 2 + 40) and a 1 m watersurface raster (from Class 2 + 41); computes water depth as the difference (watersurface − DTM); derives 1 m depth contours; calculates point density at 2 m resolution over bathymetric points (Class 2 + 40); masks depth to 0.5–2.5 m range; masks density to ≥20 pts/4 m²; and finally applies a boolean AND to produce a 2 m resolution raster indicating locations where both sufficient density and valid depth co-occur — used for quality control of topobathymetric products.

Convert polygon boundaries to single-part lines. The script converts an input polygon vector layer into a line vector layer where each line segment is a single-part geometry (i.e., no multipart features), assigns a unique integer 'fid' attribute to each line feature, preserves custom styling properties (color, ts_color, gr_color) from the input layer, and applies the original RGB color to the output layer's renderer. It uses QGIS native processing algorithms ('qgis:polygonstolines' and 'qgis:multiparttosingleparts') within a PyQGIS processing algorithm framework.

Widen taxiway buffer. The script widens taxiway centerline vector features by applying a symmetric buffer (half the user-specified distance) in a projected CRS (EPSG:3857), optionally dissolving results and converting polygons to single-part linestrings; it preserves custom layer styling properties (e.g., 'color', 'ts_color') and outputs a reprojected (back to EPSG:4326) vector layer of buffered taxiway polygons or derived linestrings.

Merge RGB and NIR bands. The script merges RGB multispectral imagery with a separately extracted NIR band (Band 1 from NED files) into a single 4-band GeoTIFF (R,G,B,NIR), preserving original data types and using GDAL merge with separate band stacking. Input files are sourced from PNEO4 or PNEO3 satellite captures under the 'IMG_01_PNEO[3/4]_MS-FS' directory structure, with '_RGB_' and '_NED_' naming conventions indicating distinct spectral products; the output replaces '_RGB_' with '_' in the filename and is saved to 'E:\2022 imagenes\'. The workflow handles fallback between PNEO4 and PNEO3 folder paths, skips existing outputs, and relies on QGIS Processing GDAL algorithms ('gdal:translate' to extract Band 1 from NED, then 'gdal:merge' to combine RGB + NIR as separate bands.

Calculate building orientation angle. The script computes the dominant orientation (azimuth) of building polygons by identifying their longest edge, then calculates the azimuth angle of that edge in degrees and radians. It outputs a point layer (centroids of buildings) with added 'angle', 'angle2' (mod 360), and 'radians' attributes; additionally, it generates auxiliary line layers visualizing the longest edge ('longest_edge'), the original azimuth direction ('orig degree'), the mod-360 azimuth direction ('mod degree'), and the 360°-complement direction ('360 degree'). The centroid layer is styled with an arrow QML to visually represent building orientation.

Generate contour stroke geometry. The script generates a 'stroke' geometry layer representing the visual line width of contour lines (elevation polygons) by computing an inner buffer (negative buffer) of selected elevation contours (where elevation % 100 == 0) and subtracting it from the original polygon geometry — effectively creating a polygonal representation of the cartographic stroke for map rendering. Input is a vector layer of contour-derived polygons; output is a clipped, memory-based polygon layer ('stroke_geom_layer') aligned to the extent of the 'rata_rectangle1' raster layer, intended for high-quality thematic mapping of elevation intervals.

Generate cloud- and shadow-corrected NDVI. The script processes Landsat 8 Level 1 TIR data to generate cloud- and terrain-shadow-masked NDVI rasters for the Parque Nacional do Tricântico (PNT) in Brazil. It performs: (1) extraction and clipping of all bands and MTL metadata to the park boundary; (2) cloud masking using BQA band reclassification (via cloud_mask.txt rules); (3) top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiometric correction using reflectance multipliers/additives and solar elevation from MTL; (4) 8-bit scaling and GRIR (Green+Red+IR)/3 compositing for shadow detection; (5) SAGA filter-based shadow enhancement and shadow mask generation (via shadow_GRIR8BITS.txt); (6) application of shadow mask to red (B4) and near-infrared (B5) bands; and (7) final NDVI calculation ((B5−B4)/(B5+B4)) on shadow-free bands. Outputs are per-scene GeoTIFF NDVI rasters (e.g., 'LC08_..._ndvi.TIF') alongside preserved MTL metadata in the 'ndvi' directory.

Extract land cover image chips. The script automatically extracts georeferenced image chips (50 m × 50 m, ~250 px at 20 cm resolution) from high-resolution orthoimagery (ORTHOHR) by intersecting vector-labeled ground truth polygons (e.g., 'classe' attribute) with raster extents, generating a regular grid aligned to the intersection geometry, filtering out incomplete tiles (area < 90% of full tile or non-5-point polygons), splitting by class, and clipping the source orthoimage to each class-specific tile polygon — outputting classified TIFF chips organized in directories by class (e.g., '/outputs/Agriculture/', '/outputs/Forest/', etc.).

Define urban scope and constraints. The script supports urban renewable energy planning by enabling users to manually digitize and save geographic layers as 'scope' (study area boundaries) or 'constraints' (policy/technical restrictions) within QGIS. It identifies the largest existing scope layer to clip new inputs, assigns integer scores (1–4) to constraints based on user selection, saves outputs to structured project directories ('/Scope/', '/Aspects/Policy aspects/', '/Aspects/Technical aspects/'), and writes a 'Score' attribute to clipped vector layers. Outputs include shapefiles for scope boundaries and scored constraint layers, integrated into QGIS layer tree groups ('Scope', 'Policy', 'Technical'). No satellite imagery or automated classification is used — all geospatial operations are vector-based (clipping, attribute editing) and driven by interactive QGIS workflows. The study area is implicitly defined by the user-loaded city shapefile in '/Processing scripts/Shapefile conversion/City/', and no time-series or remote sensing analysis is performed.

Compute weighted risk map. The script computes a spatially explicit, normalized, and weighted overlay risk map by integrating multiple user-provided geospatial risk factor layers (vector or raster) within a defined study area. Each factor is processed through proximity conversion (if vector), min-max normalization to [0,1], optional inversion for inverse-risk correlation ('Lower values = Higher Risk'), and then combined via weighted linear combination. The final output is a clipped raster risk map (0–1 scale) named '{project_name}_RiskMap_Clipped.tif', loaded into the QGIS project.

Compute weighted risk overlay map. The script computes a spatially explicit, normalized, and weighted risk map by integrating user-provided risk factor layers (vector or raster) within a defined study area. Each factor is processed through proximity analysis (if vector), normalization to [0,1], optional inversion for inverse correlation ('Lower values = Higher Risk'), and then combined via weighted linear combination. The final output is a clipped raster risk map (GeoTIFF) named '{project_name}_RiskMap_Clipped.tif', loaded into the QGIS project. No specific study area name, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are referenced in the code — all inputs are provided at runtime as QGIS layers (QgsVectorLayer or QgsRasterLayer), with no hardcoded paths, dates, or Earth Engine assets. The resolution, weights, and correlations are user-specified parameters. Output is purely a static, single-date, deterministic weighted overlay — not time-series, not cloud-masked, not sensor-derived.

Identify suitable land for afforestation. The script identifies areas in Cascais municipality suitable for afforestation by integrating land use (COS2018), soil productivity (Carta de Solos + ProdS.csv), road proximity buffers (RedeViaria + ProtRV.csv), and main watercourses (LAgua). It performs geometric cleaning, spatial clipping, attribute-based filtering (e.g., 'Florestas', 'Matos', 'SAF'), table joins, buffer generation using road protection distances, difference operations to exclude road-adjacent zones, dissolution, single-part conversion, and intersection with streams. Final output is a GeoPackage layer ('final.gpkg') containing only polygons >300,000 m² that meet all suitability criteria.

Generate raster value boxplot. The script allows the user to interactively select a loaded raster layer in QGIS and optionally define a spatial extent using either the current map canvas extent or a selected feature from an active vector layer. It then clips the raster to that extent, converts the clipped raster pixels to point features with attribute values, samples up to 1000 pixel values (with user confirmation for larger datasets), and generates a matplotlib boxplot visualizing the statistical distribution (min, Q1, median, Q3, max, outliers) of the raster values within the defined area.

Crop Sentinel-2 raster to Alcoutim municipality. The script loads a Sentinel-2 Level-2A (surface reflectance) GeoTIFF (S2A-T29SNB-B2348-2021-8-22.tif), clips it spatially to the Alcoutim municipality boundary extracted from the official Portuguese CAOP 2022 administrative vector dataset (Cont_Conc_CAOP2022.shp), sets nodata value to 0 for all four bands (B2, B3, B4, B8), removes intermediate layers, and saves the final clipped raster as a GeoTIFF named 'S2SR-B2348_alcoutim.tif' in the output_subfolder. The workflow uses QGIS Python Console (PyQGIS) with native and GDAL processing algorithms — no GEE (Google Earth Engine) API calls are present; this is a local QGIS geoprocessing script, not a GEE script.

Reproject and package GIS layers. The script processes all vector layers loaded in the current QGIS project: (1) appends geometry-type–specific suffixes (_point, _line, _polygon, _no_Geometry) to layer names; (2) reassigns their CRS to MSK-64 (custom user CRS USER:100026, corresponding to Moscow System of Coordinates 1964, tailored for Leningrad region); (3) fixes geometries using QGIS 'native:fixgeometries'; (4) exports each layer individually as a GeoPackage (.gpkg); (5) merges all exported GeoPackages into a single consolidated GeoPackage (_Merged_Package.gpkg) using 'native:package'; (6) converts that merged GeoPackage into a File Geodatabase (.gdb) named Package_YYYY_MM_DD.gdb using GDAL's convertformat. All outputs are saved in the user-specified directory (D:\wrk_genplan\Data_2023).

Clip vector data by administrative regions. The script performs spatial clipping of vector layers (e.g., buildings, greenery) using an administrative boundary layer (e.g., districts or islands), producing one output file per region — named with a '_data' postfix — in GeoPackage format. It first splits the boundary layer by a unique name field (e.g., 'Name'), then iteratively clips all loaded vector layers against each boundary part, filters out empty results, merges non-empty clipped layers per region, and cleans up intermediate files.

Clean road network topology. The script performs topological cleaning of a vector road layer using GRASS GIS v.clean tools within QGIS. It applies two sequential v.clean operations: first with tool=0 (snap) to resolve small gaps and overlaps, then with tool=6 (break) to split lines at intersections. Errors from the second clean are joined to the cleaned layer, and features without errors (i.e., 'e_fid IS NULL') are filtered into a new memory layer. The final cleaned road network is saved as a Shapefile, added to the QGIS project, and logged with feature count statistics and processing time.

Generate Voronoi polygons for road network centroids. The script processes an input vector layer (typically OSM-derived road or linear infrastructure data) to generate Voronoi tessellations representing spatial influence zones around road segments. It first cleans the geometry (deletes holes, removes null geometries, converts multipart to singlepart), renumbers duplicate 'osm_id' attributes to ensure uniqueness, computes centroids of the cleaned single-part features, constructs a buffer around those centroids (distance scaled to CRS units), generates Voronoi polygons from the centroids, indexes the Voronoi layer, clips the Voronoi polygons to the buffer extent, and saves the clipped Voronoi polygons as a Shapefile. It also saves the intermediate centroid layer and logs processing metadata including timing and output paths.

Compute proximity distance ranges. The script computes the minimum Euclidean distance from each polygon (e.g., administrative units, land parcels, or buildings) to the nearest input point feature (e.g., service facilities, infrastructure nodes), generating a vector layer where each polygon is attributed with its shortest distance (in meters) to any point. It performs spatial join, geometry centroid extraction, distance calculation, group-wise minimum aggregation, and thematic rendering using graduated symbology based on distance ranges. Output is a styled vector layer named 'Distance ranges in meters' added to the QGIS project layer tree with feature count enabled.

Dissolve burnt area polygons. The script dissolves adjacent or overlapping polygon features representing burnt areas into single, non-overlapping polygons. It first applies geometry validation and correction using QGIS's 'native:fixgeometries' algorithm, then performs a dissolve operation with no attribute field specified (i.e., merges all input polygons into one or more contiguous geometries based on spatial contiguity). The input is a user-provided vector layer of burnt areas; no raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or classification logic is involved. The output is a vector feature sink containing the dissolved polygon geometry. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified — this is a pure vector topology operation in QGIS Processing, not a Google Earth Engine (GEE) script despite the prompt’s mischaracterization.

Rasterise burnt areas by FSID. The script converts a vector layer of burnt areas (polygons attributed with an FSID field) into a raster map at 10m resolution, then merges it with an existing regional raster mapping layer; the output is a single merged raster where burnt areas are encoded by their FSID values and background/overlap is handled via GDAL merge with NODATA=0, followed by application of a color table for visualization.

Crop raster layer to extent. The script crops a user-selected QGIS raster layer (e.g., SAR or optical TIF) to a user-defined geographic extent drawn interactively on the map canvas or provided in batch mode. It computes the corresponding pixel-aligned bounding box using GDAL geotransform and GCP_TPS transformation, optionally grows the pixel window to meet a minimum size (100×100 pixels), executes gdal:translate with -srcwin for lossless subsetting, builds overviews, preserves ICEYE-specific metadata (e.g., 'ICEYE_PROPERTIES'), and adds the resulting clipped GeoTIFF as a new raster layer named with '_CROP_' suffix and SHA-1 hash of the extent. A temporary vector mask layer is displayed during cropping and removed upon completion.

Identify unpaid hunting licenses by monte intersection. The script identifies hunting zones (manchas) scheduled for hunting within the next 7 days that intersect with municipal forest parcels (MUP montes) not yet licensed—by spatially joining mancha polygons with MUP monte polygons, calculating intersection area ratios, and cross-referencing against an Excel list of paid monte identifiers (Etiqueta column). Outputs include console-printed warnings (e.g., 'X% of mancha Coto Y is in MUP Z that has not paid') and populates two Python lists: listadecotosaestudiar (matriculation IDs of affected hunting zones) and listademontesaestudiar (Etiqueta IDs of non-paying montes). No persistent GIS layers are added; all processing is in-memory using QGIS Python API (QgsVectorLayer, processing.run, geometry.intersects()).

Estimate treatment gain surface. The script implements a geostatistical workflow to estimate and compare two agricultural treatment surfaces (T1 = control, T2 = experimental) over a study area using ordinary kriging. It partitions field-measured point data by treatment (T1/T2), performs 80/20 train/test splits, builds kriging models (with user-selected semivariogram: linear/exponential/gaussian/spherical) on the 80% training subsets to predict full-area rasters, computes prediction errors on the 20% test subsets, then applies a second round of kriging (using linear model only) on those errors to generate error-correction surfaces. Finally, it sums each treatment’s prediction raster with its corresponding error-correction raster, clips both to the study area polygon, and computes the Gain raster as T2 − T1 — representing spatially explicit estimated gain (e.g., yield increase, nutrient response) of T2 over T1 in original measurement units. Outputs include three rasters (T1, T2, Gain) and HTML statistics for Gain.

Extract river network from DEM. The script extracts a vector river network from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) by performing hydrological preprocessing (depression breaching and sink filling), computing D8 flow direction and accumulation, thresholding flow accumulation to delineate channels, building reach-level topology (FromN/ToN nodes), and populating a line vector layer with 22 mandatory D-CASCADE attributes—including reach_id, Slope, Length, elevations at upstream/downstream nodes (el_FN/el_TN), contributing area (Ad), and initialized sediment transport parameters (Wac, Q, n, D16/D50/D84, etc.). Output is a shapefile-compatible line vector layer ready for input into the D-CASCADE sediment transport model.

Generate vector-based tile boundaries. The script processes input GeoJSON vector layers representing administrative or thematic boundaries (e.g., land parcels, murabba units), computes group keys based on attribute logic (e.g., 'M', 'MN', 'B', 'Type' fields), dissolves and cleans nested/contained geometries, and exports XYZ tile directories (PNG tiles) covering zoom levels 10–20 for web mapping. Outputs include cleaned outline layers with group-key labeling, styled QGIS layers, and raster tile directories with blank-tile cleanup.

Export infrastructure layers to map package. The script prepares QGIS vector layers for export into a standardized map package format. It selects visible vector layers (points, lines, polygons) from the current QGIS project, optionally filters by selection, applies geometry simplification (1.5 m tolerance), exports them as ESRI Shapefiles and WGS84 GeoJSON files, enriches GeoJSON with symbology properties (fill color, stroke color, stroke width, opacity), stores symbology metadata in an SQLite database (Symbologie.db), generates a configuration JSON file containing site metadata (entrepreneur, chantier name, WFS info, date, geometry counts), and packages all artifacts (shapefiles, GeoJSONs, SQLite, JSON) into a ZIP archive. The script interfaces with a custom .NET DLL (Recup_data.dll) for license management and FTP upload, and uses SQLite databases (ms_machine-tracking-point.Sqlite, User.conf) to manage client/chantier metadata. No remote sensing or Earth observation data is loaded, processed, or analyzed — all inputs are local QGIS vector layers and configuration databases.

Assess wetland vulnerability index. The script computes a normalized Wetland Vulnerability Index (WVI) by integrating three domain layers — Exposure (Land Cover, NDBI, Population), Sensitivity (Degradation, Ecosystem), and Resilience (NDVI, MNDWI) — using weighted linear combination. It first calculates domain-specific rasters (Exposure, Sensitivity, Resilience) via GDAL raster calculator with user-defined weights, then combines them into a raw vulnerability score using domain-level weights (Exposure, Sensitivity, Resilience), and finally normalizes the result to [0,1] range using min-max scaling. Outputs include four rasters: Exposure, Sensitivity, Resilience, and the final normalized Wetland Vulnerability Index (WVI), optionally styled with QGIS layer styles.

Compute wetland vulnerability index. The script computes a Wetland Vulnerability Index (WVI) by combining three user-provided raster inputs — Exposure, Resilience, and Sensitivity — using domain-specific weights (default: 0.40, 0.20, 0.40 respectively) in a weighted linear combination: WVI = (Exposure × wₑ) + (Sensitivity × wₛ) + (Resilience × wᵣ). It then normalizes the resulting index to the [0,1] range using min-max scaling (i.e., (value − min) / (max − min)) and applies a QGIS layer style. The final output is a single-band normalized raster representing spatially explicit wetland vulnerability scores.

Validate traffic signal point positions. The script validates the positional accuracy of traffic signal points collected via QField by buffering road centerlines (5 meters), selecting only those points that fall within the buffered road polygons, and then assigning municipality names from administrative boundaries to each validated point. Outputs include a validated point shapefile, a CSV export with geometry as XYZ coordinates, and intermediate layers for visualization and quality control.

Estimate demand catchment by travel time. The script computes isochrones (travel-time polygons) around candidate retail shop locations using the ORS Tools plugin in QGIS, then spatially joins these isochrones with census-based demand points (LSOA-level population data) to determine which population falls within each travel-time threshold (1–30 minutes) for each shop. It aggregates total population per shop-time combination (e.g., 'shop_5_10' = shop ID 5, 10-min isochrone) and outputs a CSV table listing each unique shop-time-id pair with its associated total demand (population), enabling spatial accessibility analysis and retail catchment modeling.

Calculate country area in square kilometers. The script computes the area (in km²) of each country polygon from the Natural Earth 10m Admin 0 Countries dataset. It drops all fields except 'ADMIN' and 'ISO_A3', reprojects the vector layer from WGS 84 to World Cylindrical Equal Area (ESRI:54034), fixes invalid geometries, then adds a new field 'km2area' using the field calculator with the expression 'area($geometry)/1000000'. The final output is a CSV file containing only the 'ADMIN', 'ISO_A3', and 'km2area' fields, written to 'C:/Users/se.4537/Dropbox/PoliteconGIS/LBS_2020/PhD/lecture_2/gis_data/_output/country_areas.csv'. The study area is global (all countries), no time dimension is involved, and no satellite, sensor, or band data is used — only static administrative boundary vector data.

Calculate country area in square kilometers. The script computes the area (in km²) of administrative country polygons from the Natural Earth 'ne_10m_admin_0_countries' dataset. It first drops redundant attribute fields, reprojects the vector layer to an equal-area projection (ESRI:54034), fixes invalid geometries, calculates a new field 'km2area' using the planar area of each geometry divided by 1,000,000 (to convert m² → km²), and finally reprojects the result back to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) for output as a vector layer with the computed area attribute.

Clean language boundary geometry. The script cleans a vector layer of language boundaries (langa.shp) by fixing invalid geometries, adding a unique auto-incrementing GID field, copying the 'NAME_PROP' attribute into a new shorter-named field 'lnm', and dropping all other attributes except 'GID', 'ID', and 'lnm'. The final output is a simplified shapefile (wlds_cleaned.shp) containing only those three fields and topologically valid geometries.

Compute country-level population density statistics. The script computes zonal statistics (mean values) of four raster datasets — land quality, 1500 AD population density, 1990 AD population density, and 2000 AD population density — over country boundaries (admin-0 level) from Natural Earth. It fixes geometries and retains only 'ADMIN' and 'ISO_A3' attributes before running zonal statistics. The output is a CSV file ('country_level_zs.csv') containing country names (ADMIN), ISO-A3 codes, and mean values for each raster prefixed as 'lqua_', 'pd15_', 'pd19_', and 'pd20_'. Study area is global (countries shapefile), time range is explicitly 1500 AD, 1990 AD, and 2000 AD for population layers; land quality has no temporal annotation. Data sources include HYDE population rasters (1500, 1990, 2000 AD), a custom land quality raster, and Natural Earth admin-0 countries — all non-satellite, GIS-derived raster/vector products. No satellite, sensor, or spectral band processing occurs.

Calculate country area in square kilometers. The script computes the area (in km²) of each country polygon from the Natural Earth 10m Admin 0 Countries vector dataset. It drops all fields except 'ne_10m_adm', 'ADMIN', and 'ISO_A3'; reprojects the layer to World Cylindrical Equal Area (ESRI:54034) for accurate area calculation; fixes invalid geometries; then adds a new field 'km2area' using the expression 'area($geometry)/1000000' and exports the result to a CSV file at 'C:/Users/se.4537/Dropbox/PoliteconGIS/LBS_2020/PhD/lecture_3/gis_data/_output/country_areas.csv'. The study area is global (all countries), no time dimension is involved, and no satellite, sensor, or band data is used — it is a pure vector-based geoprocessing workflow on static administrative boundaries.

Generate grid-cell country intersection polygons. The script generates a global 2.5°×2.5° regular grid in WGS84, intersects it with Natural Earth Admin-0 country boundaries, dissolves resulting fragments by grid cell ID, cleans topological errors using GRASS v.clean (snap tool), fixes geometries, and outputs a cleaned, attribute-minimized vector layer (vcountries.shp) where each feature is a single polygon per grid cell representing the union of all country overlaps within that cell — effectively producing a grid-aligned, country-masked, topology-corrected spatial partition for spatial aggregation or zonal analysis.

Extract language-free virtual country areas. The script processes vector layers to isolate portions of 'virtual countries' (vcountries) that do not intersect with language distribution polygons (TEMP_wlds), using GRASS v.overlay with 'not' operator (operator=2), followed by geometry fixing, dissolving by cell-id (a_cid), field renaming to 'cid', and attribute cleanup. It separately processes the intersected portions (TEMP_int) to produce a harmonized version retaining only the 'cid' field. Outputs are two cleaned shapefiles: TEMP_nolangs (areas of virtual countries with no language coverage) and TEMP_withlangs (areas of virtual countries overlapping languages), both topologically cleaned and attribute-minimal.

Calculate virtual country land and water area. The script computes the total land area (km²) for each virtual country (defined by polygon features with attribute 'a_cid') and the intersecting water area (km²) from global lake polygons (Natural Earth 10m lakes). It performs geometry cleaning, reprojection to World Cylindrical Equal Area (ESRI:54034), area calculation via field calculator, intersection between virtual countries and lakes, dissolution by country ID, and outputs two CSV files: 'vcareas.csv' (country total areas) and 'vcwaterareas.csv' (country-specific water-covered areas).

Compute centroid-to-coast distance. The script computes the Euclidean distance from the geographic centroids of virtual countries (vcountries) — each associated with language data — to the nearest point on the Natural Earth 10m coastline. It outputs a CSV file containing, for each vcountry centroid, its ID (cid), latitude and longitude coordinates (cent_lat, cent_lon), and the latitude and longitude of the nearest coastal point (coast_lat, coast_lon). The workflow involves geometry fixing, centroid generation, coordinate export, GRASS v.distance-based proximity analysis, vertex extraction to isolate coastal endpoints, field renaming and cleanup, and final attribute consolidation into a tabular CSV.

Compute population density zonal statistics. The script computes mean zonal statistics (mean values) of population density rasters (1500 AD, 1990 AD, 2000 AD) for two vector layers: 'virtual countries' (vcountries.shp) and 'virtual countries without languages' (vcnolangs.shp). It applies geometry fixing to both shapefiles, then runs QGIS zonal statistics (statistic ID 2 = mean) for each population raster, appending prefixed columns (e.g., 'pd15_', 'pd19_', 'pd20_') to the attribute tables. Finally, it exports the updated vector attribute tables — now containing mean population density per polygon — as CSV files (vc_level_zs.csv and vcnl_level_zs.csv). The workflow intentionally skips large climate/elevation rasters and focuses only on the three HYDE population density datasets.

Generate grid-cell country intersection polygons. The script generates a global 0.5°×0.5° regular grid (WGS84), intersects it with cleaned administrative boundaries of countries (from Natural Earth 10m), dissolves resulting fragments by grid cell ID, cleans topological errors, and outputs a shapefile (dyadcells.shp) containing one polygon per grid cell that overlaps land territory — each assigned a unique integer 'cid' — effectively producing a vector-based, land-masked, globally consistent spatial discretization for dyadic or cell-level analysis.

Join language data to dyad cells. The script spatially joins language boundary polygons (from TEMP_wlds.shp) to dyadic administrative cell polygons (dyadcells.shp) using a containment predicate (‘within’ or ‘intersects’, default predicate 0), retains only the 'cid' (cell identifier) and 'GID' (language identifier) fields in the output CSV, and writes the result to langs_in_dyadcells.csv. It first repairs invalid geometries in both input layers to ensure robust topological operations, then performs the spatial join, and finally drops all non-essential attribute fields to produce a minimal many-to-many mapping table linking dyad cells to languages present within them.

Calculate virtual country water area. The script computes the area of water bodies (lakes) intersecting with pre-defined virtual country cells (dyadcells.shp) and outputs two CSV files: (1) 'dyadareas.csv' containing the total area (km²) of each virtual country cell projected to World Cylindrical Equal Area (ESRI:54034), and (2) 'dyadwaterareas.csv' containing the summed water-covered area (km²) per virtual country cell ID ('cid'). Input data includes Natural Earth 10m lakes (vector, global coverage), and dyad cells — a custom gridded partitioning of the world surface into equal-area cells ('dyadcells.shp'), likely derived from a dyadic geopolitical unit scheme. The workflow involves geometry fixing, reprojection, GRASS v.clean and v.overlay for robust vector intersection, dissolve by cell ID, field calculation of areas in km², and field cleanup. No time dimension is involved; all operations are static spatial overlays. Study area is global (inferred from use of Natural Earth global lakes and 'world cylindrical equal area' CRS).

Generate Tanaka contours from DEM. The script generates Tanaka-style illuminated contour lines from a digital elevation model (DEM) raster input in QGIS. It first extracts elevation contours at a user-defined interval, optionally filters short segments by length and smooths geometry using iterative angular constraints, then explodes multilines into single-segment features, computes azimuth for each segment, assigns a unique FID, and applies Tanaka shading logic: stroke color varies with HSL lightness based on the absolute angular deviation of contour orientation from the dominant illumination direction (45°), and stroke width scales with the deviation from perpendicularity to illumination — producing visually enhanced, 3D-like terrain representation. Outputs include a styled vector layer added to the QGIS project and exported as GeoPackage or Shapefile.

Interpolate digital elevation model. The script performs iterative cubic spline interpolation on a point layer (probkowanie.gpkg) containing elevation samples (field 'SAMPLE_1') to generate nsteps=20 realizations of a DEM raster surface. Each realization is produced by first randomly subsampling the input points (80 points per iteration), then applying SAGA's 'interpolatecubicspline' with fixed parameters (K=140, cell size=100 m, extent matching the original layer). Finally, it computes ensemble statistics — mean and standard deviation — across all 20 interpolated rasters, producing two final output rasters: a mean DEM and its spatial standard deviation (uncertainty surface).

Reclassify suitability raster. The script reclassifies a continuous input suitability raster into discrete suitability classes (e.g., low/medium/high) based on user-defined value ranges (MANUAL method) or equal-interval binning (not yet implemented), then clips the reclassified raster to a vector mask layer. It outputs a clipped, reclassified raster with LZW-compressed GeoTIFF encoding, intended for suitability mapping applications such as habitat, agriculture, or land-use planning.

Compute land cover density masks. The script processes a classified raster (ExtraTrees.TIF) to generate six binary density rasters per folder: one for each land cover class (0–5), where each output raster (e.g., c0_sea_water.TIF) represents the spatial density (via 5-cell neighborhood averaging) of pixels assigned to that class. It does so by first applying GDAL Raster Calculator to isolate each class (e.g., A==0), then smoothing with GRASS r.neighbors (method=0, size=5), and finally deleting intermediate binary rasters. The outputs are six named GeoTIFFs per subfolder under '/Users/jonny.sanchez/Documents/tesis/9-cover_density/barranquilla', explicitly mapped to 'Agua de mar', 'Agua dulce', 'Construcciones', 'Nubes', 'Suelo desnudo', and 'Vegetación'.

Convert DXF to Orange-compliant shapefiles. The script converts AutoCAD DXF files—originating from French DFT (Dossier de Fourniture Technique) submissions—into standardized ESRI Shapefile outputs required by ORANGE (a major French telecom operator). It performs layer-type-based routing (Point/LineString/Polygon), applies domain-specific QGIS Processing Model algorithms (dxf_to_shapes_model_aer and dxf_to_shapes_model_gc) for AER (aerial) and GC (underground) network variants, merges outputs, applies consistent styling (e.g., 'support_aer.qml'), refactors field schemas to match ORANGE’s mandatory attributes ('ref_comman', 'num_siren', 'operateur', 'type'), and packages final layers (support.shp, cable.shp, bpe.shp, and optional _gcor variants) into ZIP archives—one with only GCOR-labeled layers and one without.

Generate H3 hexagonal grid from layer extent. The script generates a series of H3 geohash-based hexagonal grids (at user-specified resolutions 0–9) that cover the geographic extent (bounding box polygon) of the currently active QGIS vector layer — optionally restricted to selected features. It reprojects the input layer to a geographic CRS (EPSG:4617), computes the axis-aligned bounding rectangle, uses h3.polyfill_polygon to fill that rectangle with H3 hexagons at each resolution, converts each H3 ID to its boundary polygon in WGS84 decimal degrees, and writes each resolution level to a separate ESRI Shapefile with 'id' attribute; all outputs are added to the QGIS project.

Convert LST raster to Celsius. The script converts a raw satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST) raster layer from digital numbers (DN) to physical temperature values in degrees Celsius using a linear radiometric calibration formula: LST(°C) = (DN × 0.00341802) − 124.15. It then vectorizes the resulting Celsius raster into polygon features representing contiguous temperature zones, applies Chaikin’s smoothing algorithm (3 iterations) to eliminate pixelated jagged boundaries, and applies a dynamically classified graduated symbology (5 equal-interval classes, inverted RdYlGn color ramp) to the final GeoPackage vector layer for visual thermal pattern analysis.

Extract connected hydrographic network. The script constructs a topologically connected reference hydrographic network by starting from buffered outlet points (exutoire) and selecting all upstream/downstream connected stream reaches (troncons) from a corrected BD TOPO IGN hydrographic dataset. It first removes duplicate geometries, identifies network nodes (NODEA/NODEB), selects reaches intersecting the outlet buffer, then applies connected component selection to retain only the hydrologically connected subset. It further simplifies the network to a principal stem (single-path upstream route to source) and aggregates reaches into continuous segments between network junctions (intersections), producing two outputs: (1) a troncon-level layer preserving original BD TOPO geometry and attributes (minus NODEA/NODEB), and (2) a segment-level layer where linear features are merged between confluences, with working fields (GID, LENGTH, CATEGORY, NODEA, NODEB) removed. All outputs are saved to a GeoPackage.

Remove canal features from hydrographic network. The script processes a corrected hydrographic network layer (troncon_hydrographique_cours_d_eau_corr) by identifying network nodes, extracting outlets intersecting a buffered exutoire (outlet) layer, filtering out canal-related features based on the 'nature' attribute (excluding 'Canal', 'Conduit forcé', 'Conduit buse', and 'Ecoulement canalisé'), merging the outlet and non-canal network segments, and then applying network connectivity correction using the fct:fixnetworkconnectivity algorithm with the merged subset. The final output is a cleaned hydrographic network layer with canals removed and topologically fixed, saved back to the original GeoPackage under a new layer name (e.g., troncon_hydrographique_cours_d_eau_corr_suppr_canal).

Classify roof types from building predictions. The script classifies building roof types (e.g., 'płaski', 'dwuspadowy', 'czterospadowy') by joining AI-generated building-level predictions (from external CSV: building_predictions.csv) with a QGIS vector layer of buildings ('budynki_z_szer_elew_front'), then interactively validates and refines classifications using a GUI dialog. It outputs: (1) a CSV file ('klasyfikacja_dachow.csv') logging ID_BUDYNKU → roof category mappings; (2) a joined and styled vector layer ('budynki_parametry') with added 'Kategoria' and corrected 'nachylenie' values for flat roofs; (3) an additional joined layer for point cloud data ('Classification_6_with_roofsKategories'); and (4) GeoPackage exports of all derived layers. Critical preprocessing includes ID normalization (replacing '/' with '_'), join validation, ID-matching diagnostics, and automatic fallback handling for missing prediction fields ('PREDYKCJA', 'PEWNOSC').

Merge cadastral map and parcel layers. The script downloads, extracts, and merges Italian cadastral GML files (MAP = cadastral maps; PLE = land parcels) for a user-selected Italian region from the Agenzia delle Entrate WFS service. It organizes extracted GMLs by type (MAP/PLE), merges all files of each type into a single vector layer using QGIS native merge algorithm, filters attributes to retain only 'fid', 'gml_id', and 'ADMINISTRATIVEUNIT', exports the result in user-specified format (GML/GPKG/Shapefile/GeoJSON), and optionally loads the outputs into QGIS. The workflow includes full temporary file management, error-resilient cleanup, and timing reporting.

Generate terrain analysis from DEM. The script auto-detects a user-provided DEM/DTM raster (e.g., DEM.tif or DTM.tif) and computes four core terrain derivatives: slope (in degrees), aspect (compass direction), flow accumulation (using GRASS r.watershed), and hillshade (with azimuth=315°, altitude=45°). It optionally incorporates orthomosaic, boundary, and road vector layers for context but does not use them in the terrain calculations. Outputs are GeoTIFFs saved to an auto-created 'outputs' subfolder, with metadata (CRS, dimensions, statistics) printed and all valid results loaded into QGIS map canvas.

Classify slope terrain. The script computes slope from a digital elevation model (DEM) in degrees, classifies it into five standardized LandWise slope classes (0–5°, 5–15°, 15–25°, 25–35°, 35°+), applies professional cartographic styling (color ramp, opacity, hillshade blending), generates a fully branded A3 print layout with legend, scale bar, north arrow, and grid, and exports high-resolution PNG (4000px) and PDF (300 DPI) deliverables alongside slope statistics (area %, ha, pixel count per class), technical report, and JSON metadata — all following the LandWise Technical Specification & Map Style Standard.

Calculate footprint overlap area. The script calculates the spatial overlap among aerial imagery footprint polygons using QGIS's 'Join Attributes by Location Summary' tool with intersection predicate, then removes duplicate geometries to produce a cleaned overlap layer. Input is a vector polygon layer representing aerial imagery footprints; output is a vector layer containing summarized overlap attributes and deduplicated geometries.

Smooth Voronoi polygons for point-based administrative units. The script generates smoothed, boundary-constrained Voronoi tessellations from input point features (e.g., settlements, monitoring stations, or administrative centroids), using a multi-stage geometric processing workflow: (1) filtering input points and base polygon layer; (2) generating raw GRASS Voronoi polygons; (3) clipping to the base map extent; (4) densifying edges; (5) perturbing vertices stochastically within a user-defined tolerance to break straight-line rigidity; (6) reconstructing closed polygonal paths per unique ID group; (7) buffering and re-clipping to soften corners and ensure topological integrity within the base boundary; and (8) joining original point attributes back to the final smoothed polygons. The output is a vector layer of smoothed, non-overlapping, topology-clean Voronoi-derived polygons aligned to a base geographic boundary (e.g., country or region), preserving per-point attribute associations via join on a unique field.

Identify live cetacean monitoring suitable areas. The script identifies spatially explicit 'SUITABLE AREA(S)' for live cetacean monitoring by intersecting ERA5-derived monthly 'Total Cloud Cover' and '10m Wind Speed' vector layers that have been thresholded (e.g., cloud ≤20% and wind ≤5 m/s); it further merges and dissolves these with cloud-thresholded areas for stranded/floating cetaceans to produce integrated suitability maps for 'live cetaceans and/or floating carcasses, and stranded cetaceans'. Outputs are shapefiles (e.g., '_final_aoi_cloud20_wind5_live.shp', '_float_and_strand.shp') stored in location-specific folders, styled with colorblind-accessible dashed-fill symbology, and overlaid with EEZ, land, and image extent base layers for cartographic interpretation.

Simplify building footprints by buffer subtraction. The script processes building footprint vector data to simplify geometry by first computing minimum bounding geometries (convex hulls), dissolving them into a single polygon, converting multiparts to single parts, then subtracting street buffer polygons (5 m wide) via geometric difference. It filters resulting polygons by minimum area (50 m²), adds geometry attributes (area, perimeter), drops redundant fields, and joins maximum building height attributes from the original building layer using spatial join-by-location (‘contains’ predicate). The final output is a cleaned, simplified, area-filtered, height-annotated building footprint GeoPackage (`cleaned.gpkg`).

Dissect and dissolve polygon overlaps.
