The script detects geometric overlaps in a single input polygon layer using self-intersection analysis; it then optionally dissects overlapping polygons into non-overlapping parts (by splitting at intersection boundaries) and/or dissolves selected overlaps based on adjacency criteria (largest adjacent, smallest adjacent, or largest common boundary). Outputs include: (1) a temporary 'Intersected' vector layer containing dissected polygons with cleaned geometries and area attributes, saved as a shapefile with timestamped filename; (2) a 'Dissolved' vector layer resulting from elimination of selected overlaps, also saved as a timestamped shapefile; and (3) interactive zoom-to-selection of overlapping features in QGIS. The workflow relies on QGIS native and SAGA NextGen processing algorithms (e.g., 'sagang:polygonselfintersection', 'qgis:eliminateselectedpolygons'), geometry fixing, attribute filtering, and auto-increment ID assignment for topological disambiguation.

Generate pipe topology for thermonet. The script generates a pipe topology file for a district heating network (thermonet) by processing two input vector layers: main pipes with hierarchical 'Level' field and service pipes with 'id.lokalId' heatpump identifiers. It reprojects layers to a projected CRS (EPSG:3857), computes geometry lengths, resolves heatpump ID connectivity based on spatial proximity (buffer distance of 0.1 m for service pipes and 1 m for higher-level main pipes), deduplicates IDs, and outputs a GeoJSON layer with fields Section, SDR, Trace_(m), Number_of_traces, Max_pressure_loss_(Pa), and HP_ID_vector — plus a tab-separated DAT file with identical attributes for use in pythermonet.

Compute PS statistics and plot distribution. The script intersects two user-provided polygon layers (Polygon 1 and Polygon 2) to define a masking region, clips a point layer (PS) to that intersection, computes a new numeric field for the clipped points using a user-defined QGIS expression formula, exports descriptive statistics (median, std, max, etc.) of that field to a CSV file, and generates an interactive histogram (via Plotly) of the field’s value distribution saved as an HTML file.

Model biodiversity dispersal corridors. The script models species dispersal across a landscape by generating a friction surface from land cover layers (e.g., agriculture, forests, infrastructure) and computing cost-distance accumulation from biodiversity reservoirs (polygon features). It produces two primary outputs: (1) a 'Friction' raster where pixel values represent resistance to movement (based on user-defined coefficients per land cover class or interval), and (2) a 'Dispersion' raster generated via GRASS r.cost, showing cumulative cost distance from reservoir centroids up to a user-specified maximum cost threshold — effectively mapping potential ecological corridors and connectivity pathways.

Generate cross-sectional profiles along river axis. The script processes input survey tracks (e.g., bathymetric or geodetic transects) and a reference river axis line to generate ordered, regularly spaced cross-sectional lines perpendicular to the axis. It computes longitudinal abscissas along the axis, optionally resamples track points at fixed distances (either strictly spaced or preserving original vertices), assigns section IDs, projects points onto the axis-aligned geometry, and imports elevation values from a DEM to attribute each section with terrain height (e.g., 'zfond'). The final output is a vector layer of oriented section lines, ordered by section ID, with geometry, abscissa, and DEM-derived elevation attributes.

Interpolate cross-section points. The script interpolates point-based river cross-section data along a defined axis line to generate a regularly spaced, densified set of 3D points (with elevation and optional layer attributes) for hydraulic modeling. It refactors input section points to conform to TatooineMesher’s expected field schema (e.g., 'Zzfond', 'Zlayer1'), optionally merges and augments constraint lines (including left/right bank envelopes derived from section ordering), then invokes an external Python CLI ('densify_cross_sections.py') to perform longitudinal and lateral interpolation using user-specified step sizes (in meters). The output is a shapefile of interpolated points with geometry and Z-attributes, reprojected to match the input sections’ CRS.

Compute raster comparison error zones. The script computes pairwise spatial intersections of raster bounding boxes, generates 200m-spaced point grids within each intersection polygon, samples pixel values from the two overlapping rasters at each point, calculates the root mean square error (RMSE) of differences between corresponding pixel values, and outputs vector polygon layers named after the raster pair with an 'Eqz' (error) attribute. All output layers are grouped under 'Saída Script' in the QGIS project.

Visualize network kernel density. The script computes and visualizes network-constrained kernel density estimation (NKDV) for input point features (e.g., traffic incidents, crime events, or service locations) along a road network. It downloads or loads an OpenStreetMap-based street graph, projects points onto the nearest edges, splits edges into uniform-length segments (lixels), computes density values per lixel using a configurable kernel (Gaussian, Triangular, Epanechnikov, or Quartic), and outputs a styled GeoPackage layer where each lixel segment is colored by its computed density value — enabling fast, accurate, and cartographically refined density visualization on transportation networks.

Visualize temporal kernel density on road networks. The script performs Network Temporal Kernel Density Visualization (NTKDV) on point event data (e.g., traffic incidents, GPS traces) projected onto OpenStreetMap-derived road networks. It partitions road edges into lixels (linear pixels), computes spatiotemporal kernel density estimates using Epanechnikov or Quartic kernels across user-defined time slices (either uniformly spaced or manually specified), and outputs a series of styled GeoPackage/Shapefile layers — one per time slice — where each lixel is attributed with its density value and rendered with Turbo color ramp and graduated line symbology in QGIS. The workflow includes automatic time parsing, network caching, geometry projection, distance computation, and CRS-aware output reprojection to EPSG:4326.

Analyze watershed morphometric parameters. The script performs hydrological basin analysis using vector and raster inputs to compute morphometric parameters (e.g., basin area, stream length, slope, hypsometric integral) and their geomorphic interpretations. It clips a DEM to the basin boundary, computes slope statistics, identifies the pour point from the highest-order Strahler stream segments, calculates parameters via external `calculate_parameters()` function, and generates a hypsometric curve with HI and stage classification via `generate_hypsometric_curve()`. Outputs include a point-based attribute table (with Parameter, Value, Unit, Interpretation fields) anchored at the pour point, plus temporary hypsometric curve files (e.g., CSV, plot images) saved in QGIS temp folder. All operations are CRS-consistent, and no remote sensing time-series or satellite-derived indices are computed — inputs are local GIS layers only (not GEE ImageCollections). Study area, time range, satellite data, and explicit geographic names are not specified in the code.

Quantify nitrogen and phosphorus purification value. The script calculates the water purification ecosystem service value for nitrogen (NitroPurVal_channel) and phosphorus (PhoshPurVal_channel) removal in river channels, using SWAT+ model output from baseline and restoration scenarios. It computes channel-scale nutrient retention capacity (CWAN/CWAP) via first-order kinetic equations incorporating flow, temperature, and nutrient concentration gradients; ranks top n monthly retention increments per channel (ntop); aggregates the top values to derive mean annual phosphorus and nitrogen purification capacity per channel; and monetizes this capacity using a power-law cost function (149.34 × (capacity/10000)^0.69 × 1000), discounted over life expectancy with actualisation rate, plus annual operation/maintenance costs. Outputs are two vector layers (one per nutrient) joined to the input channel shapefile (rivs1), each containing the monetary valuation per channel feature.

Extract building vertex coordinates. The script processes a vector layer of LOD-1 buildings (polygons or TINZ geometries) to extract all geometry vertices, optionally clip them to a user-defined extent, assign sequential row IDs, transform vertex coordinates from EPSG:3301 (Estonian national coordinate system) to UTM zone 35N (EPSG:32635), and export the resulting point features—including X_UTM, Y_UTM, and optional Z values—as a CSV file with 'row_id' as the first field. It is specifically designed for Estonian national spatial data infrastructure workflows where input is in EPSG:3301 and output requires metric UTM coordinates for downstream building modeling or BIM integration.

Extract road vertex coordinates. The script processes one or more input vector line layers representing roads, standardizes their attribute schemas (resolving string field length inconsistencies across layers), merges them, removes duplicate geometries, extracts all vertices of the resulting road lines, assigns a unique row ID to each vertex, computes UTM X and Y coordinates (transforming from EPSG:3301 — Estonian Coordinate System 1997 — to EPSG:32635 — WGS84 UTM zone 35N), and exports the final vertex table as a CSV with columns ordered as ['row_id', 'X_UTM', 'Y_UTM'] followed by all original attributes. The output is a georeferenced point CSV suitable for downstream spatial analysis or integration into GIS databases.

Identify flood-prone buildings. The script identifies buildings potentially at risk of flooding by buffering rivers by 150 meters, computing building centroids, extracting those centroids that intersect the river buffer, and sampling elevation (DTM) values at those buffered building locations. Outputs are: (1) a vector layer of building centroids within the flood buffer zone ('Estrazione'), and (2) a point layer with sampled DTM elevation values ('Campionato_valore') for further flood depth or vulnerability analysis.

Classify flood depth pixels. The script converts a flood depth raster layer into vector polygons where each polygon represents a group of contiguous raster pixels with identical (rounded) depth values. It applies optional unit conversion (cm → m), classification binning (rounding to nearest multiple of a user-defined cm threshold), and optionally merges adjacent pixels into larger polygons. The resulting polygons are exported to a PostgreSQL database table with standardized field names (e.g., 'vanddybde_m' for depth in meters, 'geom' for geometry), and metadata (schema/table name, primary key, depth field, geometry field) is registered in an admin parameter table ('fdc_admin.parametre') for downstream flood damage cost modeling.

Convert flood depth raster to polygon pixels. The script converts a user-provided flood depth raster layer into vector polygons (one per pixel), rescales depth values (centimeters → meters if specified), names the output PostgreSQL table using a dynamically constructed string combining return period, year, climate scenario, and optional suffix, imports the polygons into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database schema, and updates administrative parameter tables in the same database to register the new flood dataset’s geometry, primary key, and depth field names for downstream flood damage cost modeling.

Detect pond depressions in DEM. The script detects topographic depressions (ponds/sinks) in a digital elevation model (DEM) raster by applying a sink-filling algorithm, computes pond depth as the difference between filled and original DEM, polygonizes valid depth areas (depth > MIN_DEPTH), filters polygons by minimum area, assigns unique IDs (PONDid), and calculates key hydro-geomorphic attributes: maximum/minimum pond elevation (PONDRLmax/PONDRLmin), pond volume (PONDvolume = DEPTH_sum × pixel_area), depth statistics (DEPTH_sum, DEPTH_mean, DEPTH_max), and pond area (PONDarea); outputs include a vector layer of pond outlines with rich attribute table and optional filled/depth rasters.

Resample Copernicus land cover to 1km. The script resamples Copernicus Global Land (CGLS) vegetation biophysical products (e.g., NDVI, FAPAR, LAI) from native 333 m resolution to 1 km resolution while preserving the spatial extent and temporal consistency of existing 1 km time series. It applies two parallel resampling workflows: (1) 'average' resampling for continuous variables (e.g., NDVI), including scaling and georeferenced cropping to a global bounding box (−180° to 180° longitude, −60° to 80° latitude); and (2) 'mode' resampling for categorical or discrete land cover values, applied after reclassification using a user-defined lookup table (e.g., '[-0.08,0.92,1,0.92,255,0]'). The outputs are combined via raster multiplication ('A@1 * B@1') and exported as a compressed GeoTIFF. The script is designed specifically for Copernicus PROBA-V (pre-July 2020) and Sentinel-3 (post-July 2020) vegetation products, with explicit handling of resampling method selection and reclassification logic. Study area is global (fixed bounding box), no temporal filtering is performed — input raster is assumed pre-selected. Final output is a single resampled GeoTIFF at 1 km resolution.

Compute primary forest area statistics. The script computes total and per-zone area (in kha) for binary raster layers representing primary forest, pre-connectivity forest, and input forest. It uses GDAL to read rasters, QGIS processing algorithms to reproject and rasterize vector zones, and NumPy to mask and sum pixels equal to 1. Outputs include a CSV table with per-zone or total area values and optionally a vector layer joined with area statistics.

Generate aspect-slope composite map. The script computes aspect and slope rasters from an input DEM, reclassifies both into ordinal categories (aspect into 8 cardinal directions + 'no preference' label; slope into 5 gradient classes), sums the reclassified rasters to produce a combined aspect-slope index raster (values 10–88), and applies a user-selected, aspect-preference-driven color ramp for visualisation — resulting in a single pseudo-colored raster layer named 'Aspect-Slope – [preference]' with custom interpolated color mapping. Intermediate outputs include optional standalone aspect and slope rasters.

Generate scaled STL terrain models. Generates one or more STL (stereolithography) 3D printable files from a digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer, where each STL corresponds to a feature in an input vector layer (e.g., polygons representing administrative units or land parcels); the script clips the DEM by each vector feature, computes a uniform scale factor ensuring all resulting terrain models fit within the user-specified 3D printer bed dimensions (accounting for line width resolution), and exports scaled, base-included STLs with configurable model height and base thickness.

Generate scaled STL terrain models. The script generates one or more 3D printable STL files from a digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer, clipped and scaled to fit within user-specified total width and length constraints (in mm), using vector features (e.g., polygons) to define individual model boundaries. Each STL is generated with uniform model height and base thickness, and all models are proportionally downscaled by a single global scale factor computed from the merged extent of all clipped rasters — ensuring their combined footprint fits the target print bed dimensions while respecting the user’s 3D printer line width. Outputs are STL files saved to a user-specified folder.

Generate hillshade and contour lines. The script computes a hillshade raster from an input digital elevation model (DEM) using azimuth 300° and vertical angle 40°, then derives contour lines at 10-unit elevation intervals from the hillshade output (though note: contouring is incorrectly applied to the hillshade raster instead of the original DEM, which is a logical flaw; the intended purpose remains topographic visualization and line extraction). Outputs are a hillshade raster ('hill') and a vector line layer of contours ('contour').

Generate hachure points from DEM. The script generates a vector point layer where each point lies along elevation contours extracted from a DEM, with attributes for elevation (ELEV), contour ID (ID), distance along contour (distance), contour direction (angle), slope steepness (slope_1), and aspect direction (aspect_1); these attributes are used in QGIS geometry generator styling to render monochrome hachure lines perpendicular to contours, with length modulated by slope and opacity modulated by aspect (simulating hillshading from north).

Generate feature descriptions. The script augments a user-provided vector layer with two new fields: (1) a 'description' field populated by executing a user-defined Python function (defaulting to pyrealb-based natural language generation) that accesses feature attributes via a dictionary 'f', and (2) a 'metadata' field containing a JSON-serialized dictionary of key-value pairs entered by the user in a matrix parameter. The output is a new vector layer identical to the input but enriched with these two text fields for documentation, labeling, or semantic annotation purposes.

Extract wind turbine locations. The script retrieves OpenStreetMap (OSM) point features tagged with 'generator:method'='wind_turbine' within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It downloads OSM data via Overpass API, clips the resulting points to the study area, parses the 'height' value from the 'other_tags' field using string operations, and outputs a cleaned point layer with standardized attributes including 'nome', 'alturaTorreAer', 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm', 'nome_osm', and 'alturaTorreAer_osm'. The workflow is fully OSM-centric and does not involve satellite imagery or time-series analysis.

Extract OSM police facilities. The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) features tagged as police-related (default: amenity=police) within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It queries the Overpass API, downloads the raw OSM data, separates points and multipolygons, clips both to the study area, converts polygon geometries to centroids where needed, applies a tiny buffer to polygons for robust spatial matching, excludes points disjoint from buffered polygons (to avoid duplicate representations), merges point and centroid layers, harmonizes the 'osm_id' field (prioritizing 'osm_id' over 'osm_way_id'), and refactors attributes into a standardized output layer with fields: 'nome' (name), 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm' (always 'Sim'), and 'nome_osm' ('Sim' if name exists, else 'Não'). The final output is a vector point layer of police facilities.

Extract OSM park features. The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) features tagged with user-specified key-value pairs (e.g., 'leisure'='park') within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It downloads Overpass API query results, isolates multipolygon geometries, fixes invalid geometries, clips to the study area, decomposes multipart features, filters for names containing variants of 'Praca', 'Pracinha', 'Largo', or 'Parquinho', and outputs a cleaned vector layer with standardized attribute fields including 'nome', 'geometriaAproximada', 'turistica', 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm', and 'nome_osm'.

Identify road displacement gaps. The script identifies discrepancies between reference road linework (user-provided) and OpenStreetMap (OSM) road data within a user-defined area of interest. It downloads OSM highway features (filtered to exclude minor paths/footways), buffers both the reference and OSM layers by 0.000225 decimal degrees (~25 m), computes the geometric difference (OSM buffer minus reference buffer), calculates the percentage of OSM buffer area not overlapping the reference buffer ('percentualExtraBaseRef'), filters OSM segments where this excess percentage exceeds a user-defined threshold (e.g., 40%), and outputs the selected OSM road segments enriched with attributes including 'osm_id', 'nome' (name), 'geometria_osm', 'nome_osm', 'sigla' (extracted from OSM's 'other_tags'), and 'codtrechorod_osm', serving as candidate road segments requiring geometric correction or validation.

Identify power line segments with OSM validation. The script identifies candidate power line segments from OpenStreetMap (OSM) within a user-defined area of interest, compares them against a reference line layer (e.g., official utility network), computes geometric excess (percentage of OSM line buffer area not overlapping the reference buffer), filters segments where excess ≥ user-defined threshold (e.g., 70%), and outputs a cleaned line layer enriched with OSM attributes (osm_id, description from other_tags) and quality flags (geometria_osm, nome_osm). The workflow uses Overpass API to fetch OSM 'power=line' features, applies identical buffering (0.000452 decimal degrees ≈ 50 m at equator) to both OSM and reference lines, computes area-based discrepancy via difference and field calculations, and performs attribute parsing from OSM's 'other_tags' string field to extract descriptive metadata.

Identify road police facilities. The script identifies road police facilities (e.g., traffic police stations) by querying OpenStreetMap (OSM) for points tagged with user-specified OSM key-value pairs (default: 'police'='traffic_police') within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It buffers the input reference point layer (e.g., official police station locations), downloads OSM points matching the query, clips them to the area of interest, and performs a spatial disjoint test to extract OSM points *outside* the buffered reference points — implying potential unmapped or unverified road police facilities. It then parses OSM 'name' tags, standardizes attribute fields (e.g., 'nome_osm' = 'Sim' if name exists, else 'Não'; 'geometria_osm' = 'Sim'), and merges the processed OSM points with the original reference layer (after adding a default 'nome_osm' = 'Não' field), finally refactoring all attributes into a standardized output schema aligned with Brazilian national geospatial standards (e.g., IBGE/BNGb fields like 'id', 'nome', 'municipio', 'osm_id', 'nome_osm', 'geometria_osm'). The output is a unified point vector layer ('Pol_rod_p') containing both reference and OSM-derived road police features with harmonized metadata and OSM validation flags.

Identify helipad locations. The script identifies helipad (heliponto) features by querying OpenStreetMap (OSM) data using the OSM tag 'aeroway=helipad' within a user-defined polygon area of interest, then cross-references these OSM points and polygons against a user-provided reference point layer (e.g., official IBGE helipad inventory) using spatial buffering (0.000452° ≈ 50 m at equator) and location-based extraction. It harmonizes attributes—including OSM ID, name presence ('nome_no_osm'), geometry source ('geometria_osm'), and name match status ('nome_osm')—and merges OSM-derived points and centroids of clipped OSM polygons with buffered reference points to produce a unified output layer 'Heliponto_p' containing standardized fields aligned with IBGE’s geospatial schema (e.g., 'tipopista', 'osm_id', 'nome_osm', 'geometria_osm').

Map point locations by search terms. The script converts a CSV table containing X and Y coordinate fields into a point vector layer, reprojects it (and a provided base map) to a user-specified CRS, then splits the point layer into multiple subsets based on exact or substring matches in a user-selected attribute field against comma-separated search terms. Each subset is saved as a named shapefile with a unique marker symbol and color, and added to the QGIS project as a rendered vector layer. The base map is also reprojected and output as a separate layer.

Buffer features without overlaps. The script creates non-overlapping buffers around input vector features (points, lines, or polygons) using QGIS native and SAGA GIS algorithms. It first fixes geometries, applies a buffer with configurable end cap and join styles, detects self-intersections to identify overlapping areas via 'sagang:polygonselfintersection', calculates intersection area, removes null geometries, and deletes features with near-zero area (≤0.0000001). The final output is a cleaned, non-overlapping buffer layer saved as a Shapefile and added to the QGIS project.

Estimate flood depth from DEM and inundation polygons. The script estimates flood depth by overlaying flood extent shapefiles (inundation polygons) onto a digital elevation model (DEM) using a custom QGIS processing script 'fwdet_v21'. It first cleans the input flood polygons by eliminating small holes (min area 50000) and fixing geometries, then computes water depth rasters and filtered versions. Inputs include detention basin area shapefiles and corresponding DEM TIFFs; outputs are per-date flood depth rasters and intermediate cleaned vector files.

Snap network geometries to infrastructure points. The script improves the geometric consistency of fiber-optic network vector layers by snapping endpoints and vertices of linear features (D-Cables, F-Cables, DropCables, D-Ducts) to precisely aligned point infrastructure (Paal, Aerial Boxes, Termination Boxes, Riser, DP, HPs, CO) using tolerance-based topological alignment. It first fixes invalid geometries (e.g., self-intersections, gaps) via 'fixgeometries', then applies sequential snapping with behavior=4 (move endpoints only, prefer aligning nodes) or behavior=2 (prefer aligning nodes, no new vertices) at 5 mm tolerance (0.005 map units, assumed metric). Outputs are five cleaned-and-snapped vector layers: Snapped_aerialboxes (points), Snapped_dcables (lines), Snapped_fcables (lines), Snapped_dropcables (lines), and Snapped_dducts (lines), each topologically constrained to their respective reference infrastructure points.

Calculate valley confinement index. The script computes the Confined Valley Index (VB_RB-index) as the ratio of ValleyBottom width to Riverbank width along a river axis. It generates transects perpendicular to the river line at regular intervals (user-defined step), intersects them with left/right river banks and valley bottom polygon boundaries, calculates minimum distances from the river centerline to each intersection, aggregates left/right distances separately, and derives metrics including VB_RB-index = (min-VB-L + min-VB-R) / (min-RB-L + min-RB-R), total valley bottom width (VB-W), total riverbank width (RB-W), and individual minimum distances. Output is a point layer along the river centerline with SEZ-ID as transect identifier and all computed metrics as attributes.

Measure river bank distances. The script computes perpendicular distances from a river centerline to its left and right banks at regular intervals (defined by 'step') along the channel. It generates transects orthogonal to a simplified centerline, identifies their intersections with both riverbanks, calculates minimum and maximum distances for each transect section (SEZ-ID), and outputs three vector layers: left bank intersection nodes with distance metrics, right bank intersection nodes with distance metrics, and transect lines enriched with min/max distances to both banks (min-RB-L, max-RB-L, min-RB-R, max-RB-R). The workflow relies on geometric operations (points along lines, line intersections, transect generation, spatial joins) and field calculations—not satellite imagery or time-series analysis.

Generate riverbank safety offset lines. The script computes asymmetric safety buffer zones along left and right riverbanks using erosion rate fields and a user-defined multiplicative factor (M factor). It creates single-sided buffers (left side buffered to the left, right side buffered to the right), unions and dissolves the resulting polygons, removes internal holes, and converts the outer boundary to a multiline vector layer ('Offset line') representing the safety band centerline or envelope boundary. This output is a GIS vector feature class suitable for floodplain management, riparian zoning, or erosion risk mitigation planning.

Segment river banks by reach. The script segments left and right riverbank line features into homogeneous reaches using transect limit lines as cutters, then spatially joins each resulting riverbank segment with the nearest river centerline reach to inherit its attributes (e.g., erosion rate). It outputs two vector layers: 'LRB' (Left River Bank segments with inherited centerline attributes) and 'RRB' (Right River Bank segments with inherited centerline attributes). The workflow consists of: (1) splitting both riverbanks using transect limit lines; (2) computing the maximum length of those transects; (3) performing a nearest-neighbor spatial join between cut riverbanks and centerline reaches, using the max transect length as the search distance threshold to ensure topological correspondence between segments and reaches.

Calculate vector overlaps by class. The script calculates the area and percentage of overlap between input polygon features and overlay polygon features grouped by a user-specified class field. It processes each input feature individually, extracts intersecting overlay features, computes intersection areas per class using QgsDistanceArea with ellipsoidal measurement, and outputs a table with columns: source_id, class, area (in CRS units), and percentage (relative to input feature's total area). The algorithm uses QGIS native processing tools ('extractbyattribute', 'extractbylocation') and QgsGeometryEngine for efficient intersection computation.

Clean building footprints. The script cleans OpenStreetMap-derived building polygon layers by (1) removing interior holes, (2) deleting null geometries, (3) converting multipart polygons to singlepart, (4) ensuring unique OSM ID field presence, (5) removing duplicate buildings based on rounded centroid coordinates (6 decimal places), and (7) generating Voronoi tessellations clipped to a 50-meter buffer around the cleaned buildings. Outputs include a GeoPackage file containing the cleaned single-part building layer and a second GeoPackage layer containing the clipped Voronoi polygons — both saved in a user-specified folder with auto-generated unique filenames.

Clean road network topology. The script performs topological cleaning of a road vector layer using GRASS v.clean tools in QGIS. It executes three sequential cleaning steps: (1) snapping road endpoints within a threshold (0.5 map units), (2) breaking overlapping line segments, and (3) removing duplicate geometries. Before step 3, it optionally sorts features by priority derived from an external CSV mapping of 'fclass' values to integer priorities. Errors are captured in a separate layer, and only features without errors (i.e., no join match on 'cat') are retained in the final output. The cleaned layer is saved as a GeoPackage with '_cleaned.gpkg' suffix, preserving original fields plus an optional 'priority' field, and emits logs, progress, and layer-add signals.

Generate Voronoi and hexagonal tessellations. The script computes spatial tessellations (Voronoi polygons and regular hexagonal grids) anchored to input point or polygon features (e.g., building centroids or OSM structures). It buffers and clips Voronoi cells to the input layer’s extent, generates multiple hexagonal grids at user-specified spacings (converted to map units), filters hexagons intersecting the input layer, assigns the nearest input feature’s ID (e.g., osm_id) to each hexagon, and computes numeric summaries (sums and counts) of all numeric attributes from the input layer’s centroids falling within each hexagon. Outputs are saved as GeoPackage layers: one for Voronoi (if enabled) and one per hexagon spacing, all dissolved by the input ID field.

Generate lidar-derived land cover and LAI. The script processes airborne LiDAR point cloud data (LAS format) in conjunction with vector building footprints to generate five core geospatial raster products: (1) a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) representing bare-earth elevation (masl), derived via FUSION's gridsurfacecreate using ground-classified points (class 2); (2) a Digital Surface Model (DSM) representing top-of-surface elevation (masl), generated by merging building (class 1) and ground points and applying canopymodel; (3) a Canopy DSM (CDSM) representing height above ground (magl), computed from non-building vegetation points (class 1) relative to the DEM, then filtered to remove low-height vegetation (<2.5 m), buffered-building artifacts, and small/noisy patches via morphological raster logic; (4) a land cover (LC) raster (lc.tif) classified into six thematic classes (paved, building, deciduous, grass, etc.) using a rule-based combination of building footprint rasters, CDSM-derived vegetation presence, and intensity-derived grass likelihood (thresholded at intensity 175); and (5) a Leaf Area Index (LAI) raster (lai_10m.tif) estimated at 10 m resolution using the empirical formula −1.94 × ln(Rground/Rtotal), where Rground and Rtotal are return densities over ground (class 2) and all vegetation (class 1) points respectively, computed via FUSION's returndensity.

Delimit pole service areas. The script computes individual service areas for electrical utility poles named 'lv_poles_nalusanga' by generating 30-meter buffers around each point, constructing Voronoi polygons to partition space among neighboring poles, and clipping those polygons to the buffer extent—yielding non-overlapping, distance-constrained service zones (e.g., for load balancing or maintenance planning). The output is a vector layer of clipped Voronoi polygons added to the QGIS map canvas.

Generate pseudo-DSM from building height and topology. The script generates a pseudo-digital surface model (pseudo-DSM) by joining building maximum absolute height (AbsHMax) attributes from a CSV file to Ordnance Survey TopographicArea vector features (GML), then rasterizing the joined layer at 0.5 m resolution using the building height field. It subsequently computes rooftop shading statistics (e.g., shading_mean) for input building footprints (GeoJSON) using this pseudo-DSM, and exports filtered attribute tables (including UPRN, postcode, calculatedAreaValue, AbsHMax, and shading_mean) as GeoJSON files.

Analyze dental clinic accessibility to transit and roads. The script performs spatial accessibility analysis for dental clinics in Tokyo's Setagaya-ku ward, quantifying how many are within 250 m of railway stations (using buffered station points) and how many lie beyond 500 m from road networks. It further identifies wards adjacent to Nakano-ku, wards intersecting highways, computes the proportion of supermarkets located within station buffers, and joins commercial sales volume (SELL) to population polygons via spatial aggregation. Outputs include quantitative metrics (counts and percentages), clipped and derived vector layers (e.g., station buffers, Setagaya-subset features, adjacent wards), a graduated-color map of aggregated sales per population unit, and two PDF map layouts — one comprehensive multi-layer map and one sales-only thematic map with legend, scale bar, and compass.

Extract raster values at field polygons. The script extracts pixel values from multiple user-provided raster layers (e.g., soil moisture, NDVI, elevation) at the locations of a user-specified field polygon. It optionally applies an internal buffer to the polygon, clips each raster to the buffered extent, generates a point grid aligned to the first raster’s resolution and extent, samples all rasters at those points, renames output columns uniquely per raster (handling multi-band rasters with B1/B2 suffixes), and exports the resulting point layer with all sampled values to both a GeoPackage (with geometry and CRS) and a CSV (attribute-only). The outputs are automatically loaded into the QGIS project for inspection.

Compute landmark-influenced street routes. The script computes three shortest paths on a dual graph representation of Münster's street network, where edge weights are modified by angular change values scaled by landmark proximity (via buffer intersection). It filters landmarks using a 'landmark_status = 1' attribute, buffers them at 50 m, joins landmark influence to dual edges, refactors the angular cost field to incorporate landmark weighting (beta = 0.5), runs Dijkstra’s algorithm for three predefined origin–destination pairs, maps the resulting dual-node paths back to the primal street network via streetID joins, and outputs three finalized polyline route layers ('polyRoute1.shp' to 'polyRoute3.shp') in the primal geometry — all within a local coordinate reference system (EPSG:3044).

Identify sugarcane planting failures. The script identifies gaps (failures) in sugarcane planting rows by analyzing high-resolution drone imagery (RGB or NIR+Red) against pre-defined planting line vectors and field boundary polygons. It computes a vegetation index (GLI for RGB or NDVI for NIR+Red), applies thresholding to generate a binary vegetation mask, filters noise via sieve, optionally resamples and simplifies, converts non-vegetated areas intersecting planting lines into vector line segments representing planting failures, filters out segments shorter than a user-defined minimum length (e.g., 0.5 m), and outputs the resulting failure lines with length attribute (comp_m) plus comprehensive statistics including total failure length, count, mean/max length, and percentage of failed planting relative to total line length.

Filter NDVI for crop plots. The script filters NDVI values to retain only those pixels where underlying land cover classification (from a separate 'bands' raster) equals class 4 or 5 (e.g., cropland or vegetation classes), then computes zonal statistics (count, mean, standard deviation) of the filtered NDVI over a user-selected plot polygon (buffered inward by 10 units), and outputs a vector layer enriched with these statistics. The output shapefile retains the plot geometry and appends NDVI summary metrics per plot.

Calculate NDVI-based vegetation statistics for plots. The script processes vector plot boundaries (selected by an attribute ID) and raster bands + NDVI layers to compute zonal statistics (count, mean, standard deviation) of NDVI-derived vegetation pixels within buffered plot geometries. It outputs a shapefile enriched with these statistics as new attribute fields.

Match GPS tracks to road network segments. The script performs map matching of GPX/GPS track data to a road network (segments and nodes), identifying which road segments and nodes are intersected by a buffered GPS track (20 m buffer). It calculates intersection length and percentage per segment, flags segments with ≥75% overlap as matched, outputs matched segments and their statistics (length, count, etc.), and identifies associated network nodes within the matched segment buffer. Outputs include matched segments (geojson), matched nodes (geojson), segment and node statistics (CSV), track buffer (polygon), reprojected and clipped network layers, and intermediate intersection layers.

Calculate protected area percentage per zone. The script computes the percentage of protected area (from WDPA points and polygons) within user-defined administrative or ecological zones. It processes WDPA data by filtering out 'Proposed' and 'Not Reported' status sites and excluding UNESCO-MAB Biosphere Reserves; buffers points using radius derived from REP_AREA (converted to km²), intersects buffered points and filtered polygons with input zones, dissolves and merges protection geometries, joins protection area back to zones, calculates zone area and protection percentage (prot_area_km2 / zone_area_km2 × 100), and exports the result as a PostgreSQL table with an API comment. Output is a vector layer (EPSG:4326) containing per-zone attributes: zone_id, prot_area_km2, zone_area_km2, and pc_prot.

Identify species presence cells. The script identifies grid cells containing species presence points and buffer zones (0.5° radius) for 16 triatomine bug species in Mexico/Central America. It loads species occurrence CSVs (with 'DecimalLongitude' and 'DecimalLatitude' columns, EPSG:4326), overlays them onto a 0.05° vector grid (grid_005d_process4.shp), performs spatial selection-by-location (using INTERSECT, CONTAIN, OVERLAP, ARE WITHIN predicates), assigns binary 'count' or 'b_05' flags to grid cells, exports results as CSV files per species, and cleans up temporary attributes and buffer layers. The study area is implied by species names (e.g., 'mex', 'maz', 'san', 'rub') and GitHub repo name 'r_chagasM' (Chagas disease in Mesoamerica), with grid resolution and coordinate system confirming regional-scale analysis. No satellite, sensor, or band data is used — all inputs are vector-based point and polygon layers.

Delineate upstream catchment polygons. The script delineates upstream catchment areas (Poly_A) for stream gauges by recursively identifying and merging all subbasins that drain to each gauge, using topological relationships (HYDROID/NEXTDOWNID) in a subbasin network layer. It then derives intermediate catchments (Poly_B or Poly_C) by unioning and deduplicating Poly_A polygons, reassigning IDs to match the outlet gauge ID. Outputs are three shapefile sets: (1) individual dissolved upstream polygons per gauge (Poly_A_*.shp), (2) merged upstream basin layer (Poly_A.shp), and (3) either Poly_B.shp (for basin delineation B) or Poly_C.shp (for basin delineation C), both representing non-overlapping, gauge-anchored intermediate catchments.

Delineate catchment area. The script delineates a catchment (watershed) area from a digital elevation model (DEM) using GRASS GIS hydrological tools within QGIS Processing. It computes flow direction and flow accumulation raster layers from the input DEM; identifies the contributing area upstream of a user-specified outlet point using r.water.outlet; extracts a stream network based on a user-defined flow accumulation threshold using r.stream.extract; converts the catchment raster to a vector polygon layer; and clips the stream network to that catchment polygon. All outputs are derived solely from the provided DEM and outlet coordinate — no time-series, spectral bands, or external geospatial datasets beyond the input DEM and point are used. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

Create sanitation planning base layers. The script creates standardized polygon layers for sanitation planning: Area of Interest (AOI), Administrative Boundaries, Existing Sanitation Area, and Water Availability Area — each with UUID fields, domain-specific attribute schemas (e.g., 'SanitationType', 'WaterAvailable', 'AverageWaterConsumption'), default value expressions (e.g., uuid('Id128'), 'true'), and pre-defined QML styles. Optionally, it generates a population density grid by aggregating population data (raster or vector) into user-specified hexagonal/rectangular/diamond grids, applying annual growth projection to estimate target-year population, and computing population density (persons/km²) using $area-based normalization.

Create gridded population density. The script generates a vector grid (rectangle, diamond, or hexagon) over a user-defined extent, aggregates population counts from either a raster or vector input layer into each grid cell, applies exponential population growth to project population to a target year, computes population density (persons per hectare) for each cell, and outputs a styled vector layer with attributes including 'popDensity', 'population', 'YEAR_popdensity', and 'PARAM_AnnualGrowthRate'. It enforces exclusive use of one population source (raster or vector), handles reprojection and spatial indexing for efficiency, filters out empty grids, and applies a predefined QML style.

Generate road-aligned square patches. The script generates square polygon patches aligned to road centerlines using width and orientation derived from road attributes (R22_005) and geometry. It reads a road centerline shapefile and a precomputed buffer polygon layer, reprojects the road layer to EPSG:6675, iteratively places squares along each road segment at intervals equal to their width, rotates each square to match the local road angle, and retains only those squares intersecting the buffer layer. Final output is a FlatGeobuf file of squares reprojected to EPSG:4612, saved in the 'SquarePatches' folder.

Generate transit stop walksheds. The script generates pedestrian catchment areas (walksheds) for public transit stops using a street network dataset. It first buffers all stops at 804.672 meters (½ mile), clips and splits the pedestrian network to that buffered extent, then performs service area analysis (shortest-path network traversal) from each stop to identify reachable network segments within the walking distance. For each route (grouped by 'rte' field), it computes individual walksheds via concave hull refinement of service lines, merges them into route-level dissolved polygons, and outputs three geopackage layers: (1) individual walksheds per stop, (2) dissolved walksheds per route, and (3) the traversed network segments ('service lines'). The workflow relies on QGIS native algorithms including buffer, clip, splitlinesbylength, serviceareafromlayer, convexhull, concavehull, and dissolve.

Assess property suitability for energy infrastructure. The script evaluates land parcels in Bendigo, Australia for suitability as energy infrastructure sites by integrating proximity to transmission lines, solar radiation potential, and parcel area—while excluding protected lands, built-up areas, and restricted planning zones. It performs vector-based spatial erasure (multidifference), centroid generation for raster sampling, and lays groundwork for standardized 0–100 suitability scoring across criteria; outputs include an erased property layer (Property_Suitability.gpkg), a point layer of property centroids (Property_Point.gpkg), and intermediate dissolved exclusion layers.

Compute isochrone polygon union. The script processes isochrone polygons (e.g., travel-time catchments around infrastructure points like water fountains 'fontanelle') to compute a topologically cleaned, area-filtered, and aggregated summary layer. It converts input isochrone polygons to lines, re-polygonizes them to resolve overlaps and slivers, unions them with the original polygons to capture intersections and gaps, filters resulting fragments by minimum area (>1.0 m²), then groups and counts overlapping isochrones per unique area class — assigning a count ('nro') and concatenated list of source IDs ('ids', stripped of 'tp_' prefix) — finally dissolving by 'ids' and removing redundant 'ID' field. The output is a simplified vector layer where each feature represents a spatially contiguous zone sharing the same set of contributing isochrones (e.g., overlapping service areas), with attributes summarizing cardinality and membership.

Fix and dissolve polygonized MBES survey shapes. The script processes shapefiles derived from multibeam echosounder (MBES) data: it first fixes invalid geometries (e.g., self-intersections, ring errors) using QGIS's native:fixgeometries algorithm with method '0 — Try to fix geometries (default)', then dissolves all features into single-part polygons per input shapefile (no attribute-based grouping), and finally merges all dissolved shapefiles into a single unified shapefile (abp49_id001-054_merged.shp) in EPSG:32634. The workflow targets vector geometry integrity and topological simplification of seafloor polygon interpretations, not raster analysis or time-series modeling.

Map localist mapper activity zones. The script analyzes OpenStreetMap (OSM) node edit history to identify and map three types of mapper activity per grid cell: (1) '@localist' — mappers with concentrated, locally weighted activity in their core zones (enhanced by neighbor-grid activity thresholds and multiplicative weighting), (2) '@activist' — the most *recently* active mapper per grid (weighted by edit timestamp decay: 1.0 for <1 yr, down to 0.05 for ≥5 yrs), and (3) '@master' — the mapper with the highest raw edit count per grid. It computes grid-level metrics including '@nodecount' (total edits), '@agesum' (time-weighted edit sum), and '@currentness' (normalized time-weighted average). Outputs include updated grid vector layer attributes, a dissolved single-part 'localist' thematic map (grouping contiguous grids sharing the same '@localist'), and an optional CSV user statistics table listing per-user total edits, time-weighted edits, grid coverage, and counts of localist/activist/master grid assignments.

Convert vector layer to GPX format. The script converts an input vector layer (points, lines, or polygons) into a GPX file suitable for GPS devices. It first fixes geometries, converts polygons to lines if needed, optionally dissolves non-point features (unless a name field is specified), splits multipart points into singleparts, refactors the attribute table to include a 'name' field (either a static display name or dynamic field value), and writes the result using GDAL’s GPX driver with extensions enabled and forced GPX tracks. The output is a valid GPX file containing waypoints (for points), tracks (for lines), or routes — with metadata conforming to GPX 1.1 schema.

Count point features within dissolved polygons. The script dissolves a base polygon layer (e.g., administrative or thematic boundaries) and then, for each selected point layer, subsets points by a categorical field (e.g., land cover type, species ID), counts occurrences per category within each dissolved polygon, outputs individual shapefiles with integer count fields, exports each to CSV, and finally merges all CSVs into a single consolidated CSV file where columns represent counts of distinct point categories per polygon — enabling cross-tabulated spatial aggregation of point data by polygon and attribute class.

Convert SU 3D geometry to polygon. The script converts a 3D OBJ mesh file—representing the top surface of an archaeological Stratigraphic Unit (SU)—into two cleaned, attribute-enriched 3D polygon shapefiles: one in local coordinates (e.g., arbitrary site grid) and one georeferenced to EPSG:32632 (UTM zone 32N). It uses Blender (with BlenderGIS addon) in headless mode to import the OBJ and export an initial shapefile; then applies QGIS processing steps—including geometry fixing, dissolving, hole removal, coordinate translation (by fixed delta: ΔX=452000, ΔY=4413000), projection assignment, and field population (Year, Trench = floor(SU/1000)*1000, SU) —to produce final 3D polygon layers for archaeological spatial documentation and integration into GIS projects.

Convert 3D OBJ surface to 3D polygon. The script converts a 3D Wavefront OBJ file—representing the top surface of an archaeological Stratigraphic Unit (SU)—into two cleaned, attribute-enriched 3D polygon shapefiles: one in local coordinates (unprojected, retained for internal use) and one projected to EPSG:32632 (UTM zone 32N), with fields 'Year', 'Trench' (derived as floor(SU_number/1000)*1000), and 'SU' (user-provided integer). The workflow uses Blender (via BlenderGIS addon) in headless mode to import the OBJ and export an initial 3D shapefile ('POLYGONZ'), then applies QGIS geometry cleaning steps (fix geometries → dissolve → delete holes → fix again), followed by coordinate translation (ΔX=452000, ΔY=4413000), CRS assignment, and field population. Output files are saved to a user-specified folder and loaded into QGIS for verification.

Generate aggregated isochrones for transit accessibility. The script computes multi-temporal isochrones (travel-time polygons) from point locations using the OpenTripPlanner (OTP) routing engine via HTTP API calls. For each input point feature, it iterates over a user-defined datetime range at specified intervals (e.g., every 300 seconds), constructs OTP isochrone request URLs with configurable parameters (mode, walk speed, wheelchair, maxWalkDistance, etc.), downloads zipped shapefile responses, validates geometries, and aggregates results using one of three modes: (1) Max Dissolve (dissolving by time), (2) All Union (spatial union + statistical summary per time bin), or (3) No Agg Raw (individual isochrone polygons per datetime). Outputs a memory vector layer containing all isochrone geometries plus rich metadata attributes — including source feature fields, AggIsochrone_UID/ID, error logs, base URL, datetime range, request interval, requested dates/times, total requests, and time-derived statistics (e.g., time_min, time_mean, time_stddev) — enabling quantitative analysis of temporal accessibility variation.

Generate bounded polygons from frame and delimiter layers. The script generates bounded polygon features by using a selected polygon frame layer as the outer boundary and one or more line or polygon delimiter layers to internally partition or constrain the geometry. It merges all delimiter geometries (converting polygon boundaries to lines), dissolves and fixes them, polygonizes the resulting line network, clips the resulting polygons to the frame layer, optionally removes overlaps with input delimiter polygons, and outputs a memory vector layer with fields 'id' (UUID), 'description' (NULL-initialized), and 'area_otf' (area in square meters calculated in EPSG:31985), grouped under 'istools-output' in the QGIS layer tree.

Convert RGB raster to color-based polygons. The script converts an RGB raster layer named 'map' into a vector layer where each unique RGB color (encoded as R*65536 + G*256 + B) is represented by a single dissolved polygon (i.e., one multipolygon per distinct color). It achieves this by: (1) locating the input raster in the QGIS project; (2) computing a single-band integer raster via raster calculator using band 1 (R), band 2 (G), and band 3 (B) with 8-bit assumptions; (3) polygonizing the resulting integer raster, assigning each pixel’s value to the 'DN' field; (4) dissolving all geometries sharing the same 'DN' value into unified polygons; and (5) adding the final dissolved vector layer named 'map_provinces' to the QGIS project. The output is a thematic vector layer where each feature corresponds to a unique color class — typical for manually digitized or symbolically rendered thematic maps (e.g., land cover legends encoded as RGB pixels).

Generate SWAT+ to MODFLOW connections. The script intersects SWAT+ HRU polygons and channel/reach lines with a MODFLOW active grid (structured, NROW=125, NCOL=222, NLAY=3), computes area fractions for HRU-to-grid cell overlaps and line-length fractions for channel-to-grid cell intersections, filters connections by minimum area fraction (0.05), maps grid IDs to row/column indices using integer division/modulo arithmetic, assigns default MODFLOW layer (1), and exports a GeoPackage table with attributes: swat_obj_type ('hru' or 'channel'), swat_obj_id (hru_id or reach_id), mf_layer, mf_row, mf_col, fraction (for HRUs), and length_m (for channels). The output is used for coupling SWAT+ hydrologic modeling with MODFLOW6 groundwater simulation.

Reclassify and combine NLCD land cover. The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for Alaska to reclassify tree canopy classes (41, 42, 43) into a unified forest class, warp both tree canopy and land cover rasters to EPSG:4326, combine them using conditional pixel replacement, replace urban/clutter classes with grass-related codes, reclassify urban classes (21–24) into simplified urban types (10, 1, 2), apply GRASS median filtering to clean urban features, merge cleaned urban and grass layers, upsample the result by factor 8 using GDAL Warp, smooth with GRASS r.neighbors (size=11, method=median), and compress to 8-bit LZW TIFF. Outputs include 11 intermediate and final rasters named with suffixes like '_Trees-Combined', '_Tree_Canopy_4326', '_Grass-Only_4326', '_Reclassed-Urban_4326', '_Urban-Only_4326', '_Combined-Clean_4326', '_Combined-Clean-HD_4326', '_Smoothed-HD_4326', and '_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326'.

Merge and mask satellite image stacks. The script batch processes satellite imagery by merging multiple raster files per ID from a CSV input table, then clips each merged raster to a user-provided masking shapefile using GDAL's merge and cliprasterbymasklayer algorithms. It deletes intermediate merged rasters after masking. The workflow is executed in QGIS Python console using processing.run() with fixed GDAL algorithm parameters and no dynamic time or band selection logic.

Model river bathymetry surface. The script models high-resolution bathymetric surfaces for selected British Columbia river regions (e.g., T09UWS, T10UDA) using in-situ bathymetric point measurements (ellipsoidal height 'z_el'/'ellipsoida') and river boundary vector data. It performs multilevel B-spline interpolation (SAGA 'grid_spline' module) on WGS84 points to generate a continuous raster surface, clips it to the river corridor, reprojects the surface and points to regional UTM-based CRS (EPSG:3156 or EPSG:3157), re-runs interpolation at 10 m ground resolution, clips again, and tiles the final clipped surface into VRT-aligned GeoTIFFs — retaining only tiles intersecting bathymetric points. Outputs include: (1) QGIS project with styled bathymetry points and clipped surface rasters (WGS84 and projected), (2) CSV files for SDB/SNAP processing containing reprojected coordinates and depths, (3) tiled GeoTIFFs for downstream hydrodynamic or remote sensing applications.

Compute elevation-based volume curves. The script computes a series of cut-and-fill volumes for a clipped DEM by iteratively applying horizontal reference planes (contour levels) from minimum to maximum elevation in 10% increments of the total elevation range. It uses QGIS’s native:rastersurfacevolume algorithm to calculate volumetric earthwork (fill volume above, cut volume below each level), converts results to km³, and exports a CSV table with columns: Level (m), Fill Volume (km³), Cut Volume (km³), Net Volume (km³). The workflow relies on GDAL raster clipping and QGIS raster statistics, not satellite or time-series data.

Extract water level and inundation depth from rasters. The script extracts water level (in cm) and inundation depth (lame_eau) from GeoPackage-stored raster layers, matched to user-provided point features using date-based correspondence. It supports two modes: (1) interval mode — duplicates each input point for every date in a user-specified date range and samples corresponding rasters; (2) field mode — matches each point’s date attribute to the nearest raster (named by water level in cm) and samples a single raster value per point. Outputs include a new QGIS vector layer with added fields 'date_releve_terrain', 'niveau_eau_cm', and 'lame_eau', added to the current project.

Identify thermal refugia patches. The script identifies spatially contiguous thermal refugia patches by polygonizing a binary thermal patch mask raster (value = 1), filtering by minimum area, computing the mean surface temperature (from a co-located thermal raster) within each patch via zonal statistics, calculating the centroid (in WGS84 lon/lat), and exporting both a QGIS vector layer of polygons with attributes (area, mean temperature, lon, lat) and a CSV table listing patch ID, centroid coordinates, area, and mean temperature.

Simplify segmentation line geometry. The script simplifies a vector line layer representing image segmentation boundaries by topologically merging lines adjacent to small polygons (area < 30 units) into those surrounding larger polygons. It achieves this through a multi-step GIS workflow: (1) deriving the input layer’s extent and converting it to a bounding polygon boundary; (2) unioning that boundary with the input segmentation lines; (3) polygonizing the resulting line network to reconstruct polygons; (4) computing polygon areas; (5) selecting and eliminating small polygons (<30 area units) by merging them with neighboring larger polygons; (6) converting the merged polygons back to lines; (7) applying a tiny buffer (1e-5) to the original extent boundary; and (8) computing the symmetrical difference between the new simplified lines and the buffered extent boundary — effectively extracting only the interior simplified segmentation lines, excluding the outer frame. The output is a cleaned, topology-consistent line vector layer with reduced complexity, optimized for cartographic generalization or downstream vector processing.

Generate travel time isochrones. The script computes travel time isochrones from starting points along a road network, using road speed attributes to rasterize roads, assign off-road speeds, calculate per-pixel travel time in minutes or hours, and generate a cost-distance raster representing cumulative travel time. It then applies discrete color-ramped styles for user-defined time intervals (e.g., 5,15,30 minutes) and optionally supports vector isochrone generation (currently commented out). Inputs include a vector roads layer with speed field, vector starting points, resolution, and extent; output is a styled raster of travel time in minutes.

Validate land cover classification accuracy. The script performs comprehensive accuracy assessment of a classified raster map against reference point data. It extracts class values at point locations, constructs an error (confusion) matrix, and computes over 30 validation metrics including Overall Accuracy, Producer/User Accuracies, Kappa coefficients (standard, weighted, conditional), Classification Success Index (CSI/GCSI), Ground Truth Index (GT), entropy-based measures (AMI, NMI, EC), Aickin's alpha, and disagreement components (QD, AD). Outputs include 'error_matrix.txt', 'global_indexes.csv', and 'per_class_indexes.csv' saved to the specified output folder.

Assign stream order to catchments. The script computes catchment boundaries from a depressionless DEM using GRASS r.watershed, rasterizes a drainage line vector layer (with 'ORDER' attribute) to a matching resolution and extent, then assigns the maximum stream order value from the drainage raster to each catchment polygon's corresponding raster cells. The final output is a catchment raster where each cell's value represents the highest stream order intersecting that catchment. Temporary rasters are cleaned up after processing.

Derive protected site boundaries. The script processes vector GIS layers to derive and refine administrative and protected area boundaries (e.g., 'site-ja', 'zone-ja', 'gga-ja') through sequential clipping and difference operations. It starts from input shapefiles (Adp.shp, Gwp.shp, vast_az.shp, gga.shp, bes_arch_site.shp, wrzja.shp, wrzneen.shp) located in local file paths under 'G:/geo-ict-Qgis/', constructs a bounding box from the 'Adp' layer, clips other layers to that extent, then performs cascading set-difference operations (e.g., ADP minus site → siteneen; siteneen minus gebieden → gganeen; gganeen minus zone → zoneneen; etc.) to isolate non-overlapping or conditionally included zones. Final outputs are cleaned, mutually exclusive polygon layers ('cleanzone', 'cleangga', 'cleansite') representing 'yes' subsets (e.g., 'zone-ja') for visualization and integration with pre-processed WRZ (Wetenschappelijke Raad voor het Rijkslandschap?) layers. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is used — all operations are vector-based geometric Boolean logic in QGIS Processing Toolbox (qgis:clip, qgis:difference, saga:difference). CRS is explicitly set to EPSG:31370 (Belge 1972 / Lambert 72), confirming Belgium as the geographic context. Study area is not named explicitly but inferred from CRS, path structure, and layer names (e.g., 'wrz' likely refers to Belgian 'Wetenschappelijke Raad voor het Rijkslandschap').

Generate catchment mask grid. The script generates a regular 5 km × 5 km fishnet grid aligned to the British National Grid (EPSG:27700) covering a user-provided catchment boundary shapefile; it assigns SHETRAN_ID = 0 to grid cells intersecting the catchment and SHETRAN_ID = -9999 to all others; then pivots the attribute table into a raster-like 2D integer array (Y-indexed descending, X-indexed ascending), appends an ESRI ASCII grid header (ncols, nrows, xllcorner, yllcorner, cellsize, NODATA_value), and saves it as a space-delimited text file ('final_mask_SHETRAN.txt') compatible with SHETRAN hydrological modeling software.

Count points within polygons by date. The script counts the number of point features (e.g., observations or events) falling within each polygon feature, then identifies the earliest date among those points per polygon and exports a subset of points corresponding to that minimum date per polygon. It adds a count field to the polygon layer, builds a spatial index for efficient point-in-polygon testing, writes intermediate results to temporary shapefiles named by polygon ID and min date, and finally merges outputs into a single result vector layer. The log file tracks processing steps and errors.

Detect large linear feature changes. The script detects significant geometric changes between two vector line layers (e.g., roads, rivers, pipelines) by buffering each layer and computing geometric differences. It identifies line segments from the Original_Layer that lie outside the buffer of the Updated_Layer (and vice versa), splits multipart geometries, filters segments by minimum length outside buffer (50 m), and writes qualifying features to two output vector layers with error metadata fields. The workflow includes fixed-distance buffering, geometry difference operations, multipart handling, and optional feature deletion based on ID matching.

Calculate road network length within region. The script calculates the total length of road network lines intersecting or contained within a user-provided polygon region. It first reprojects both the road network (line) and region (polygon) layers to the project's CRS, then uses QGIS's 'Sum line lengths' algorithm to compute the sum of road lengths per polygon feature (storing result in a new 'LENGTH' attribute), and outputs a polygon layer with this aggregated length value attached to each region feature.

Compute Largest Empty Circle radii. The script computes the Largest Empty Circle (LEC) radii for a set of input point sites by calculating the Euclidean distance from each Voronoi polygon vertex to its nearest site. It first removes duplicate geometries, generates Voronoi polygons bounding the sites, extracts and deduplicates their vertices, assigns unique IDs to cleaned sites and vertices, computes bounding geometry statistics (diagonal, max search distance, lag distance), performs nearest-hub distance analysis (HubDist) from vertices to sites, and outputs: (1) LEC point layer with HubDist radii, (2) bounding geometry polygon, (3) cleaned sites with Sites_ID, (4) cleaned vertices with Vertices_ID, (5) Voronoi polygons, and (6) HTML statistics report of HubDist values (min, max, mean, std, etc.).

Generate contour lines and polygon areas. The script processes a pre-computed kriging raster (e.g., interpolated elevation or concentration surface) to generate contour lines at user-defined intervals, converts those lines into closed polygons, dissolves polygons by contour elevation (Z) value, computes polygon area and number of parts, and finally counts the number of input point sites (e.g., sampling locations) falling within each contour-derived polygon — outputting both the contour line vector layer and an attribute-enriched polygon layer with area and site count per isoline.

Map gun crime rates by ward. The script analyzes spatial patterns of firearm-related incidents in Washington, D.C. wards by (1) filtering 2017 crime incidents to only those with METHOD = 'GUN', (2) filtering ShotSpotter gunshot detections to those occurring in 2017, (3) performing spatial joins to count gun crimes and shooting incidents per ward using point-in-polygon containment, and (4) computing and printing ward-level rates per 10,000 residents using 2010 population (POP_2010) from the ward boundary layer. Outputs are two shapefiles (join_crime.shp and join_shootings2017.shp) with added per-capita rate fields, and console-printed ward names with their respective gun crime and shooting incident rates per 10,000 people.

Calculate gun crime rate per capita. The script calculates and prints the number of gun crime incidents and ShotSpotter-detected gunshots per 10,000 residents in each Washington, D.C. ward for 2017, using vector-based spatial joins (count points in polygon) and population-normalized field calculations. It loads three local shapefiles — DC ward boundaries (2012), 2017 gun crime incidents, and 2017 ShotSpotter gunshot detections — filters gun crimes by attribute ('METHOD' = 'GUN'), aggregates counts per ward, and computes rates using 2010 ward-level population ('POP_2010') from the boundary layer. Outputs are printed to console as ward-number–rate pairs and saved as new shapefiles with normalized rate fields ('GunCrimePer10K', 'ShotsPer10K').

Extract shoreline from satellite imagery. The script extracts the shoreline as a vector line layer by computing a user-selected water index (NDWI, MNDWI, AWEI, NIR, WI1, or WI2) from multi-band satellite raster input; applying Otsu’s automatic thresholding for binarization; performing morphological opening to remove noise; polygonizing the binary water mask; extracting water polygons (DN = 1); converting them to lines; clipping to input extent (or full raster extent); and simplifying the resulting shoreline geometry using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm with a pixel-size-derived or user-defined tolerance.

Identify crevasse polygons in DEM. The script identifies crevasses (low spots) in a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) using a neighborhood-based statistical comparison: for each pixel, it computes either the mean or maximum elevation within a user-defined (square or circular) neighborhood and flags pixels where the local deviation from that statistic exceeds a user-specified threshold. The result is a binary raster of crevasse locations, converted to vector polygons. Inputs include a DEM raster, optional polygon mask, neighborhood radius, aggregation type (mean/max), deviation threshold, and circularity flag; outputs are a binary crevasse raster and a vector layer of crevasse polygons.

Adjust road gradient and platform elevation. The script auto-adjusts road segment gradients to comply with a user-specified maximum gradient limit (e.g., 1:25) by iteratively modifying endpoint elevations of line segments (Segmentz), propagating adjustments to connected segments via shared nodes (Nodez); it then computes feasible internal access ramp locations and lengths on platform polygons (Platformx) based on perimeter-to-ramp-length ratio and ramp gradient constraints, generates access point features at interpolated positions along intersecting road-platform boundaries, and adjusts platform elevations (platz) to ensure vertical accessibility — outputting four layers: adjusted Nodez (with z, oldz, adj), adjusted Segmentz (with updated grad, styl, oldgrad), updated Platformx (with new Z values), and Access points (with platid, platz, accz, lid, etc.).

Calculate platform cut and fill volume. The script calculates earthwork volumes (cut and fill) for engineered platforms by comparing a digital elevation model (DEM) against platform elevation polygons. It first optionally merges an adjusted platform layer (with updated 'platz' elevation values) with the base platform layer, rasterizes the combined platform elevations to match the DEM resolution and extent, computes the height difference raster (platform elevation minus DEM), then applies QGIS's raster surface volume algorithm to compute total cut (volume below zero) and fill (volume above zero) in cubic meters. Outputs include volumetric totals, total platform area in hectares, average cut/fill height, and applies a QML style to the final platform layer; results are printed to the Log tab.

Identify drainage deadspot at road node. The script identifies drainage deadspots—road nodes where connected road segments have both endpoints at higher elevations, indicating potential water accumulation points due to inadequate downstream gradient. It processes vector layers: (1) a point layer of road nodes with Z-values (elevation), and (2) a line layer of road segments with Z-enabled geometry. Using 'Join by Nearest', it associates each segment with its two nearest nodes; then computes start- and end-point Z-values (sz, ez) via geometry expressions. Aggregating by node ID, it filters for nodes linked to ≥2 segments and calculates the vertical deficit (z_node − min(sz, ez)); nodes with deficit < 3 meters are flagged as deadspots. The result is a point layer of deadspot locations with original node geometry and attributes, styled via a QML file and deduplicated by geometry.

Generate landuse polygons from vector lines. The script generates landuse polygon features by merging input line layers (Road casing, Landuse line, Site boundary line), polygonizing the merged lines to form closed polygons, assigning a 'rod' (road) landuse code to polygons intersecting Road segment lines, and outputting a vector layer with fields 'plotid' (sequential ID) and 'luc' (landuse code). It computes total area and road area in hectares, reports statistics in feedback, and applies a predefined QML style. The workflow assumes topologically clean input lines; users are instructed to snap/trim intersecting lines if polygons fail to form correctly.

Calculate road segment gradient. The script calculates the gradient (expressed as a 1:X ratio) for each input road segment by extracting elevation (Z) values from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) at segment endpoints and nodes, interpolating Z-values for intermediate vertices along the segment length, computing gradient as segment length divided by elevation difference (dz), classifying segments as steep if gradient < (GRADLIM − 0.5), and outputting two layers: (1) 'Segmentz' — a line layer with added fields 'lid' (segment ID), 'wid' (width), 'grad' (gradient 1:X), and 'styl' (styling flag: 1=steep, 0=not steep); and (2) 'Nodez' — a point layer with 'id' and interpolated 'z' (elevation) values. Z-values are extracted via QGIS native:setzfromraster using DEM band 1, and styling is dynamically applied post-processing using categorized rendering based on the GRADLIM parameter.

Reclassify NDWI raster to water/land and compute zonal counts. The script reclassifies an input NDWI raster (values −1 to 1) using a fixed 2-class lookup table ([−1,0,0,0,1,1]) to produce a binary raster where pixel value 0 represents land and 1 represents water; it then computes, for each polygon in the input sites shapefile, the count of land (0) and water (1) pixels within that polygon, appending two new columns (named using an 8-character substring from the raster filename — e.g., year — suffixed with '_0' and '_1') to the output polygon feature class.

Analyze soil moisture percentiles. The script computes zonal statistics of monthly soil moisture percentile raster data (sm_pct_Actual_month.nc) over Australian Local Government Areas (LGA_2020_AUST.shp), classifies mean soil moisture values into seven qualitative vulnerability categories (e.g., 'Extremely Below Average' to 'Extremely Above Average'), and applies a graduated color symbology based on the '_mean' field to visualize spatial patterns of soil moisture conditions across LGAs in Australia.

Reclassify NDWI raster and compute zonal water/non-water counts. The script reclassifies an NDWI raster (values -1 to 1) into two classes (0 = non-water, 1 = water) using a fixed 2×3 reclassification table, then computes the count of each class within polygon features from an input shapefile using zonal histogram. The output is a polygon shapefile with two appended columns named after the raster’s filename substring (e.g., year/month), where '_0' contains non-water pixel counts and '_1' contains water pixel counts per polygon.

Preprocess thin section imagery. The script preprocesses georeferenced thin section scans (TL, XPL, and optional RL images) by merging them into a multi-band raster and then clipping that raster to a user-defined area of interest (AOI) polygon. It uses GDAL's merge and cliprasterbymasklayer algorithms via QGIS Processing Framework. Inputs are multiple georeferenced .tif files and a .shp polygon; outputs are a merged multi-band raster and an AOI-clipped version, both in .tif format, intended for subsequent classification (MiGIS 2) and spatial statistics (MiGIS 3).

Evaluate ROI spectral statistics. The script computes per-band mean and standard deviation of pixel values within user-defined Regions of Interest (ROIs) — polygons representing training classes (e.g., 'clay coating', 'quarz') — overlaid on a clipped multi-band raster of a thin section. It performs zonal statistics for bands 1–9, merges results into a single vector layer with prefixed band statistics (e.g., b1_mean, b1_stdev), exports the merged table as a CSV ('ROI/band statistics'), and generates nine interactive HTML box plots (one per band) showing class-wise distribution of band means (with standard deviation bars), using the class label field for grouping. This supports spectral separability assessment and training dataset validation for thin-section mineral/texture classification.

Classify thin section components. The script classifies mineralogical and textural components (e.g., rock, sediment, soil constituents) in petrographic thin sections using a pre-trained machine learning model (Random Forest via dzetsaka plugin). It takes a clipped multi-band raster containing transmitted light (TL), crossed polarized light (XPL), and reflected light (RL) spectral bands as input; applies the model to generate a per-pixel classification map; computes a confusion matrix against an independent vector-based ROI reference layer (with integer class IDs and string labels); calculates class-wise area statistics in square meters by aggregating raster pixel counts using the spatial resolution metadata; joins class labels from the ROI layer; and generates an HTML bar plot visualizing class areas. All outputs are derived solely from the input raster and reference vector data — no time-series or external geospatial datasets are involved.

Calculate retention basin volume. The script calculates the volumetric capacity (in m³) of a retention basin by generating a 3D artificial surface from an input query line (abfragelinie), based on user-defined barrier height and sedimentation slope (Verlandungsgefälle). It clips a high-resolution ALS-derived DGM (1 m), samples elevation along the line and perpendicular profiles, constructs a 3D polygon representing the theoretical water surface, interpolates it into a raster (TIN), computes the difference raster against the clipped DTM, sums negative differences (i.e., volume below the artificial surface), and outputs both the total retention volume and a smoothed, simplified polygon layer ('stauraum.shp') representing the inundated area. The result is added to QGIS with labeling showing the volume in m³ and semi-transparent blue fill.
