It processes clustered, grouped, and hexagon-labeled point features (e.g., optimized survey targets), applies coordinate transformation to a proprietary UGCS-aligned projection (via empirical affine scaling), inserts a base takeoff point, and exports one JSON file per hexagon cluster (e.g., 'cluster-01.json') into a user-specified folder. The output includes safe RTH altitude, max flight altitude, vehicle/payload profiles, and failsafe configurations.

Calculate demographic indicators by administrative units. The script computes population-based demographic indicators (e.g., aging index, dependency ratios, foreign population share, child-to-women fertility ratio) by aggregating census microdata to user-selected spatial units (ILLES, PARCELES, SECCIONS, BARRIS, DISTRICTES POSTALS, DISTRICTES INE) or custom legend layers. It constructs SQL queries to join census records with geometry tables via cadastral or address matching, applies filters (age, gender, education, origin, nationality), computes absolute counts, relative percentages, densities, and standardized indices, then renders the results as styled vector layers in QGIS with graduated symbology and optional labels.

Generate elevation profile along line. The script generates an elevation profile graph (distance vs. elevation) by sampling a digital elevation model (DEM) at regularly spaced points along a user-defined line path derived from input point features. It computes cumulative geodesic distances between consecutive sampled points using WGS84 ellipsoid, extracts corresponding elevation values, and plots the profile with min/max/mean elevation reference lines, grid, and shaded fill; outputs a matplotlib figure and prints summary statistics (min, max, mean elevation in feet, total distance in feet).

Identify sub-basin outlet points. The script identifies, for each sub-basin polygon, a single target point on the river network — either the most upstream (first vertex), most downstream (last vertex), or a specific-index vertex — assuming consistent digitization direction of river polylines. It achieves this by extracting all vertices from the input river layer, spatially joining them to sub-basin polygons, then selecting one vertex per sub-basin based on vertex index extremum or exact match. The output is a memory-based point vector layer with attributes 'Subbasin' (ID) and 'vertex_index', added to the QGIS project.

Generate sub-basin virtual precipitation stations. The script generates time-series 'virtual station' files (e.g., '123_precip.txt') for each sub-basin by computing a Thiessen-polygon-weighted average of observed point precipitation data from .txt files; it also produces a weights CSV ('thiessen_weights_precip.csv') linking stations to sub-basins via intersected polygon areas, and a summary CSV listing generated virtual stations with date ranges and filenames.

Resample elevation raster to finer resolution. The script resamples a digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer named 'DEM' from its original resolution to a finer resolution using a two-step geoprocessing workflow: (1) standardizing the input raster via GDAL warp/reproject to a clean GeoTIFF at original resolution, then (2) applying GRASS r.resample to upscale resolution by a user-defined scale_factor (e.g., 2 → halving pixel size). Inputs and outputs are local file paths (e.g., 'E:/Project_folder/UTM_DEM_resample_input.tif', 'E:/Project_folder/UTM_DEM_scaled.tif'); no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or classification is involved. The final output is a newly resampled raster layer added to the QGIS project with verified pixel dimensions and CRS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified — the script operates on an existing local DEM layer loaded by name ('DEM') in QGIS.

Align raster layers to reference geometry. The script aligns user-selected raster layers to a chosen reference raster layer by (1) warping/reprojecting/clipping each source raster to match the reference’s CRS, extent, and cell size using GDAL’s warpreproject algorithm, and (2) applying a multiplicative mask using the reference raster’s values via GDAL’s raster calculator (A*B). Outputs are aligned, masked GeoTIFF files (Float64) saved to a user-specified folder; optionally, they are added to the QGIS project under a dedicated '01. Aligned layers' group.

Replace raster NoData values. The script replaces undefined or existing NoData pixel values in input raster layers with a user-specified numeric value (e.g., -9999 or 0), using GDAL Translate to inject NoData where missing (especially for Byte/UInt16 rasters) and GDAL Raster Calculator to conditionally substitute pixels matching the original NoData value. It outputs new GeoTIFF files with consistent NoData handling, optionally adding them to the QGIS project.

Map PEB noise zone impact. The script generates standardized PDF cartographic layouts for French aerodromes, each showing the official Plan d'Exposition au Bruit (PEB) noise zones (A–D), impacted buildings (clipped to PEB), and intersected constructible urban planning zones (PLU), with statistics on building counts per noise zone and total constructible surface area (m²); outputs include a GeoPackage archive of PEB, clipped buildings, and PLU-PEB intersection layers, plus a branded PDF map with legend, scale bar, north arrow, metadata, and DGAC logo.

Model retention pond site suitability. The script performs a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compute a site suitability score for retention ponds by spatially joining and weighting four precomputed grid layers: Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), Rainfall, Land Cover/Land Use (PL), and Soil Type (JTNH), all aligned by a common 'id' field. It calculates MCDA = 0.30×S_Rain + 0.30×S_TWI + 0.20×S_PL + 0.20×S_JTNH, then classifies the result into four qualitative categories ('Tidak sesuai' to 'Sangat sesuai') in a new vector layer containing all input scores plus MCDA and K_MCDA fields.

Sum monthly CHIRPS rainfall. The script computes annual rainfall by summing 12 monthly GeoTIFF rasters from the CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group Infrared Precipitation with Stations) dataset, all belonging to the same year and stored in a user-specified local folder. It enforces NoData handling (-9999) via GDAL VRT preprocessing, performs pixel-wise summation with strict NoData propagation (using QGIS Cell Statistics or fallback GRASS r.series), and outputs a compressed, georeferenced annual rainfall raster in mm. Input filenames must conform to a configurable pattern (e.g., 'chirps-v2.0.-2024-01_jawa.tif') to identify months 01–12; the script validates presence, sorts chronologically, and fails gracefully if any month is missing.

Compute multi-year mean rainfall. The script computes the multi-year mean annual rainfall raster by first aggregating monthly CHIRPS GeoTIFFs (01–12) per year into annual totals (sum), then calculating the arithmetic mean across all years in the specified range (e.g., 1981–2024). It enforces strict NoData propagation: any pixel with missing data in ≥1 monthly input within the stack results in NoData in the final output. Input rasters are preprocessed to enforce -9999 as NoData via GDAL VRT, and fallback GRASS-based averaging with validity masking ensures robustness. The final output is a compressed GeoTIFF with NoData = -9999.

Map museum locations in Paris. The script retrieves museum records for Paris from the Île-de-France regional open API, creates a point layer with full attribute preservation in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), applies green marker symbology, loads a Paris administrative boundary GeoJSON, generates individual A6-sized PNG map exports (300 dpi) centered on each museum and framed by the Paris boundary, and additionally extracts and maps railway stations intersecting Paris using spatial overlay — all within a cleaned QGIS project environment.

Map museum accessibility by walking isochrones. The script maps walking accessibility (5- and 10-minute isochrones) from officially designated 'Musée de France' institutions in Paris, using OpenRouteService API. It integrates museum locations (from Île-de-France Open Data API), Paris administrative boundary (Paris.geojson), and railway station locations (Gares_4326.gpkg). Key workflow steps include: (1) fetching museum records via REST API with filter 'commune = "Paris"'; (2) creating WGS84 point layer with all API fields; (3) extracting stations within Paris using 'extractByLocation'; (4) computing foot-walking isochrones (300m/600m) per museum via ORS API; (5) identifying stations intersecting the 10-minute isochrone; (6) applying categorized symbology to gares (SVG markers for accessible stations, red circles for others); (7) generating individual A6 PNG location maps centered on each museum; and (8) producing detailed PDF layouts per museum including title, metadata, Wikipedia-derived summary text, scale bar, north arrow, legend, logo, and inset location map. Study area is Paris (city), data sources are regional open data (Île-de-France), Wikipedia (scraped), ORS API, CartoDB Positron tiles, and local GPKG/GeoJSON files. No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used.

Simulate flood depth from rainfall and land use. The script simulates flood inundation depth for six administrative districts in Beijing under multiple future scenarios (2021 and 2031) using the SCS-CN hydrological model. It dynamically maps land use codes to Curve Numbers (CN), computes runoff volume from design rainfall (100-year event), and solves for equilibrium flood elevation via binary search on a high-resolution DEM; outputs are per-watershed, per-scenario GeoTIFF rasters of flood depth (in meters), clipped to Level 12 micro-watersheds.

Simulate flood depth. The script simulates flood inundation depth (in meters) for three rainfall return periods (10-yr, 50-yr, 100-yr) using the SCS-CN hydrologic model and topographic filling logic. It processes watershed polygons (Beijing_Watersheds_L8.shp), a 30-m DEM (Beijing_DEM_30m.tif), and a 10-m Curve Number raster (Beijing_CN_10m.tif) to compute runoff volume per watershed, then applies binary search on the clipped DEM to derive the water surface elevation that matches that volume; final output is a set of GeoTIFF rasters (Float32) named 'Flood_{HYBAS_ID}_{scenario}.tif', where pixel values represent local water depth (m) above ground, with NoData = 0. Study area is Beijing, China; no satellite or time-series data used — all inputs are static, pre-processed geospatial layers.

Generate concentric buffer rings. The script generates a series of non-overlapping, geometrically precise concentric ring-shaped polygons (annuli) centered on input point features. Each ring has an exact width ('Shape Width') and exact spacing between successive rings ('Buffer Distance'), calculated as absolute distances from the original base points—not cumulatively—ensuring consistent geometry across iterations. Rings are constructed via buffered outer/inner circles (with configurable segment count, cap/join styles), followed by geometric difference and dissolution. The output is a single merged vector layer containing all rings as polygon geometries.

Detect parcel evolution by geometry. The script performs a geometric change detection analysis between two agricultural parcel vector layers (T1 and T2) using QGIS processing tools. It harmonizes CRS, fixes geometries, computes a topological union to decompose overlapping and non-overlapping polygon areas, then calculates per-geometry surface area for each time step (surf_T1, surf_T2), absolute and relative change (var_abs, var_pct), and classifies each resulting geometry into one of five status categories: 'nouvelle' (new parcel at T2 only), 'disparue' (parcel present at T1 only), 'conservee' (area change < user-defined % threshold), 'augmente' (positive % change ≥ threshold), or 'diminuee' (negative % change ≥ threshold). Outputs include a GeoPackage or Shapefile vector layer with these attributes and an optional CSV export of the attribute table.

Identify disconnected poles and chambers. The script performs spatial quality control on utility infrastructure layers: (1) it fixes geometries of the 'route' (line) layer to ensure topological validity; (2) it identifies 'poles' that are spatially disjoint (i.e., not intersecting or touching) the fixed routes, outputting them as a new layer named 'Diconnected_Poles'; (3) it first extracts chambers that *touch* the fixed routes, then identifies chambers that are *disjoint* from those touching chambers — effectively isolating chambers with no topological connection to the route network — and outputs them as 'Disconnected_Chambers'. All outputs are vector layers added to the QGIS project with descriptive names and printed status messages.

Analyze masonry component dimensions. The script performs quantitative analysis of architectural masonry components (e.g., stones, bricks, blocks) from vector polygon survey data. It computes oriented minimum bounding boxes (OMBBs) for each component to extract geometric attributes — width, height, angle, perimeter, and area — then calculates modular metrics relative to a user-defined module (e.g., Roman foot = 0.296 m), including integer modulo counts (width_modulo, height_modulo) and remainders (Δwidth_modulo, Δheight_modulo). It applies optional material-based filtering, separates components by 'intera'/'parziale' surface condition if the field exists, computes aggregate statistics (count, min/max/mean/stddev/range) on width, height, and area, and generates binned frequency distributions ('range' tables) for width and height using configurable step intervals. Outputs include: (1) oriented bounding box polygons with geometric fields; (2) enriched survey layer with all computed metrics and virtual modulo fields; (3) tabular aggregate statistics; (4) categorical count tables for width and height ranges.

Analyze dry-stone component dimensions. The script performs quantitative analysis of dry-stone masonry components (e.g., stones, blocks) from vector polygon survey data. It computes oriented minimum bounding boxes (OMBB) for each component polygon to extract geometric metrics: width_bbox, height_bbox, angle_bbox, perimeter_bbox, and area_bbox. It then calculates modulo-based metrics (width_modulo, Δwidth_modulo, height_modulo, Δheight_modulo) using a user-defined module value (default 0.296 m, corresponding to the Roman/Attic foot). Statistics (count, min, max, mean, stddev, range) are aggregated over width, height, and area fields — restricted to 'intera' (full) components if the optional 'superficie' field is present, otherwise applied to all components. Outputs include: (1) OMBB polygons with geometric attributes; (2) enriched survey layer with bbox metrics and modulo fields; (3) tabular aggregate statistics; (4) categorical frequency distributions for width and height ranges (binned by user-specified step sizes). No remote sensing or raster data is used — input is strictly vector-based survey polygons. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

Identify post-earthquake building construction. The script identifies buildings constructed within a user-specified time interval (e.g., 1–10 years) after selected earthquake events, using buffer zones around earthquake point features to spatially constrain the analysis. It loads two local vector layers: 'Edifici.gpkg' (buildings with 'Data Edificio' attribute) and a QGIS active layer containing earthquake points (with 'Anno' attribute). For each selected earthquake, it creates a buffer polygon (distance input by user), clips buildings intersecting that buffer, filters them by construction year ('Data Edificio') falling in [Anno, Anno + intervallo], and outputs a final clipped layer 'ritaglioFinale' of qualifying buildings. The output is added to the QGIS project as a new vector layer. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are local vector files. Study area and time range of earthquakes/buildings are not specified in the code.

Generate stage-discharge sensitivity curves. The script performs a dual-zone (channel + floodplain) hydraulic modeling workflow to generate stage-discharge (Q–h) sensitivity curves by systematically varying Manning’s n roughness coefficients per land cover class across 30 water level multipliers (0.1–3.0× base water level). For each stage factor, it computes inundation depth using HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) and base water level rasters, classifies pixels as channel or floodplain using a vector mask, assigns land cover–specific roughness values, calculates cross-sectional hydraulic properties (flow area, wetted perimeter, hydraulic radius), and applies the Manning equation to compute discharge for all combinations of n values. Outputs include: (1) per-stage inundation rasters, (2) individual Excel files containing all n-combination discharges and flow areas, and (3) aggregated discharge values written into a pre-existing summary Excel workbook ('QGIS-Calculations-San-Isidro.xlsx') under the 'Cabula Curve List' sheet for hydrologic curve number (CN) or rating curve analysis.

Split monthly climate raster bands. The script splits a multi-band raster into individual single-band GeoTIFF files (monthly mode) or yearly multi-band GeoTIFF files (yearly mode), with automatic labeling using month names and years (e.g., 'tmax_Jan_2023.tif') or year-only labels (e.g., 'ppt_2023.tif'). It applies a consistent pseudocolor renderer (using min/max statistics across bands) to newly created yearly rasters. The input is any multi-band raster (not sensor-specific), but the algorithm’s documentation and group name ('TerraClimate Downloader') strongly indicate it is designed for TerraClimate datasets — gridded, global, monthly climate variables (e.g., precipitation, max temperature) spanning 1958–present at ~4.5 km resolution. No spatial subsetting, reprojection, or classification is performed; only band extraction and file export via GDAL translate. Outputs are georeferenced GeoTIFFs with LZW compression, optionally added to QGIS map canvas with styling.

Download TerraClimate climate variable. The script downloads and clips TerraClimate gridded climate data for a user-defined polygon area of interest. It connects to the TerraClimate OPeNDAP server (http://thredds.northwestknowledge.net:8080/thredds/dodsC/TERRACLIMATE_ALL/data) to fetch NetCDF files (e.g., TerraClimate_ppt_2024.nc) for selected variables (e.g., 'ppt', 'tmax', 'pdsi') and years (1958–2025). It subsets spatially using bounding box with optional buffer (in degrees), optionally selects one month or all 12 months per year, concatenates multi-year/multi-month data into a raster stack, writes a temporary GeoTIFF, then clips it precisely to the input polygon using GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer. The output is a single GeoTIFF file with band(s) corresponding to time steps (e.g., 12 bands for monthly 2024; 24 bands for Jan–Dec 2024 & 2025), styled with variable-specific pseudocolor ramps (e.g., 'precipitation' ramp for 'ppt'), and added to the QGIS map canvas. No study area, satellite, sensor, or custom geometry is hardcoded — the AOI is fully user-provided via input vector layer.

Offset itinerary stroke points at intersections. The script processes vector layers representing itinerary strokes (strokes_iti) and intersection nodes (noeuds_graph) to generate displaced (offset) point features at each stroke–node intersection. It buffers nodes, computes line–buffer-boundary intersections, identifies whether each intersecting point lies near the start or end of the corresponding stroke segment (using geometry extremity logic), calculates local line direction and normal vectors, and places offset points perpendicular to the stroke at a distance scaled by an 'offset' attribute and a user-defined 'largeur' parameter. Outputs are: (1) a memory vector layer 'points_offset' containing displaced points with attributes including angle, dx/dy components, offset value, stroke/route IDs, and extremity flag; and (2) a difference layer 'layer_iti_visu' showing itinerary strokes clipped outside node buffers — intended for visual separation of overlapping strokes at junctions in cartographic rendering.

Export vector layers to file formats. The script exports selected QGIS vector layers to various geospatial file formats (e.g., GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage, CSV, DXF) with optional reprojection to a user-specified CRS. It handles geometry-preserving and non-geometry formats separately, warns about attribute-only exports (e.g., CSV/XLSX), applies filename sanitization, logs progress and errors, and supports French/English UI localization.

Aggregate building volume to grid cells. The script processes building footprint (Hausumringe) and LoD2 3D building data to compute per-building floor area and volume (floor_area × measuredHeight), then spatially overlaps these buildings with a user-provided grid, aggregates total floor area and total building volume per grid cell, and joins the aggregated metrics back to the original grid geometry. It outputs two GeoPackage files: (1) individual buildings with attributes 'floor_area' and 'building_volume', and (2) grid cells enriched with 'total_floor_area' and 'total_building_volume' — enabling urban morphology and density analysis at the grid level.

Calculate building floor area per grid cell. The script computes the total floor area of buildings (from vector building footprints) within each grid cell by geometric intersection and aggregation. It first verifies and reprojects the building footprint layer (Hausumringe) to match the project CRS, clips it to the Coburg administrative boundary, calculates planimetric area per building feature, performs vector overlap analysis to determine how much of each building falls into each grid cell, aggregates overlapping areas by grid cell ID, and finally joins the aggregated floor areas back to the original grid layer—producing a grid-layer GeoPackage with an attribute 'floor_area_per_grid' representing the summed building floor area per cell.

Map roof area per urban grid cell. The script computes total rooftop area per grid cell by spatially joining 3D building roof geometries (from a CityGML/3DCityDB database) with a regular grid, then aggregates roof area values by grid ID. It outputs a GeoPackage file (geodataframe_newwip_cleaned_roof_grid.gpkg) containing grid cells enriched with summed roof area, alongside intermediate layers including stripped/merged GML buildings, PostGIS-joined roof-area attributes, and spatially joined roof–grid features.

Assess radioactive leak impact area. The script assesses the geographic impact area of a radioactive leak at the Asco Nuclear Power Plant by generating concentric buffer zones (2 km, 3 km, 5 km) around a fixed incident point (296590.70333919115, 4564089.212024709) in EPSG:25831, clipping municipal boundaries from a GeoPackage layer to the 5 km buffer, calculating total affected population from the 'POBLACION' attribute, labeling municipalities with 'NOMCAP', overlaying an SVG nuclear plant marker, and producing a PDF map layout with title, footer (population count), north arrow, and legend-equivalent visual hierarchy via colored buffers.

Extract water polygons from binary mask. The script converts an input binary raster layer (where pixel value 1 = water, 0 = non-water) into clean vector polygons by: (1) pixel-to-polygon conversion using GDAL’s polygonize algorithm; (2) filtering to retain only features where the 'is_water' attribute equals 1; (3) dissolving all adjacent water polygons into a single multipart geometry to eliminate internal boundaries; and (4) converting the dissolved geometry into individual singlepart polygons (e.g., separate river segments, lakes, or disconnected water bodies). The final output is a vector layer of simple, non-overlapping, water-only polygons suitable for area calculation, spatial analysis, or cartographic display.

Calculate weighted mean radon levels per parish. The script computes a weighted mean radon concentration (based on 'CLASS_MAX' values from the Radon Indicative Atlas v3) for each parish polygon, using area-weighted intersection with radon polygons. It reprojects input GeoPackage and MBTiles layers to EPSG:27700 (OSGB 1936 / British National Grid), loads three key layers (parish boundaries, radon atlas, ceremonial county boundaries), performs spatial intersection and area-weighted aggregation, writes the result into a new 'mean_radon' attribute in the parish layer, applies a Jenks natural breaks graduated color ramp (green-to-red) for visualization, and exports one A4 landscape PNG map per ceremonial county showing the parish-level radon means masked to that county’s boundary — including custom gradient legend, scale bar, and title. The study area is implicitly the UK (EPSG:27700 CRS, 'ceremonial counties', 'parish' administrative units, 'Radon_Indicative_Atlas_v3'). No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are vector geospatial datasets (GeoPackage, MBTiles).

Calculate composite curve number. The script calculates area-weighted composite Curve Numbers (CN) for hydrological modeling by intersecting subbasin, land use, and soils polygon layers; it performs geometry repair, CRS reprojection (to EPSG:3361), sequential intersections (land use × soils → result × subbasins), area recalculation from post-intersection geometries (in acres), CN lookup via user-provided CSV/Excel table mapping land use and soil hydrologic group (A–D) to CN values, and outputs a shapefile with decimal (CN_Comp) and integer-rounded (CN_Int) CN fields, plus detailed and summary CSVs including area validation metrics (reference vs. intersection area difference %).

Calculate area-weighted composite runoff coefficient. The script calculates area-weighted composite runoff coefficients (C values) for catchments by intersecting user-provided polygon layers — catchment boundaries, land use/land cover, and soil hydrologic groups — then applying slope-category–specific C values from an external lookup table (CSV or Excel). It outputs: (1) a shapefile of catchments with added 'C_Comp' (composite C) and 'Area_acres' attributes; (2) a detailed CSV listing each intersected land-use/soil/slope sub-area, its C value, and C×area product; and (3) a summary CSV with per-catchment total area, sum of C×area, and final composite C. The workflow includes reprojection to EPSG:3361, sequential vector intersections, soil group parsing (e.g., handling 'A/B' → 'B'), and validation-driven GUI controls.

Classify forest stand povoamento. The script processes point-based SB_AZ (Arborização) data — likely field-surveyed tree locations with 'PAP' (probably 'Perímetro à Altura do Peito', i.e., trunk circumference at breast height) measurements — to identify and map forest stand povoamento (i.e., self-sustaining, closed-canopy forest patches meeting minimum density and size criteria). It computes crown radius ('RAIO_COPA') from PAP using a piecewise linear lookup, buffers points by that radius, applies a 10 m continuity buffer and dissolves to form contiguous patches ('manchas'), filters for patches ≥ 0.5 ha, assigns ID_MANCHA, joins tree attributes back to patches, aggregates per patch (count of trees, mean PAP, class), calculates tree density (N_ARVORES / AREA_HA), and classifies povoamento as 'SIM' if density thresholds are met per PAP-derived class (1–4). A two-pass classification is performed: first on original patches, then a repescagem (re-evaluation) of non-classified patches using mean PAP from associated points, followed by reclassification and merging. Final output is a dissolved polygon layer '23_POVOAMENTO_FINAL' representing classified forest stands. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; input is purely vector point data ('Camada SB_AZ (pontos)') with attribute-driven geometric and statistical operations. Study area, time range, and external data sources are not specified in the code.

Model drainage classes from water level points. The script models surface drainage conditions by interpolating point-based water level measurements (vandspejlspunkter) using Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), then subtracting the interpolated water surface raster from a Digital Height Model (DHM) to compute depth-to-water-table (in cm). It reclassifies the resulting difference raster into seven hydrologically meaningful drainage classes (e.g., '< 0 cm Frit vandspejl', '0–25 cm Sump', up to '100–125 cm Mark'), converts the classified raster to polygons, assigns descriptive class names via field calculation, and applies a categorized fill symbology with predefined colors and black outlines. The final output is a vector polygon layer representing spatially explicit drainage condition classes.

Interpolate terrain elevation. The script interpolates a continuous, filled high-resolution digital elevation model (DEM) for a user-defined polygonal area ('Område') by sampling elevation values from an input DEM ('DHM'), generating dense sample points along the boundary and interior of the area, applying Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation with power=5 and radius=100 m, clipping the interpolated surface to the input polygon, and merging it with the original DHM raster to produce a seamless 'Fyldt højdemodel' (filled elevation model) that preserves original terrain data outside the interpolation zone while filling or refining elevation within the target area.

Extract terrain elevation along offset transects. The script processes point features representing a linear survey (e.g., VASP survey points), converts them into a path, offsets that path left or right by 10 meters to define a terrain sampling line, generates equally spaced sample points (1 m interval) along the offset line, assigns station numbers starting from a user-defined integer, samples elevation values from a digital height model (DHM) at each point, and exports the resulting point layer—including station number, sampled terrain elevation ('bundkote'), an empty 'vsp' field, and a fixed 'Bemærkning' = 'Terrain'—to an Excel spreadsheet for engineering/terrain analysis.

Classify and buffer hydrographic network by order. The script processes a vector-based hydrographic network layer by clipping it to an administrative boundary, then classifying stream segments into Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary orders using the 'Codigo' attribute (values 1, 2, 3), assigning distinct colors for visualization, and generating order-specific buffers (100 m, 50 m, and 20 m respectively); outputs are three temporary vector layers — 'Buffer_Primaria', 'Buffer_Secundaria', and 'Buffer_Terciaria' — each representing buffered zones for their respective stream order.

Extract OSM buildings and roads. The script queries the Overpass API to extract OpenStreetMap (OSM) building and road features within a user-defined polygon area. It constructs an Overpass QL query targeting 'way' elements with 'building' or 'highway' tags, parses the JSON response, reconstructs geometries from node coordinates, assigns relevant OSM tags as attributes, reprojects to the project's CRS if requested, clips the extracted features to the input polygon, and outputs three layers: (1) a clipped polygon layer of individual buildings, (2) a dissolved polygon layer of merged (adjacent/touching) buildings, and (3) a clipped line layer of roads.

Derive slope and stream networks. The script processes a digital elevation model (DEM) mosaic to compute terrain slope, reclassify slope into restriction classes (0–25°, 25–45°, ≥45°), extract stream networks and spring points (as vector features), and clip all outputs to a user-provided polygon area of interest. It uses GRASS GIS hydrological tools (r.fill.dir, r.stream.extract) for flow direction and stream delineation, GDAL slope computation, raster reclassification, and vector clipping to generate five final products: (1) clipped slope raster, (2) raster of areas with slope >45°, (3) raster of areas with slope 25–45°, (4) clipped stream network vector, and (5) clipped spring point vector.

Delineate riparian and spring protection areas. The script delineates Areas of Permanent Preservation (APP) in Brazil by generating buffer zones around hydrographic features (rivers/streams) and springs (point sources), merging and dissolving the buffers into a single polygon layer, and clipping the result to a user-provided administrative or study area boundary. It outputs a vector layer ('APP') representing legally mandated environmental protection zones adjacent to water bodies and headwaters, as defined by Brazilian environmental legislation (e.g., Law 12.651/2012).

Clip airports buffer to county boundary. The script selects the 'Nueces' county from a counties shapefile, creates a new layer containing only that county, loads an airports point layer, generates a 5000-meter buffer around airports (without dissolve), and clips that buffer layer to the Nueces county boundary. The output is a clipped polygon layer ('clippedbufferAirports.shp') representing only the portions of the airport buffers intersecting Nueces County.

Generate hunting lot-parcel intersection layers. The script processes vector layers representing hunting lots and land parcels to generate two new output layers: (1) a parcel-lot intersection layer ('parclot') containing geometric intersections with calculated surface area and proportional 'contenance' (a land management attribute), and (2) a dissolved lots layer ('nwlots') aggregating intersected geometries by lot ID, enriched with total contenance per lot; both outputs are saved in a GeoPackage, styled with categorized symbology, aliased field names, and inserted at the top of the QGIS layer panel.

Quantify urban land area near rivers. The script calculates the surface area (in hectares) of urban land cover (LULC classes DN=1 and DN=2) within 50 m of rivers (SWAT-referenced waterways), then computes an aesthetic service metric (Hpd) by multiplying the urban area (ha) by a fixed coefficient (194.129488213811). It also clips urban LULC to a 500–50 m buffer annulus around rivers for comparative spatial analysis. Outputs include a vector layer with a new 'Hdp' attribute representing the computed aesthetic service value per feature.

Simplify boundary geometry. The script simplifies the input polygon boundary layer using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm with a user-defined tolerance (in meters), after reprojecting to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) for metric consistency; it computes and appends vertex counts before and after simplification, then reprojects the result back to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) and fixes geometries to ensure topological validity. The output is a vector layer of simplified polygons with two new integer fields: 'vertices_boundary' and 'vertices_simplified'.

Convert application points to rectangles. The script converts point features representing agricultural as-applied data (e.g., fertilizer, pesticide, or seed application) into oriented rectangular polygons. It reads heading (azimuth), distance (length), and width attributes from input points; converts units from feet to meters; computes rectangle vertices by rotating and translating a centered axis-aligned rectangle; reprojects input points to UTM using an automatically computed zone (based on extent centroid longitude/latitude); constructs polygons in UTM coordinates; then reprojects the resulting rectangles back to WGS 84. The output is a polygon vector layer where each rectangle represents the spatial footprint of an application event, oriented per heading and sized per distance and width.

Reclassify land cover raster. The script reclassifies an input land cover raster using a user-defined lookup table, then reprojects it to an equal-area CRS (ESRI:54009) and resamples to a specified pixel size (e.g., 1000 m); the primary output is a reclassified and reprojected land cover raster ('LC_reclassified'), intended for subsequent CoE (Convergence of Evidence) layer computation in a QGIS plugin context.

Calculate D'Hondt seat allocation. The script calculates parliamentary seat allocations per constituency using the D'Hondt method (highest averages method) applied to party vote counts. It reads a vector layer with total votes, per-party vote columns, and seat counts per region; applies an optional electoral threshold (percentage-based on total votes across all regions); filters out parties below threshold; then iteratively assigns seats by dividing each party's votes by (mandates+1) and awarding the next seat to the party with the highest quotient (with tie-breaking by raw vote count). Output is a vector layer with original attributes plus new integer fields named 'SEATS_<party_column>' containing allocated seat counts per party per feature.

Export ERT profile topography. The script processes electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) line vector layers and a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to extract elevation-sampled points along electrode-spaced profiles. It reprojects point coordinates into an optional additional CRS, writes topographic data to .attab (profile-ordered tabular elevation/distance), .top (aggregated topography summary), and augments existing .dat resistivity files with appended topographic sections (as _topo.dat) including median-filtered DEM values. It optionally generates Res2DInv batch (.bth) files and triggers inversion runs via system calls.

Import geoelectrical survey metadata. The script imports and processes geoelectrical resistivity survey data from .dat and optional .2dm files located in a user-specified directory. It extracts per-profile metadata—including profile length, electrode spacing, array type (e.g., Wenner-Alpha, Dipole-dipole), device info, operator, notes, and acquisition time—from structured ASCII files; joins this metadata to an input QGIS line vector layer (representing survey profiles) using profile ID; computes GIS-derived profile length, azimuth, cardinal direction, and length error percentage; and outputs an enriched vector layer with all attributes plus a companion CSV docsheet summarizing key parameters per profile.

Identify suitable terrain areas. The script identifies terrain areas suitable for development or land use based on slope constraints (15°–45°) derived from LiDAR point cloud data (LAZ), then excludes zones within specified buffer distances of buildings (30 m), roads (100 m), watercourses (50 m), railways (60 m), and protected areas (via direct difference). It outputs two vector layers: (1) 'Vyselektovaneuzemi' — the final filtered area after all exclusions, and (2) 'Vysledekrastru' — intermediate candidate terrain polygons (>15,000 m²) meeting slope criteria before infrastructure/environmental exclusions.

Calculate DRASTIC groundwater vulnerability index. The script computes the DRASTIC index — a standardized, weighted-sum groundwater pollution vulnerability assessment — by processing seven geospatial factors: Depth to water (D, derived from inverse distance weighting interpolation of well elevation data), net Recharge (R, reclassified from annual rainfall raster), Aquifer media (A, reclassified from geology vector layer using user-provided CSV lookup), Soil media (S, reclassified from soil vector layer using user-provided CSV lookup), Topography (T, derived from slope of digital elevation model), Impact of vadose zone (I, reclassified from soil vector layer using a second user-provided CSV lookup), and hydraulic Conductivity (C, implicitly assigned weight 1 but not computed — the script contains a placeholder comment "acabou C" with no actual C-layer generation or calculation; the final expression includes '+ 1' as a fixed offset, not a raster-based C term). All layers are resampled to 25 m resolution within a user-defined extent, reclassified to DRASTIC rating scales (1–10), and combined using standard DRASTIC weights (D×5, R×4, A×3, S×2, T×1, I×5) plus a constant +1. Outputs include intermediate rasters (d.tif, r.tif, a.tif, s.tif, t.tif, i.tif), a final DRASTIC index raster (drastic.tif), and optional intermediate files in a user-specified output folder.

Plan door-knocking visit routes. The script plans field-based door-knocking campaigns by spatially clustering address points within a user-defined polygon area, then computing shortest-path road-based visit sequences for each crew starting from a designated start location. It outputs (1) an ordered point layer of visit locations with crew ID, visit order, travel cost, and QField-ready configuration (default value + ValueMap editor for 'Outcome'), and (2) a CSV-compatible table layer containing the same visit metadata plus editable tracking fields ('Inquiry Date', 'Inquirer ID', 'Outcome', etc.) for offline data collection.

Calculate zonal area statistics. The script computes area-based zonal statistics (either pixel count or sum) for multiple raster datasets over administrative polygon boundaries. For each raster, it extracts the suffix after the last underscore in the filename (e.g., '2020' from 'lc_2020.tif') to generate consistent field names, runs QGIS’s native zonal statistics (count or sum), derives area in km² by multiplying the statistic by pixel area (either user-provided or computed from raster resolution), and appends the result as a new double-precision field (e.g., '_2020_km2') to the vector layer. The final output is a polygon vector layer enriched with one area field per input raster.

Calculate weighted hazard index. The script calculates a Weighted Index (WI) and a normalized Final Weighted Index (FWI) for hazard, exposure, or vulnerability by standardizing indicator values from an input CSV, applying user-provided weights (from a separate weights CSV), computing per-feature weighted averages, and joining the resulting WI and FWI back to an input vector layer (e.g., administrative units or exposure assets) via a specified join field. Outputs include a shapefile enriched with WI and FWI attributes and a companion CSV containing all computed indices.

Merge mask and reproject rasters. The script merges georeferenced TIFF rasters based on a user-defined regex pattern (e.g., grouping by date or numeric ID), clips each merged or individual raster to the geometry of an input vector mask layer, reprojects the clipped rasters to a user-specified target CRS (or preserves original CRS if none provided), and saves the final outputs in a mirrored subfolder structure within the designated output folder — all with LZW compression and consistent naming using a configurable prefix (e.g., 'mod_flood_2025-01-01_2025-01-10.tif').

Calculate monthly zonal area. The script calculates monthly zonal statistics (Count or Sum) for a polygon administrative layer over a folder of georeferenced raster files (e.g., monthly land cover or fire detection rasters), extracts date identifiers from raster filenames using user-defined string slicing (e.g., '2:7'), appends zonal statistic fields with date-based suffixes, and computes area in km² by multiplying the statistic value by pixel area (either user-provided or derived from raster resolution). The final output is a vector layer with one feature per administrative unit and one field per raster representing the computed area (km²) for that month.

Calculate zonal statistics for rasters. The script calculates zonal statistics (e.g., Sum, Mean, Min, Max, Count) for all GeoTIFF rasters in a user-specified folder, using an input polygon vector layer as zones. It extracts the text after the last underscore in each raster filename to construct unique field names with a configurable prefix, appends results as new attributes to the vector layer, and saves the final enriched vector layer as the output. The workflow uses QGIS's native 'zonalstatisticsfb' algorithm iteratively and saves the result via 'savefeatures'.

Offset multiple vector lines. The script offsets multiple input line vector layers simultaneously by leveraging QGIS Processing algorithms: it first explodes each line layer into individual segments, validates geometry, merges all layers while preserving source layer identity via a 'layer' attribute, applies offsetting using the external 'Offsetter:Offsetter' plugin (grouped by the 'layer' field), and finally dissolves the result by both 'layer' and 'offset' attributes to reconstruct continuous offset lines. The output is a single dissolved vector layer containing all offset geometries, named 'Offset' upon loading.

Download administrative boundaries. The script downloads official Danish administrative and territorial boundary datasets (e.g., Kommuneinddeling, Regionsinddeling, Postnummerinddeling) from the Danish Datafordeler API in GeoPackage (.gpkg) format. It authenticates using a user-provided API key, constructs a parameterized HTTPS GET request for a specific entity and temporal type (current/bitemporal/temporal), downloads the file, unzips it (as the response is delivered in a zip archive containing the .gpkg), and loads the first geopackage layer into QGIS as a vector feature layer output. No on-the-fly processing, classification, or analysis is performed — it is purely an ETL (Extract-Transform-Load) utility for acquiring authoritative Danish geospatial boundary data.

Download matrikel cadastral data. The script downloads official Danish cadastral data (Matriklen2) from the Datafordeler API, selecting a specific entity (e.g., 'Jordstykke', 'BygningPaaFremmedGrundFlade') and temporal variant ('current', 'bitemporal', or 'temporal'), then unzips the downloaded GeoPackage and loads the first layer as a vector feature layer into QGIS. The output is a feature sink containing the selected cadastral geometry (e.g., parcels, buildings, boundaries) in vector format (points, lines, or polygons), ready for mapping or spatial analysis.

Join cadastral parcels with agricultural water rights data. The script performs a spatial-attribute join between a cadastral parcel layer (cadastre) and a business application layer ('Role') containing agricultural water rights information (e.g., ASA — Association Syndicale Autonome). It validates field presence (e.g., 'asa_id_parcelle', 'asa_nom', 'asa_cp', 'asa_cod_tarif'), executes a field-value join on 'idu' (cadastre) ↔ 'CLEF_2' (Role), then refactors and renames output fields to standardized ASA schema (e.g., 'asa_id_parcelle', 'asa_nom', 'asa_adresse', 'asa_commune') while prefixing cadastre fields with 'cad_'. The final output is a merged vector layer with joined attributes and a success/error message string.

Calculate watershed morphometric parameters. The script performs a comprehensive hydrological basin analysis by clipping a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to the input basin polygon, computing slope statistics, identifying the pour point from the highest-order Strahler stream segments, and calculating 15+ standard morphometric parameters (e.g., basin area, perimeter, form factor, circularity ratio, elongation ratio, relief ratio, dissection index, drainage density, stream frequency, texture ratio, bifurcation ratio, length ratio, gradient ratio, hypsometric integral). It outputs a point vector layer with each parameter as a feature at the pour point location, including value, unit, and expert interpretation (e.g., 'youthful', 'mature', 'senile' stage), plus an optional interactive HTML hypsometric curve visualization.

Download OpenTopography DEM. The script downloads digital elevation models (DEMs) from the OpenTopography API for a user-defined geographic extent. It supports 13 DEM types including SRTM, ALOS, Copernicus, NASADEM, EU DTM, GEDI L3, and GEBCO bathymetry products. The workflow includes: (1) accepting an extent parameter (with automatic reprojection to EPSG:4326 if needed), (2) mapping user-selected DEM names to internal API codes, (3) constructing a GET request URL with bounding box coordinates and API key, (4) downloading the GTiff-formatted DEM via QGIS's native:filedownloader algorithm, (5) optionally saving the API key in QGIS settings, and (6) loading the downloaded raster into the QGIS project. Outputs include a georeferenced GeoTIFF raster file and optional in-project layer visualization.

Scale Landsat surface reflectance and thermal bands. The script applies radiometric scaling factors to Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Reflectance (SR_B1–SR_B7) and Surface Temperature (ST_B10) bands: for multispectral bands it computes (DN × 0.0000275) − 0.2 to yield unitless surface reflectance; for thermal band B10 it computes ((DN × 0.00341802) + 149) − 273.15 to yield land surface temperature in °C. It outputs a 7-band corrected multiband raster with descriptive band names (aerosol, blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2) and a single-band thermal raster labeled 'B10_Thermal_Celsius', both preserving NoData values and metadata.

Scale Sentinel-2 L2A reflectance. The script applies a scale factor of 0.0001 to Sentinel-2 Level-2A top-of-canopy (TOC) reflectance digital numbers (DNs) across 10 spectral bands (B01, B02, B03, B04, B05, B06, B07, B08, B11, B12), resamples all non-10m bands (B01, B05–B07, B11–B12) to 10 m resolution using nearest-neighbor resampling, and merges them into a single multiband GeoTIFF raster with descriptive band names (e.g., 'Blue', 'NIR', 'SWIR1'). Input is a local filesystem folder containing a Sentinel-2 MSIL2A product (e.g., 'S2A_MSIL2A_20230515T103621_N0509_R106_T30TXL_20230515T135526.SAFE'), specifically targeting the IMG_DATA/R10m, R20m, and R60m subdirectories. No cloud masking, temporal aggregation, or spatial subsetting is performed — the operation is per-scene, local-file-based radiometric scaling and harmonization to 10 m. Output is a scaled, resampled, multiband raster with band descriptions embedded in GDAL metadata.

Calculate color distance for crop discrimination. The script computes a per-pixel color distance raster that quantifies spectral dissimilarity between input orthomosaic pixels and reference color models (Mahalanobis or Gaussian Mixture Model), derived either from annotated reference images or polygon-based pixel sampling. It processes large orthomosaics tile-by-tile with configurable overlap, applies optional radiometric transforms (Lambda or Gamma), scales output optionally to uint8, and writes a georeferenced output raster with overviews. The result supports visual and quantitative assessment of spectral homogeneity—e.g., detecting off-type plants, stress-induced color shifts, or varietal boundaries in high-resolution agricultural imagery.

Download GSI vector tile infrastructure data. The script downloads vector tiles from the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (GSI) — specifically infrastructure-related layers (e.g., administrative boundaries, roads, buildings, land use/land cover, topography) — converts them from PBF format into valid QGIS vector layers, clips them to a user-defined extent in EPSG:4326, merges across downloaded tiles, and outputs either as temporary QGIS layers or saved GeoPackage (.gpkg) files. It performs coordinate transformation, tile index calculation using Web Mercator tiling scheme (XYZ), zoom-level validation against layer-specific min/max zoom constraints, download throttling via tile count limits, and field-type-aware refactoring of PBF attribute schemas.

Map soil erodibility classes. The script generates a single-band raster soil erodibility map aligned to a reference DEM grid, where each pixel contains an integer class (1–5) representing relative susceptibility to wind erosion. Classification integrates two inputs: (1) soil texture/type polygons classified either via a user-provided CSV lookup or an internal DIN 19706–based rule set mapping 32+ soil codes (e.g., 'Tt', 'Lu', 'fS') to classes 1–6; and (2) SOM polygons classified by percent content (0–1, 1–15, 15–30, ≥30) into classes 1–4. The final raster is computed using a deterministic combinatorial rule: SOM class 4 always yields erodibility class 5; other combinations follow a lookup table encoded in a deeply nested QGIS raster calculator expression that maps (soil_class × SOM_class) pairs to final classes 0–5 (with -9999 for NoData), resulting in a final 5-class ordinal scale (very low → very high). All processing respects the DEM’s CRS, extent, and resolution; geometry validity is enforced and vectors are clipped and reprojected as needed.

Calculate landscape element height. The script computes the height of landscape elements (e.g., trees, buildings, shrubs) as the pixel-wise difference between a Digital Surface Model (DSM) and a Digital Elevation Model (DEM), i.e., DSM − DEM. It optionally masks (sets to zero) all raster cells falling within user-provided polygon features (e.g., agricultural field blocks), ensuring those areas contribute no vertical structure in the output. The result is a Float32 raster where non-masked cells contain positive real heights (negative differences are clamped to zero), preserving NoData values from inputs. The output is automatically loaded into QGIS as the final LE_Raster.

Compute wind protection maximum raster. The script groups input GeoTIFF rasters (wind-protection masks) by the first numeric substring in their filenames (e.g., '45' in 'r45a_hs_az45_alt36.tif'), then computes, for each group, a per-cell maximum raster using QGIS native:cellstatistics (STATISTIC=7). Finally, it computes an overall maximum raster ('wind_protection.tif') from all group-maximum rasters. All outputs preserve input grid geometry (CRS, resolution, extent), and the workflow is designed to composite directional wind shadow masks — typically generated by Tool 2 — into integrated wind protection layers for erosion risk assessment.

Calculate high-risk area share. The script calculates, for each input polygon (e.g., field blocks), the fractional area where wind-erosion risk raster values are ≥ user-defined threshold (e.g., ≥5, corresponding to 'very high' risk class per DIN 19706). It does so by: (1) reprojecting the vector layer to match the raster’s CRS; (2) validating and repairing geometries; (3) generating a binary mask raster (1 where risk ≥ threshold, else 0); (4) computing zonal count and sum statistics over the mask; (5) deriving true metric areas (m²) using raster pixel dimensions; and (6) appending fields: risk_count (total raster cells intersecting polygon), risk_sum (number of high-risk cells), area_m2 (polygon area), area_high_m2 (high-risk area), pct_high (percentage), and thr_val (applied threshold). Output is a vector layer enriched with these six attributes.

Cut dike segments by river mileage points. The script automatically processes riverbank-aligned dike lines (with岸别 field 'zya' = 'L' or 'R') by matching river-cutting points (labeled with 'LC' mileage values, offset every 100 m starting at 50 m) to their nearest point on the respective bank’s dike line. It generates perpendicular-like cutting lines from each point to its nearest dike location, extends those lines by configurable distances (EXTEND_START/END) to ensure intersection, then splits the original dike lines using those extended lines. Outputs include: (1) left-bank cutting lines (cut_lines_left), (2) right-bank cutting lines (cut_lines_right), and (3) a merged dike_sections layer containing all resulting dike segments — each inheriting original dike attributes (e.g., dikeName, polderCode) and preserving the 'zya' bank identifier, with segment count and length statistics reported.

Assign river centerpoint elevation to dike sections. The script performs spatial attribute transfer from river segment center points (with left/right bank elevations and mileage) to adjacent dike sections using distance-based one-to-one matching, conditioned on bank side (L/R); it selects the appropriate elevation field (zagc for left bank, yagc for right bank), assigns LC (mileage), adds match metadata (distance, type), and optionally joins municipal/county administrative attributes via spatial intersection; output is a vector layer of dike sections enriched with ddgc (assigned堤顶高程), LC, match_dist, match_type, and CITY/COUNTY fields.

Enrich grid layer with town and polder ID. The script enhances a grid vector layer by performing spatial joins with乡镇 (town) and保护片 (polder/conservation zone) layers to add 'town' and 'polderId' attributes, computes grid area in square meters, assigns sequential 'grid_id', handles NULL/empty values using configurable defaults, excludes joined fields from output, and validates field completeness. It outputs a new memory vector layer 'grid_enriched' in the 'process' group with core fields (grid_id, area, town, polderId) plus preserved original grid fields, while moving input layers to the 'input' group.

Assign grid attributes to road segments. The script processes a raw road vector layer and an enriched grid vector layer (with fields grid_id, area, polderId, town, Bathymetry) to generate a new road output layer where each road segment is spatially clipped to grid boundaries and inherits all grid attributes. It ensures geometric validity (removing Z/M, fixing geometries), reprojects for accurate length calculation, computes Shape_Leng in meters, handles nulls with domain-appropriate defaults (e.g., 'UNKNOWN' for polderId, 0.0 for area), and validates field completeness. The output is a topologically consistent line layer in the 'process' group with per-segment grid attribution and length — enabling downstream infrastructure analysis per hydrological or administrative grid unit.

Filter reservoirs near rivers. The script filters point features representing reservoir engineering projects (skgc2) to retain only those located within a user-specified Euclidean distance (e.g., 100 m, though configured as 0.1 m in the script — likely a unit or typo inconsistency) of line features representing rivers (hlsc1); it achieves this by generating a dissolved buffer around the river layer, reprojecting layers as needed for metric distance computation, performing spatial intersection filtering, and outputting a new memory vector layer containing only the proximal reservoir points with original attributes and CRS.

Calculate infiltration parameters. The script calculates spatially distributed infiltration parameters for hydrologic modeling in FLO-2D, supporting four methods: Green-Ampt (with soil texture, hydraulic conductivity, soil depth, and moisture deficit), SCS Curve Number (from polygon, raster, or multi-layer land-soil combinations), Horton (initial/final infiltration rate and decay constant), and channel-specific hydraulic conductivity. It processes user-provided soil and land use layers (vector or raster), optionally integrates SSURGO soil database or OpenStreetMap-derived land cover, computes grid-cell–level infiltration properties via zonal statistics or raster overlay, applies effective impervious area corrections, and writes results to GeoPackage tables (e.g., infil_cells_green, infil_cells_scs) for use in flood simulation.

Validate raster source coverage. The script validates whether all required raster sources (fotoskice, i.e., orthophoto or survey image mosaics) referenced in a vector layer of administrative or survey unit boundaries (SE polygons) are present in a specified folder. It checks for missing rasters by matching 'vir meritev' (measurement source ID) field values against folder names containing numeric identifiers (e.g., 'FS 123'), reports missing, unreadable, or CRS-mismatched rasters, and optionally reassigns the coordinate reference system of raster files to match the vector layer’s CRS — permanently modifying the source GeoTIFF files if enabled.

Generate digital elevation models for cadastral units. The script processes cadastral unit (SE) polygon boundaries and associated raster-based topographic maps (fotoskice) to generate clipped Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) per SE unit. It drape Z-values onto polygon vertices using the DEM, computes raster statistics (min/max/mean/stddev) within each SE boundary, appends these metrics as attributes to the output vector layer, and saves clipped DEM rasters to a user-specified folder. Input requires SE polygons with fields for SE ID ('Koda_id'), measurement source identifier ('vir meritev'), and optional FID; raster inputs are organized in folders named by numeric 'FS' codes matching the 'vir meritev' values, with configurable suffix (e.g., '_dem') and '.tif' extension.

Extract SE textures from orthophoto mosaics. The script processes cadastral or administrative spatial units (SE — 'statistične enote', i.e., statistical units) defined by polygon boundaries and clips high-resolution orthophoto raster mosaics (fotoskice) to each SE geometry. It groups and merges overlapping or duplicate SE polygons sharing the same ID and measurement source (FS), then performs raster clipping using GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' to generate individual texture rasters (GeoTIFFs) per SE × FS combination. Outputs are clipped, georeferenced GeoTIFF files named as '{SE_id}_{FS_id}.tif', stored in a user-specified output folder.

Download and clip DHM Vlaanderen. The script downloads Digital Height Model (DHM) rasters for Flanders, Belgium — specifically selecting from three variants (I DHM, II DTM, II DSM) and four spatial resolutions (1m, 5m, 25m, 100m) — determines the relevant map sheet ('kaartblad') IDs intersecting the user-provided study area polygon, downloads corresponding GeoTIFFs from AGIV's Azure blob storage, extracts and loads them as raster layers, builds a virtual raster (VRT) mosaic, and clips the result to the exact geometry of the input study area, outputting a georeferenced, clipped DHM raster file.

Generate InSAR point target grid. The script generates a regular grid (vector polygon layer) aligned to the project CRS, filtered to retain only cells intersecting both ascending and descending InSAR Persistent Scatterer (PS) points. It handles CRS mismatches by clipping and reprojecting PS layers when needed, converts metric cell sizes to degrees for geographic CRS, builds spatial indices for performance, and outputs a cleaned, named QgsVectorLayer ('InSAR_Grid') with valid grid cells intersecting co-located PS points in both acquisition geometries.

Map tsunami inundation hazard zone. The script computes a tsunami inundation hazard zone by integrating a user-provided DEM with precomputed PTHA (Probabilistic Tsunami Hazard Assessment) point data from a CSV file containing tsunami stage estimates (in meters) at fixed return periods (10–10,000 years) and uncertainty levels (median, mean, confidence intervals, percentiles). It first clips the DEM to the user-defined Area of Interest (extent), identifies the nearest PTHA point to that extent, extracts the corresponding tsunami water level (WL) value for the selected return period and uncertainty type, applies a custom scaling formula (sqrt(sqrt(|elev|)) × WL) to derive a final PTHA water level (PTHA_WL), then generates a binary flood mask where raster elevation is both < PTHA_WL and > 0. This mask is converted to polygons, buffered minimally (0.00001°), dissolved, styled as orange-filled polygons, and output as a vector layer named 'PTHA_{year}yr_Hazard_Zone'.

Model traffic emission line sources. The script processes OpenStreetMap (OSM) road network data and GPS trajectory point/line data to generate spatially aggregated, hourly-resolved traffic emission line sources for ENVI-met simulation. It filters OSM roads by functional class, splits them into uniform-length segments, counts unique vehicle trajectories (grouped by temporal ID and hour) within a search radius per segment, merges geometrically adjacent and temporally similar segments, applies scaling and emission factors (NOx, PM10), converts counts to mass emissions (g/h) using vehicle speed assumptions (3.6 m/s), and outputs (1) a GeoPackage vector layer of merged line sources with hourly traffic volumes, and (2) a JSON-formatted ENVI-met database (.edb) containing hourly NO, NO₂, PM10, PM2.5, and placeholder emissions per line source with standardized metadata and styling.

Quantify street environment stress. The script computes the Street Environment Stress Index (SESI) for road segments by integrating visual stress (advertising density, building enclosure, built coverage, canopy deficit) and thermal stress (LST anomaly, canyon effects) using expert-defined or PCA-derived weights. It segments roads, buffers corridors, performs zonal statistics on canopy height and LST rasters, normalizes indicators, computes composite VSI and TSI indices, aggregates results by corridor, and outputs classified stress segments, corridor summaries, policy priority scores (e.g., tree planting, billboard reduction), and styled GeoPackage layers with Natural Breaks symbology.

Compute travel time isochrones. The script computes travel time isochrones from starting points along a road network, using road speed attributes to generate a cost raster representing minutes (or hours) of travel time. It clips the road layer to an extent, rasterizes road speeds, assigns off-road speed values, converts pixel speeds to pixel traversal times in minutes, and computes cumulative cost distance using GRASS r.cost. The output is a raster where each cell value represents the minimum travel time in minutes (or hours) from the nearest starting point, styled with discrete intervals and a reversed RdYlBu color ramp.

Compute reservoir hypsometric curve. The script computes the hypsometric (HSV) curve — i.e., elevation–surface area–volume relationship — for a reservoir (dammed water body) using a digital elevation model (DEM) and a vector polygon delimiting the reservoir's extent. It clips the DEM to the reservoir boundary, generates elevation-contoured polygons at user-defined vertical intervals (dZ), aggregates them by ascending elevation, calculates planimetric surface area per contour, cumulatively sums surface area (to obtain surface area at each elevation), and integrates volume incrementally (using trapezoidal approximation: average area × dZ). Outputs are (1) an HTML-formatted table with columns Z (elevation), Surface (cumulative m²), and Volume (cumulative m³), exportable to Excel; and (2) a non-spatial QGIS vector layer (attribute-only) containing the same three fields.

Convert dB to linear scale. The script converts a multiband raster stack where each band is in decibel (dB) units into a new multiband raster stack where each band is converted to linear power units using the formula: linear = 10^(dB/10). It processes each band individually via QGIS Raster Calculator, then merges the resulting single-band rasters into a final multiband output raster. The input is assumed to be a SAR-derived or radar backscatter stack (e.g., Sentinel-1 GRD), and the output is suitable for radiometric calibration, ratio-based indices (e.g., ratio between polarizations), or further geophysical modeling requiring linear-scale reflectivity.

Convert linear to dB. The script converts a multiband raster stack from linear scale to decibel (dB) scale using the formula 10 * log10(value) applied band-by-band. It imports a raster layer, iterates over each band, applies the QGIS Raster Calculator with the dB conversion expression, collects the resulting single-band rasters, and merges them into a final multiband dB stack output. The algorithm is implemented as a QGIS Processing tool named 'Linear to dB' under the 'Stack tools' group.

Linear reference event mapping. The script performs linear referencing by projecting point events (e.g., infrastructure assets, inspection points) onto a single-part alignment line (e.g., road, pipeline, or rail centerline), computing the perpendicular distance from each event to the line, the measured distance along the line to the nearest projection point, side-of-line classification (Left/Right/On Line), and consolidated start/end records for duplicate event IDs. It outputs a vector table (MultiPoint geometry) with attributes including fid, event_id, event_layer, comment, distance_away, distance_line, formatted distance string, side_of_line, projected x/y coordinates, and event_type (Unitary, Start, or End). Input validation enforces planar CRS in feet, single-feature alignment, and CRS-matched event layers.

Split line features by point locations. The script splits input line vector features (e.g., rivers, roads, boundaries) at the geometric locations of input point features (e.g., sampling points, intersections, or markers), producing a new set of contiguous sub-line segments. It achieves this by extracting line vertices, snapping input points to the nearest line geometry, joining snapped points to their closest vertex indices along the line, and then reconstructing ordered polyline geometries between consecutive split points — preserving original line attributes and optionally appending beginning/ending point attributes with prefixed field names. The output is a vector layer of segmented lines with enriched attribute tables.

Calculate network-based travel time statistics. The script computes network-based and linear (Euclidean) distance statistics between source points (e.g., origins like neighborhoods or facilities) and multiple target point layers (e.g., services such as schools, hospitals, shops) using a street network. It outputs: (1) a grid-like source layer enriched with max/Q3/mean network travel times (converted from cost in meters to minutes assuming 83.33 m/s ≈ 300 km/h — likely a placeholder speed; actual interpretation depends on network units and context), (2) convex hulls centered on source points formed by nearest targets per layer (only geometrically valid for ≥3 target layers), (3) a category-level summary table aggregating statistics per target layer (e.g., 'Hospitals', 'Schools'), and (4) a target-layer output enriched with origin-wise travel time statistics. The core method uses QNEAT3’s OD matrix (m:n) over a provided line network, followed by per-origin/per-destination aggregation, duplicate removal, geometry extraction, and unit conversion (cost → time).

Generate plot grid and centroids. The script processes an input vector layer (e.g., field boundaries or administrative polygons) to generate: (1) a memory-layer of square buffers (50×50 units) centered on each input feature using 'native:rectanglesovalsdiamonds'; (2) a regular point grid (5×5 unit spacing) aligned to the extent of those squares via 'native:creategrid'; (3) centroids of each grid cell; and (4) all vertices of the grid cells. All four derived layers — squares, grid polygons, centroids, and vertices — are added to the QGIS project as temporary in-memory layers for spatial sampling or field plot design.

Map tourism pressures and opportunities. The script performs MOPST (Mapping Opportunity & Pressures for Sustainable Tourism) analysis by integrating landcover sensitivity, seasonality scores, pressure areas, opportunity areas, and user-provided factor rasters. It computes weighted seasonal (summer/winter) pressure and opportunity scores for a baseline and multiple user-defined scenarios, rasterizing vector-based sensitivity attributes using pressure raster geometry as template, applying factor-specific weights and scenario multipliers, and aggregating results via pixel-wise summation. Outputs include four rasters per scenario (pressure-summer, opportunity-summer, pressure-winter, opportunity-winter) saved in scenario-named subdirectories, plus baseline rasters, all in GeoTIFF format, along with an execution log.

Link point features to nearest line vertices. The script creates line features connecting each point feature in a Point Layer to the closest vertex (or closest segment point) on a Line Layer, using spatial proximity within a user-defined buffer distance. It computes the shortest distance from each point to candidate line features clipped by that buffer, constructs a line geometry between the point and the closest location on the line, stores the distance and optional ID attributes (from both layers), and outputs a new memory vector layer named 'relations'. Optionally, it also selects and exports points that failed to find a matching line within the buffer as a separate layer named '_rel_failed'.

Summarize fire risk classes by district. Creates an Excel spreadsheet containing counts and percentages of pixels classified as low (0–20), moderate (20–30), and high (30–40) fire risk — excluding special values (0=no data, 253=firescar, 254=water) — for each pastoral district polygon; outputs include per-district counts, normalized percentages (relative to total risk-class pixels only), and a checksum validation column.

Plot pasture growth trends. The script generates stacked, median monthly pasture growth graphs for pastoral districts in the Northern Territory of Australia, using raster time-series data from three consecutive financial years (e.g., 2021–2022 FY to 2023–2024 FY). It computes zonal statistics (mean and median) per district over monthly growth rasters, aggregates cumulative growth month-by-month across financial years, and plots smoothed or unsmoothed line graphs comparing current and prior financial years against long-term district-specific medians. Outputs are PNG files — one per district — showing monthly growth (kg/ha) across a July–June financial year cycle, with region-specific y-axis scaling and labeled legends.

Compute cumulative pasture growth medians. The script computes stacked, median monthly pasture growth values for each pastoral district in the Northern Territory of Australia across three consecutive financial years (e.g., 2022–2023 FY, 2023–2024 FY, 2024–2025 FY), using pre-processed raster (.img) time series from a local directory. It performs pixel-wise summation (cumulative stacking) over sequential monthly rasters per financial year, then applies zonal statistics (mean and median) over polygon boundaries of pastoral districts to extract district-level cumulative growth metrics. Outputs are structured as an Excel spreadsheet with one tab per district, containing columns for financial year, calendar year, month, district name, cumulative mean growth, long-term median baseline (hardcoded per district), and cumulative median growth.

Calculate district-level burnt area percentage. The script calculates the percentage of each pastoral district that has been burnt by wildfires, using vector-based spatial overlap analysis between a pastoral districts polygon layer and a NAFI (National Assessment of Fire and Fuel) firescar polygon layer. It computes two summaries: one filtered to firescarring events occurring from July onward (financial year), and another including all months (calendar year). For each district, it reports district area (km²), burnt area (km²), and percentage burnt. Results are exported to an Excel spreadsheet with two sheets: 'Area Burnt Summary Financial Year' and 'Area Burnt Summary Calendar Year'.

Summarize percentile growth by district. The script counts pixels in seven percentile-based growth classes (Extremely low, Well below average, Below average, Average, Above average, Well above average, Extremely high) for each pastoral district using an input percentile growth raster and a pastoral district vector layer. It clips the raster to each district, computes pixel counts and percentages per class using GDAL and NumPy array operations, and exports the results—including counts, percentages, and a validation checksum—to an Excel spreadsheet.

Summarize TSDM pixel counts by pastoral district. The script computes pixel count and percentage summaries for two raster datasets—AussieGRASS Total Standing Dry Matter (TSDM) and TSDM Percentile—within each Australian pastoral district polygon. For TSDM, it classifies pixels into four biomass classes (Low, Low-Moderate, Moderate, High) using region-specific thresholds (northern vs. southern districts), excludes NoData (0), and calculates percentages relative to non-zero pixels. For TSDM Percentile, it classifies pixels into three percentile-based categories (Below Average: 0–30, Average: 30–70, Above Average: 70–100), excludes special values (253 = fire scar, 254 = water, 0 = NoData), and computes percentages relative to the sum of the three main classes. Outputs are two tabular sheets in an Excel (.xlsx or .ods) workbook: one for TSDM biomass classes and one for TSDM percentile classes, both with district-level counts, percentages, and validation check sums.

Grid-based feature subdivision. The script subdivides selected non-multipart vector features into a regular grid of square cells (2.4 units) using QGIS's creategrid algorithm, then intersects the grid with the original layer to split features spatially. It deletes the original selected features and appends the intersected grid cells as new features, assigning incremented FID values and marking them with 'y' in a 'Cut' attribute. Area calculation using WGS84 ellipsoidal mode filters out cells smaller than 1000 m² before insertion.

Calculate road longitudinal slope. The script calculates longitudinal slope (%) for forest paths and roads by segmenting a 2D line vector layer (road network) into user-defined lengths (default 250 map units), draping each segment onto a DEM to assign elevation (Z) values at vertices, extracting first and last Z values per segment, computing segment length, and deriving slope as |z_first − z_last| / length × 100. Outputs a new segmented line vector layer with two added fields: 'Length' (actual segment length, including residuals) and 'Slope_%' (longitudinal slope in percent). It explicitly warns against use on engineered national roads without high-precision DSM due to terrain smoothing artifacts.

Extract PRISM temperature statistics. The script computes mean temperature values from PRISM raster layers (identified by names starting with 'PRISM') for each zip code polygon in the 'Zip_Codes' vector layer using zonal statistics. It iteratively joins the resulting mean temperature fields—prefixed by the last two characters of each PRISM layer name (e.g., '01' for January)—to a growing result layer, producing a single vector layer ('Zip_Codes' extended with multiple PRISM-derived mean temperature columns) that is added to the QGIS project.

Evaluate IDW and TIN interpolation accuracy. The script evaluates the accuracy of multiple spatial interpolation methods (IDW with varying power and search radius parameters, TIN, nearest neighbor, natural neighbor, kriging, and Topo to Raster) against a high-resolution global bathymetry/elevation reference dataset (ETOPO 2022). For each interpolated raster, it computes: (1) absolute pixel-by-pixel difference from ETOPO; (2) Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI) for both ETOPO and interpolated rasters; and (3) TRI difference. It generates histograms and statistical summaries (min, max, mean, std dev) of both difference rasters, plus timing logs for performance benchmarking across QGIS, GDAL, SAGA, GRASS, and ArcGIS implementations.

Create frontage layer from building polygons. The script creates a frontage (linear) layer from building (polygon) layers by converting polygon boundaries to lines and exploding them into individual segments. It adds standardized attributes (F_ID, F_Group, F_Type, F_Length), populates F_ID sequentially or from feature ID, computes geometry length for F_Length, applies thematic QML styling, and supports attribute transfer from building layers via spatial intersection. Outputs include a new vector layer (shapefile or memory layer) with frontage features and attributes, styled according to thematic rules (including NULL-aware styling), and integrated into the QGIS legend and editing workflow.

Generate voronoi polygons from random points.
